Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa.
Now begins the Dīkṣāprakāśa (The Illumination of Initiation).
Victorious is the Primordial Goddess, the sole agent of creation, preservation, and dissolution; the daughter of the Lord of Mountains; the bestower of the goals of human existence;
possessing the luster of a fresh rain-cloud; and worshipped by Brahmā and Viṣṇu. 1.
For the benefit of practitioners, the wise Jīvanātha composes this *Dīkṣāprakāśa* in accordance with the *Tantrasāra*.
Now, regarding the non-obligatory nature of initiation (*dīkṣā*), it is stated in the *Yāmala*: "O practitioners, listen to the fault of mortals who are uninitiated:
their food should be known as equal to excrement, and likewise their water as equal to urine. (1)
Having accepted the Śrāddha performed by one who is uninitiated, as well as the Śrāddha of one who is himself uninitiated,
his ancestors quickly fall into a terrible hell.
They certainly fall, there is no doubt, even as many as fourteen Indras;
nevertheless, the gods do not at all accept the worship of one who is uninitiated.
Therefore, upon seeing one who is uninitiated, one should perform a bath with one's clothes on;
for at the time of receiving initiation, the heap of sins is dissolved.
Intent upon that goal, he goes forth outwardly, joined to the state of Nirvāṇa.
Among all stages of life (āśramas), they proclaim the necessity of initiation (dīkṣā).
O Goddess of the Gods, for a mortal who lacks a Lord, there is no savior.
Likewise, for one who is devoid of initiation, there is no protector in this world nor in the next,
neither through austerities, recitations, modesties, ritual services, nor spiritual practices.
Because it bestows divine knowledge and brings about the destruction of sin,
it is therefore called *dīkṣā* by the sages who know that [reality].
The entire world has initiation as its root; initiation is the root of supreme austerity. (p.
2) Relying upon initiation, a person may dwell in whichever stage of life they choose. || 8 ||
And one who dies without initiation shall go to the Raurava hell;
therefore, one should joyfully receive initiation from the scriptures with great effort.
And so it is said in the Tārākalpa:
"That lowest of men who, having seen the mantra in a ritual manual (kalpa), nevertheless takes it up, shall find no atonement even throughout thousands of future births. (1)
One should not receive the mantra from one's father, nor likewise from one's maternal grandfather, nor from a younger uterine brother, nor from one who belongs to the faction of an enemy.
If one should perform the initiation of the ancestors through negligence or likewise through ignorance,
one must then perform an expiation and undergo the initiation once again.
The initiation of a father, the initiation of an ascetic, and the initiation of a forest-dweller—
any initiation belonging to those who do not belong to a stage of life (āśrama) is a source of suffering.
In another tantra it is also said:

"One should not receive the mantra of one's father, nor likewise of one who has taken refuge in an enemy. If one ever receives it from such a person, he must undergo the consecration (saṃskāra) once again. (1)
"A mantra of one's father, even if lacking in potency (*nirvīrya*), does not cause fault in the Śaiva or Śākta [traditions].
This refers specifically to the Kaulika initiation of mantras.
And likewise, in the *Yoginītantra*:

Because the initiation of ancestors is prohibited with reference to the *śakti-dīkṣā*, there is no fault anywhere when a solar or lunar eclipse occurs at a great sacred site (*mahātīrtha*). And so it is said with reference to the Viṣṇu-mantra:
Well asked by you, O Brahmin; I shall relate it all to you.
It was formerly told by Brahmā to the high-souled Vasiṣṭha, and Vasiṣṭha himself imparted it to his own grandson, my father.
"My father, whose heart was serene, pure, and a treasure-house of compassion,
gave [it] at the great sacred site of Kurukṣetra during a solar eclipse," and so forth— these are the words of Vyāsa addressed to Śaunaka in the Vaiśampāyanīya-saṃhitā.
In the Yoginītantra:
"A mantra that lacks potency from one's father, as well as from one's maternal grandfather,
or one obtained in a dream or given by a woman, is purified only through consecration."
As for that which was said:
"A woman who is virtuous, of good conduct, devoted to her guru, with senses subdued,
possessing knowledge of the true meaning of all mantras, well-behaved, and intent upon worship."
Indeed, she who is free from widowhood is fit to be a guru;
initiation for women is declared auspicious, and that of a mother is remembered as being eightfold superior.
But this refers specifically to the mantra worshipped by the Guru.
As it is said in the Bhairavītantra:
"In the case of receiving instruction in one's own mantra, one should not perform the contemplation of the Guru, provided that [the mantra] has been worshipped as one's mother."
The meaning is that the fruit is eightfold when [the mantra] is not worshipped; or, according to some, it refers to the subject of accomplished mantras (*siddhamantra*). In the *Yoginītantra*:
And when the vase has been obtained in a dream, one should cause the life-force (prāṇa) of the Guru to enter it;
having written [the mantra] with saffron on a banyan leaf, its reception is auspicious.
From that, one attains success; otherwise, it would be fruitless.
This [method] applies in the absence of a true guru; when such a guru is available, one should receive [initiation] from him alone.
For there is a statement by Nārada: "In the case of a dream, however, there is no restriction."
Now, the characteristics of the Guru:
He is peaceful, self-controlled, of noble birth, humble, and possessed of pure attire;
he is of pure conduct, well-established, clean, skillful, and highly intelligent.
One who belongs to a spiritual stage of life (āśramin), is devoted to meditation, is proficient in the Tantras and Mantras,
and is capable of both restraint and grace, is designated as a Guru.
Now, the characteristics of those who are censurable and unfit to be gurus: one afflicted with vitiligo, one suffering from oozing leprosy, one with eye disease, a dwarf,
one with deformed nails, one with black teeth, one who is a slave to women, and one with an extra limb.
One who has missing limbs, is deceitful, diseased, eats excessively, or speaks too much—
one who is free from these defects is a teacher approved by his disciples.

Now, the characteristics of a disciple: one who is tranquil, well-disciplined, pure in soul, endowed with faith, capable of retention, competent, of noble birth, wise, of virtuous conduct, and observant of vows.
A disciple is one endowed with such qualities as these, and not otherwise;
the status of being a guru or a disciple arises for those two after a year of living together.
And so it is said in the *Sārasaṅgraha*:
"A true guru should examine the disciple who has taken refuge in him for one year;
as the sin committed by a kingdom falls upon the king, and the sin of a wife falls upon her husband."
Likewise, the preceptor certainly incurs the sin acquired by the disciple;
therefore, having received initiation from a true guru, one should accomplish all ritual acts.
In that case as well, one should adopt a favorable mantra.
And so it is said:
"One should resort to mantras that are favorable to the *sutāra*, the *rāśi*, and the *koṣṭha*."
And so it is stated in the Vārāhītantra:
"The Tārā-cakra, the Rāśi-cakra, and likewise the Nāma-cakra—
if a mantra possesses good qualities here, one need not examine any other cakra."
However, this should be understood as being primary.
And so it is, for we see such statements as:
"A wealthy man should not accept counsel, nor likewise one who is of low birth," and so forth. Therefore—
Regarding the necessity of investigating the *cakra*:
one should not examine the *siddha* and other [status levels] for the *Nṛsiṃha*, *Arka*, and *Varāha* mantras, nor for the *Tāra*, *Prāsāda*, and those mantras consisting of *sapiṇḍākṣara*.
*Tāra* is *praṇava* (OM). *Prāsāda* is *HOṂ*. A *kūṭamantra* consists of syllables joined with *piṇḍa*. (p.
5) [This applies] to a mantra obtained in a dream, one given by a woman, and a three-syllabled *mālāmantra*.
Furthermore, among all Vedic mantras, one should not purify the Siddha and other categories.
Regarding the *mālāmantra*, it is stated in the *Vārāhīya*: "Mantras consisting of more than twenty syllables are proclaimed as *mālāmantras*."
Likewise, [this applies] to the eight-syllable Haṃsa mantra as well as to the five-syllable one.
One should not purify the seed-syllables of one, two, three, or more [deities] from the perfected ones (siddha) and so forth.
As for the Haṃsa mantra:
"By the letter *ha* it goes out; by the letter *sa*, it enters again.
'Haṃsa, haṃsa'—this is the mantra that the living soul recites at all times."
Kālī, Tārā, Mahāvidyā, Ṣoḍaśī, Bhuvaneśvarī,
Bhairavī, Chinnamastā, and likewise the Vidyā Dhūmāvatī.
Bagalā, Siddhividyā, Mātaṅgī, and Kamalātmikā—
these eleven Mahāvidyās are proclaimed as the Siddhividyās.

"Here there is no dependence on perfected beings (*siddha*) and the like, no consideration of lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*), no purification of time and so forth, and no purification of friends and the like"—from such statements, it follows that there is no [such] deliberation for these [practices]. However, in reality, this is merely intended as praise; [it applies] everywhere.
The traditionalists maintain that reflection (*vicāra*) is necessary. Regarding this, he first states the wheel of *kula* and *akula* in the *Nibandha*:
"The letters of the fifty [Sanskrit alphabet] correspond in sequence to air, fire, earth, water, and space."
There are five short vowels and five long vowels, ending with the *vṛddhi* vowels, which arise from euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*).

It is taught that the five beginning with *ka*—ending in *śa*, *ṣa*, *kṣa*, *la*, *sa*, and *ha*—are as follows: *a, ā, e, ka, ca, ṭa, ta, pa, ya, ṣa* are the winds (*māruta*). *i, ī, ai, kha, cha, ṭha, tha, pha, ra, kṣa* are the fires (*āgneya*). *u, ū, o, ga, ja, ḍa, da, ba, la, la* are the earths (*pārthiva*). *ṛ, ṝ, au*... [and so forth].

The *gha*, *jha*, *ḍha*, *dha*, and *bha* sounds belong to Water (*vāruṇa*). The *ḷ*, *ḹ*, *aṅ*, *tra*, *ṇa*, *na*, *ma*, and *śa* sounds belong to Ether (*nābhasa*). (p. 6) If one should know that the syllable of the practitioner and the syllable of the mantra belong to the same element and have the same deity, then that indeed constitutes one's own family (*svakula*).
The water-element is the friend of the earth-element, and the air-element is the friend of the fire-element;
the air-element is the friend of the earth-elements, while the fire-element is the enemy of the water-elements.
Everything belonging to the ether element (nābhasa) is a friend; one should never practice that which is contradictory.
Water-element (vāruṇa) is a friend to earth-element (pārthiva), while fire-element (taijasa) is said to be its enemy.
Now, for example, [consider] Jīvanātha:
its first syllable is *ja*, and that is pārthiva (the earth element). The mantra, however, is *oṃ namaḥ śivāya*.
Its first syllable is *oṃ* (*o*), and this too is pārthiva. In this case—
Because these two have become one, this supreme mantra bestows auspicious results.

If the mantra is *āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ*, then its elemental principle (*tattva*) is air (*vāyu*). Since the letter *ja* has the element earth (*bhūta*) as its enemy, this mantra is not auspicious; for it is said that "air is the enemy of those belonging to earth."
Now, the zodiacal circle (*rāśicakra*).
In the *Āgamakalpadruma*:
"Two threads, extending from east to west, [are drawn] from the center of that [mandala], according to the division between the south and Kubera (the north)."
Then, one should write the syllables individually in the northeast, the northwest, the southeast, and the southwest.
The numbers four, three, three, two, two, two, two,
five, five, five, five, five, four, and four;
these are the debts [of the months] beginning with Aries.
One should count all three letters pertaining to the girl and then write the letters beginning with 'śa'.

A Ā I Ī are in Aries; U Ū Ṛ are in Taurus; Ṝ Ḷ Ḹ are in Gemini; E AI are in Cancer; O AU are in Leo; AṂ AḤ ŚA ṢA HA ḌHA KṢĀḤ are in Virgo; the *ka*-group (5) is in Libra; the *ca*-group is in Scorpio;
the *ṭa*-group (5) is in Sagittarius; the *ta*-group is in Capricorn; the *pa*-group is in Aquarius; the *ya*-group is in Pisces. Thus.
It should be known.
The wise should calculate from one's own sign up to the end of the mantra's sign;
the purity of the signs should be understood, and one should abandon the enemy [sign], the eighth [death], and the twelfth [expenditure].

p. 7) When there is ignorance regarding one's own zodiacal sign (*rāśi*), then the practitioner (*sādhaka*) should take the sign associated with the first syllable of his well-known name and perform the calculation.
He should count from the syllable of the practitioner up to the sign of the syllable of the object of attainment (*sādhya*).
One (1), five (5), and nine (9) are known as kinsmen;
two (2), six (6), and ten (10) are servants;
and three (3), eleven (11), and seven (7) are nourishers.
Twelve, eight, and four are the slayers.
Thus [the rule] regarding Viṣṇu.
However, in the case of Śakti and others, one should avoid the sixth, eighth, and twelfth [vowels]. And so it is stated in the Tantrarāja:
"Therefore, the first letter of the mantra is not [determined] by the name nor by the first syllable."
If one should count the sixth, eighth, or twelfth [letter] from the first letter of the mantra, and that should be an enemy [vowel], by that [enemy] the [mantra] becomes harmful to him.

An example of this: the first letter of Jīvanātha is in the sign of Scorpio (vṛścika-rāśi), therefore the practitioner's [natal] sign is Scorpio. The mantra-syllable is *oṃ*, which belongs to the sign of Leo (siṃha-rāśi). Here, since the mantra-sign is in the tenth house from the practitioner's sign, this [mantra] bestows auspicious results.
The same applies elsewhere as well. Now, this wheel of constellations (*nakṣatracakra*) is described in the *Mantramahodadhi* as follows:
"One should draw four lines, extending from north to south, in succession."
Ten lines with their tips pointing westward should be drawn by the most excellent practitioners.
The arms [of the first configuration] are two eyes (2), three qualities (3), four Vedas (4), one earth (1), two mountains (2), and one earth (1).
The arms [of the second] are two moons (1), two arms (2), two oceans (2), two eyes (2), one earth (1), two eyes (2), three mountains (3), and one quality (1).
Then, among the stars, [the arms are] one (1), one (1), one earth (1), two arms (2), one pair (1), two eyes (2), and three Rāmas (3) and one moon (1).
The wise should understand that the initial letters [of the alphabet] correspond respectively to the asterisms beginning with Aśvinī;
however, the letter *kṣa* and the nasal bindu and visarga are situated within the portion of Revatī.
When the first syllable of the mantra is *ā* or *āḥ*, then its asterism is Aśvinī;

if the syllable is *i* or *ī*, it is Bharaṇī; if it is *u* or *ū*, it is Kṛttikā—and so on for the subsequent syllables as well. Thus, by means of the first syllable, one determines both the asterism and the specific lunar mansion (tārā) within that asterism, as well as the group (gaṇa).

In the same way, for the practitioner as well, one should determine the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) by means of the first syllable; from that lunar mansion, one should gain knowledge of the host of stars (*tārāgaṇa*). Here is an example: the mantra is *oṃ namaḥ śivāya*. Its first syllable is *oṃ*. Furthermore, the lunar mansion corresponding to the vowel *o* is Punarvasu.
The host of deities is the accomplisher Tārā, and the sign is Leo; the practitioner is Jīvanātha.
According to its syllable, its [corresponding] constellation is Uttarāphālgunī; its group is Nara; its star is Pratyari;
and its zodiac sign is Scorpio.
Now, he explains the knowledge of the stars from the constellation:
Birth, prosperity, downfall, security, enemy,
benefactor, slayer, friend, and supreme friend are to be reckoned starting from the sign of one's own name.
"One should abandon the asterism that causes misfortune, death, or enmity, and take another excellent asterism.
In this case, for the practitioner, the *uttarā-phālgunī* asterism is [the starting point];
from that to the mantra asterism, the count is 23; when divided by 9, the remainder is 5.
Therefore, she is known as Pratyaritārā; therefore, Tārā is to be understood as wicked.
Now he speaks of the examination of the lunar mansions (gaṇa):
"The three [mansions] of the east and north, as well as Bharaṇī, Ārdrā, and Rohiṇī..."
The lords of sages call these the lunar mansions belonging to humans.
Jyeṣṭhā, Śatabhiṣā, Mūla, Dhaniṣṭhā, Āśleṣā, Kṛttikā,
Citrā, Maghā, and Viśākhā— these have the Rākṣasas as their presiding deities.
Aśvinī, Revatī, Puṣya, Svātī, Hasta, Punarvasu,
Anurādhā, Mṛgaśiras, and Śravaṇa are the asterisms presided over by deities.
The highest efficacy is within its own class, while it is middling toward different classes;
there is destruction for Rākṣasas and humans, and enmity between Dānavas and gods.

The intermediate nature [of the mantra] is established by the statement, "Herein lies the intermediate affection between the groups of men and gods. Regarding the *ākāḍama-cakra*, it is stated in the *Mantramahodadhi*:
"One should purify [the mantra] starting from the first letter of the practitioner's name."

From the first syllable of the mantra up to its final syllable, one should take the name well-known from the birth asterism (*janmarkṣa*) and purify it according to the sequence in the *siddha* and other wheels. There should be five vertical lines and likewise five horizontal lines.
Sixteen compartments are produced there; one should draw them exactly thus.

[The years] are measured by one (1), three (3), nine (9), two (2), four (4), twelve (12), ten (10), six (6), eight (8), thirteen (13), fourteen (14), five (5), seven (7), fifteen (15), and thirteen (13). Bhū (1), Rāma (3), Śivanandā (9), Kṣi (2), Vedā (4), Arkā (12), Diśa (10), Rasā (6), and Aṣṭabhiḥ (8);
Kalā (13), Manu (14), Śara (5), Adri (7), Tithi (15), and Viśvaiḥ (13) [are the respective measures].
Within the squares are the letters of the alphabet;
therein, starting from the beginning of the name and proceeding in order up to the final syllable of the mantra, they are to be known as Siddha, Sādhya, Susiddha, and Ari.
In that tetrad where the syllable of the name is located, from there follows the fourfold Siddhas;
moving clockwise, that is the second, and the one called Sādhya is the third.
The fourth is called Susiddha, while that known as Sapatna is remembered by the wise. When two letters occupy a single square, it is proclaimed as Siddhasiddha.
Regarding that, the second [type] is cited in the mantra-text as "siddhasādhya";
the third is "siddhasuprasiddha"; and in the fourth, there is "siddhāri."
If the name consists of four syllables, there are four boxes joined with letters; if it consists of two syllables, they are in the second [set].
In that case, the first [syllable] is where the letter of the name is situated within the four.
There, beginning from that square, one should count in sequence as before:
Sādhya, Siddha, Sādhya-sādhya, Tat-siddha, and its enemy (Tad-ripu).
If the description of the mantra is in the third tetrad,
then it should be understood by the wise in due order according to the method previously stated.
The Susiddha-siddha, its Sādhya, its Susiddha, and its enemy;
in the fourth tetrad, there is the Ari-siddha and the Ari-sādhaka.
Once that is well-accomplished, the noble enemy [of obstacles] is subdued; thereafter, one should contemplate the mantra in this way:
"Siddhasiddha" as stated, and "Siddhasādhaka" with double the [repetition].
An enemy of the *siddha* class destroys one's kinsmen through firm recitation (*japa*) that is well-accomplished;
a *sādhya-siddha* [enemy] does so through double the recitation; a *sādhya-sādhya* [enemy] is useless.

If it is well-accomplished (*susiddha*) through twice the number of recitations (*japa*), it destroys those who belong to one's own clan (*gotraja*). If it is to be accomplished (*sādhya*), it kills enemies; if it is well-accomplished (*susiddha*), it [destroys] those accomplished through half the recitations, and that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*) [destroys them] through double the recitations.
A planet that is well-accomplished (susiddha) brings success to the planets themselves, while one that is accomplished by enemies (siddhāri) destroys the family.
One that is accomplished by enemies (arisiddha) kills the son, whereas one that is to be accomplished by enemies (arisādhya) kills the daughter.
When that [mantra] is well-accomplished, it slays the wife; its enemy destroys the practitioner.
Also elsewhere:
"The *siddha* [mantra] is accomplished in time, but the *sādhya* is accomplished through recitation and fire-offerings."
When perfectly accomplished, the enemy cuts off one's very root from the moment of its grasping.

Then, having first constructed a square, one should place the numbers one, three, eleven, nine, two, four, twelve, ten, six, eight, sixteen, fourteen, five, seven, fifteen, and thirteen respectively in the sixteen compartments.

Having repeatedly written the letters beginning with *a* in sequence, one should contemplate the four squares as *siddha*, *sādhya*, and so forth; then, the counting of the *siddha* group and others must be performed within those four squares.
This is the meaning: starting from whichever square contains the first letter of the name, [the counting proceeds].
One should count the *siddha*, *sādhya*, *susiddha*, and *ari* [categories] by moving clockwise. Here,
starting from the first letter of one's own name up to the first letter of the mantra, the *siddha*, *sādhya*, *susiddha*, and *ari* are to be known through groups of four squares each.
Thus it is stated in the Viśvasāra:
"In the moon, fire, Rudra, nine, eyes, pair, sun, and directions; in the seasons, eight, sixteen, fourteen, and the elemental [fifteen];"
In a square grid measuring fifteen by fifteen,
the wise one should write the letters born of the script in their proper sequence.
Starting from the first letter of the name up to the first letter of the mantra, there is one letter for each of the four squares; thus, there is a set of four squares.
Furthermore, "in the inner compartments from the left, starting from the beginning of the name.
An example here is as follows: the practitioner is Jīvanātha; the mantra is *oṃ namaḥ śivāya*.
Here, in the fourth group of four, there is the first letter of the practitioner's name; that very [letter]...
The first [mantra] is called *siddha*; therefore, in the second tetrad, there is the first syllable of the mantra, and thus the mantra is called *sādhya*.
This refers to where the first syllable of the name resides within the tetrad.

If the first syllable of a mantra is *siddha*, then the second syllable of that mantra is *sādhya*, the third is *susiddha*, and the fourth is the *ari* (enemy) mantra. For example, for a practitioner whose seed-syllable is *ja*, the mantra *aiṃ* is *siddha*, the mantra *hrīṃ* is *sādhya*, the mantra *āṃ* is *susiddha*, and *gaṃ* is the *ari* mantra.

"Mantra" means "enemy-mantra. Now, if the letters of the practitioner (sādhaka) and the mantra are in the same square, then it is *siddha-siddha*. If the mantra-letter is in the second square from that, then it is *siddha-sādhya*.
If it is in the third from that, it is *siddha-susiddha*. If the mantra-letter is in the fourth from that, then it is *siddha-ari* (mantra-enemy).

Now, if the first letter of the mantra occurs in the second group of four squares starting from the group of four squares containing the first letter of the name, then one should proceed as before, beginning from that very square in which the first letter of the name resides within the first group of four squares. In the first [case]...
In the first [square], it is *sādhyasiddha*; in the second, *sādhyasādhya*; in the third square, *sādhyasusiddha*;

and in the fourth, *sādhyāri*. Now, if the mantra-syllable is likewise in the third tetrad according to the previous method, then in the first [square] it is *susiddhasiddha*; in the second, *susiddhasādhya*; and in the third, *susiddhasusiddha*.

In the fourth [position], it is *susiddhāri*. Thus, in the fourth tetrad, there are: *arisiddha*, *arisusiddha*, and *aryari*. When calculated in this manner, there are sixteen variations, as follows:
1. *siddhasiddha*, 2. *siddhasādhya*, 3. *siddhasusiddha*, 4. *siddhāri*.
Sādhyasiddha (5), Sādhyasādhya (6), Sādhyasusiddha (7), Sādhyāri (8),
Susiddhasiddha (9), Susiddhasādhya (10), Susiddhasusiddha (11), Susiddhāri (12),
Arisiddha (13), Arisādhya (14), Arisusiddha (15), and Aryari (16). An illustration of these is as follows:

For example: from the second group of four squares starting from the square corresponding to the name [of the practitioner], if the first syllable of the mantra is in the third square, then this mantra is "Sadhyasusiddha" (easily accomplished with effort). For the letter *ja*, the mantra *em* is "Siddhasādhya" (accomplished with effort); the mantra *hrīṃ* is "Sādhyāri" (enemy to be accomplished); and the mantra *am* is [Siddhāri].

The mantra *śam* is *susiddhāri*; the mantra *gam* is *aryari*. Other cases are to be understood in the same way. Now, he describes the purification of the *siddha* and other categories by another method:
Having written down the letters of the mantra by name, one should perform the calculation of the *siddha* and other groups for each individual letter until the completion of the mantra.
If there should be a repetition of the name, the wise man should write the name again.
When [the names] have been thus corrected, there will be many enemies of the person to be accomplished (sādhya).
If the *siddha* and *susiddha* [results] are few, there is inauspiciousness; from their reversal, there is auspiciousness.
Such is the opinion of some, and that too is approved by the wise.

The word "of the name" (*nāmnaḥ*) indicates a transposition [of the order]. It is auspicious when there is a plurality of *siddha*, *sādhya*, and *susiddha* [syllables], and a scarcity of *ari* [syllables]. Now, the purification of *siddha* and the others according to another method is stated in the *Mantramahodadhi*:
One should write the letters in the twelve-spoked wheel in order, starting from the east and ending with the northeast,
beginning with the letter 'a' and ending with 'ha', excluding the letters 'bu' and 'kṣa'.

In that regard, one should count from the first letter of the name up to the first letter of the mantra in sequence; their results—such as *siddha*, *sādhya*, and so forth—are as previously described.
Siddha is in nine, one, and five (9|1|5); Sādhya is in six, ten, and two (6|10|2);
Susiddha is in three, seven, and eleven (3|7|11); and Ripu is in four, eight, and twelve (4|8|12). This Akadaṃcakra, however, pertains to the domain of Gopāla.
As it is stated in the Vārāhīya:
"The purification of the stars is for the Vaiṣṇavas, and the purification of the square (koṣṭha) is for Śiva."
"In the Traipura and Gopāla [systems], the purification of the *rāśi* (zodiacal sign) is traditionally taught as *akraḍama*.
Now, he describes the purification of *siddha* and the others by another method:
one should repeatedly write the vowels and consonants in four squares."
From the letters of the name, one should know [the results] starting from "accomplished" (siddha) and "to be accomplished" (sādhya), up to the syllables of the mantra.
Now, the purification of the *siddha* and other categories by another method:
A wise person should divide the letters of the name and the mantra by four.
From the remainder of one or more, one should know the *siddha* and other categories, with results as previously described.
Now, the wheel for the clearing of debts and assets (*ṛṇadhanaśodhanacakra*).
As it is stated in the *Mantramahodadhi*:
"Next, the complete purification of debts and assets is described, which bestows spiritual accomplishment."
One should draw seven horizontal lines and twelve vertical lines.
When this has been done, sixty-six (66) compartments are produced. In the first row, those empty squares are stated in their proper order as follows:
The asterisms (27), eyes (2), suns (12), lunar days (15), six (6), Vedas (4), and fires (3);
the Aṣṭakās (8), Vasus (8), and Nandas (9) are situated in the squares in successive order.
In the second row, one should write the five long vowels excluding [the short] *u*;
in the third row, one should write the consonants beginning with *ka* and ending with *ṭa* in their proper order.
The letters from *ṭha* to *pha* are to be written in the fourth row, while those from *va* to *ha* are to be written in the fifth;
in the sixth row, the numbers are to be written in sequence—these are now being told to you.
Ten, one, seven, four, eight, three, seven, five, and four are the oceans;
and six and the number of Rāma (three) are proclaimed as the practitioner’s digits.
One should separate the syllables of the mantra according to their form as vowels and consonants;
for as many syllables as there are in a cell, one should multiply the numerical value by that same amount.

This procedure applies to all letters using the numeral situated above the *koṣṭha*. However, for long vowels, the numerals are to be understood as those located beneath the short vowels. Having combined all the numerals, one should then divide them by eight (8).

The remaining figures shall constitute the aggregate of the mantra; this is the procedure regarding the letters of the name. All of those [letters] are to be multiplied by the figures situated in the row below.
The debtor is known as the greater quantity and the creditor as the lesser;
when the mantra is the debtor, then it should be accepted, but not the creditor.

Now, their collective meaning is as follows: "In the cell, for as many [as there are]. Here, in the wheel of wealth and debt (*dhanarṇacakra*), one should multiply the numerical value of the mantra-syllable located in whichever cell it occupies by the number situated above it. For example, the numerical value in the first cell is one (1), and the values situated above the letter *a* are fourteen.

The same applies to the letter *e*. Furthermore, the numerical value of the boxes for the letters *ka*, *ṭha*, and *ba* situated below the box for *a* is one (*1*). When multiplied by the number above them, which is fourteen (*14*), the result is indeed fourteen. Likewise, in the second box are the letters *i* and *ī*.

The measure of that square cell is 2; multiplied by the twenty-seven (27) figures situated above it, it becomes fifty-four (54). Furthermore, the measure of the square cells for the letters *kha*, *ḍa*, and *bha* situated below the letter *i* is also 2.
p. 14) That multiplied by the number 27 above results in fifty-four (54).

Thus, the letter *u* is situated in the third cell. The numbers in those cells are three (3); these three multiplied by the number 2 above result in six (6). Thus, for those situated below the letter *u*...

The three numerical values for the letters *ga*, *ḍha*, and *ma* are also multiplied by the numbers situated above their respective boxes; thus, they likewise become six (6). The same applies to those that follow. Then, one should take the letters of the name to be accomplished (*sādhya*), and having separated its vowels and consonants individually, [one should multiply them] by the numbers situated above their own respective boxes.

The meaning is that after multiplying those [numbers] and adding them together, the remainder when divided by eight is the "sādhya-rāśi" (the target number). Likewise, after multiplying the practitioner's own digits, adding them together, and dividing by eight, the remainder is the "sādhaka-rāśi" (the practitioner's number). In this context, if the mantra-number is greater, it should be taken [as is].
The creditor is known to be the higher amount, while the debtor is the lower amount.
When the mantra is the debtor, then it should be accepted as the creditor; however, not otherwise.
Furthermore, elsewhere it is said:
When a mantra has an extra syllable (*adhikāṅka*), then the wise man should recite that mantra;
he may also recite it when the syllables are equal, but he should not recite it when it is deficient (*ṛṇādhika*).
For it is said: "One should know that a zero (*śūnya*) portends death; therefore, one should avoid a zero."

An example of this is the mantra *oṃ namaḥ śivāya*. Here, since it is stated that the *praṇava* consists of three syllables—*a*, *u*, and *m*—the value for the letter *a* is 14 according to the previous method; for *u*, 6; for *m*, 5; then for *na*, 72; for the letter *a* [in *namaḥ*], 14; and finally for the *m* in *maḥ*, 5.

Of the letter *a* there are 14; of the *visarga* there are 99; then of the letter *śa* there are 24 and of the letter *i* there are 54. Then of the letter *va* there are 28 and of the letter *ā* there are 14. Then of the letter *ya* there are 48 and of the letter *a* there are 14. The sum of these is 413; the remainder when divided by eight is 5. This is the numerical total of the mantra. Thus, O Jīvanātha, the practitioner [should proceed].
Thus: according to the form of vowels and consonants, the number of consonants is 40, 49, 36, and 18;
the number of vowels is 2, 10, 10, 10, and 33. The total sum is 208. The remainder when divided by eight is (1); this is the "sādhaka" (practitioner) heap.
(15) Here, the collection of practitioners is the debtor; the collection of mantras is to be known as the creditor.
Therefore, [the mantra] is indeed not to be grasped. In this case, when the remainder is zero, the figure is to be known as being equal to the divisor (8). Enough of this;
now he states the debtor by another method:
Starting from the first letter of the name up to the first letter of the mantra,
one should count them according to the sequence of the *mātṛkā* letters and multiply the total by three.
The remainder, divided by seven, is declared to be the aggregate of names (*nāmarāśi*).
Thus, beginning from the syllable of the mantra up to the first letter of the name [is calculated].
Having counted [the letters] and multiplied by three, the wise one should divide by seven;
the remainder is known as the "mantra-heap," and it is designated as either positive or negative (debt) as before.
The example: here, starting from the letter *ja* up to the end of *oṃ*, the count is 37;
multiplied by three, it is 111; reduced by seven, it is 6. Thus, the first letter of the mantra is *oṃ*.
Therefore, from the letter *o* up to the letter *ja* (the first letter of the *sādhya*), the count is 12; multiplied by three, it is 36.
Divided by seven, [the remainder is] 1. Here too, because the mass of the mantra is small, it possesses the quality of being multiplied (ghanitva).
(p. 16) Now he states another method:
"Alternatively, having separated the syllables of the mantra here according to their vowels and consonants, one should double them and join them with the syllables of the practitioner."
The collection of mantras is declared to consist of those eight [groups] thus arranged;
likewise, the assembly of vowels is joined by doubling it.
The wise have declared that the aggregate of names is refined by eight through the syllables of the mantra;
herein, the states of being in debt and being wealthy are proclaimed as before.
Debt or wealth is to be cleared according to whichever of the aforementioned methods is applicable.
An illustration of this follows: *oṃ namaḥ śivāya*. The syllables are: *a*, *u*, *m*, *n*, *ś*, *v*, *y*; *a*, *a* (visarga), *i*, *ā*, *a*; *j*, *ī*, *v*, *n*, *ā*, *th*;

*j*, *n*, *n*, *th*; *ī*, *a*, *ā*, *a* (visarga). In that case, the number of mantra-syllables is 14. Doubled, it is 28. Added to the nine vowel-mātrās of the practitioner, it becomes 37. When divided by eight, the remainder is 5. Thus.
The number of the practitioner Jīvanātha is 9; doubled, it becomes 18;
added to the number of syllables of the mantra (14), it becomes 32; divided by eight, the remainder is 0, which is equal to the divisor.
Furthermore, a mantra that was practiced in a previous birth but did not yield fruit will bear fruit at a later time once the [karmic] obstacles have been exhausted.
If the practitioner meets his destruction in another life due to the exhaustion of his lifespan,
the mantra grants the desired goal merely by being attained, because it remains as a debt.
If both signs have equal angles, then the result comes from service;
however, a mantra that has been acquired as "wealthy" bears fruit through excessive service.
The purification of mantras is further described by another method:
one should write the letters beginning with *a* and ending with *ha*, excluding the neuter vowels, one by one starting from the eastern corner of a hexagon.
One should purify [the elements] starting from the first letter of the name up to the final syllable of the mantra.
In the first [year], there is the attainment of prosperity; in the second, the loss of wealth;
in the third, the acquisition of wealth; and in the fourth, conflict with kinsmen.
In the fifth [case], however, there will be disease; in the sixth, the destruction of everything.
Having thus purified the mantra, the master of mantras should bestow it upon the disciple.
Now follows the method for abandoning an inimical mantra: If an inimical mantra has been taken up through the power of ignorance, its abandonment must be performed; that method is now described.
On an auspicious day, one should place the pitcher within the Sarvatobhadra mandala;
while reciting the mantra in reverse order, one should fill it with pure water.
There, having invoked the deity, one should worship [the deities] beginning with Āpa and Varuṇa;
then, having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in front of that, one should subsequently establish the fire.

One should offer oblations with clarified butter one hundred times using the root mantra in reverse order; one should present bali-offerings to the lords of the directions with milk-rice mixed with clarified butter.

Having worshipped the Lord of Gods once more, one should pray with this mantra: "O Lord, whatever has been attended upon and worshipped by me— whose intellect is fickle— without having considered what is favorable, [may that be accepted] as the very form of the mantra."
Therefore, dispel this entire agitation of my mind.
"May my evil be destroyed and may eternal welfare prevail;
thereafter, may auspiciousness follow for me, and may purifying devotion be mine.
Having thus prayed to the Lord of Gods, [he should worship Him] with camphor, agallochum, and sandalwood.
One should write the mantra in reverse order on a palm leaf and worship it there.
Having awakened the deity upon his own head, one should bathe him with the water contained in the pitcher;
then, having refilled it with that same water, one should place the mantra-leaf within its mouth.

Having worshipped the jar, one should indeed cast it into a river or a pond; by feeding the Brahmins, he shall be liberated from the affliction arising from the *manu*. If purification is achieved through various means of cleansing, the *manu* attains purity.
At the outset, one should offer *māyā*, *kāma*, and *śrī* for the sake of liberation from those defects;
or else, a defective mantra becomes effective when enclosed by the *praṇava*;
or else, it is perfected when recited through the sequence of the *varṇamālā* in both direct and reverse order.
Whichever supreme Mantra one has devotion for, that becomes one's most excellent;
even if it enters the treasury of an enemy, it becomes the bestower of desired fruits for that person.
Thus ends the section on the purification of the six chakras. Now follows the determination of the time for initiation:
The commencement of mantra practice should take place in the month of Caitra, as it bestows all human goals.
In Vaiśākha there shall be the acquisition of jewels, but in Jyeṣṭha death will occur.
In Āṣāḍha there will be the loss of kinsmen; in Śrāvaṇa, an increase in wealth;
in Bhādrapada, the destruction of progeny; and in Āśvina, an accumulation of jewels.
In Kārttika there shall be the attainment of mantra-perfection; likewise it shall be so in Mārgaśīrṣa.
In Pauṣa there shall be affliction from enemies, while in Māgha there is an increase in intelligence.

In the month of Phālguna, all desires may be fulfilled; one should avoid the intercalary month (mala-māsa). However, initiation (dīkṣā) in Caitra yields fruit regarding the worship of Gopāla, because it is stated by Gautama. Initiation in the month of Madhu (Caitra) leads to suffering, according to the scriptural statement; therefore, it should not be performed at any other time. There is also a prohibition against [initiation] in Āṣāḍha.
Regarding subjects other than Śrīvidyā: "In the month of Jyeṣṭha it bestows death, and in Āṣāḍha it brings wealth and prosperity," according to the *Yoginīhṛdaya*.
Now, the observance of the days of the week.
On Sunday there will be wealth; on Monday, peace is proclaimed;
on Tuesday it destroys longevity, so one should avoid initiation on that day.
One attains beauty under Mercury, while wisdom is gained under Jupiter;
one attains good fortune under Venus, but there is a loss of fame under Saturn.
The specific distinction in the *Gāruḍatantra* is as follows:
on Thursday, one should know that [the worship] is auspicious for the Vidyā; for Śakti, Sunday is praised;
for Śiva, Thursday is appropriate; and for Saura, Monday is praised.
On Wednesday, initiation is fruitless and destructive to knowledge.
Now, the rule regarding lunar days:
initiation performed on the first day (pratipad) is considered to cause the destruction of knowledge.
Practice should be undertaken in the second [stage], and in the third, one should be pure.
On the fourth lunar day there will be loss of wealth; on the fifth, an increase in wealth;
on the sixth, the loss of knowledge is proclaimed; and on the seventh lunar day, there will be happiness.
On the eighth day, there would be loss of intellect; on the ninth, the decay of the body;
on the tenth, sovereignty and good fortune; and on the eleventh, one becomes pure.
On the twelfth day there shall be all success; on the thirteenth, poverty;
on the fourteenth, birth as an animal; and at the end of the month, loss.
At the end of a lunar fortnight, one should maintain a sense of dharma and avoid Vedic recitation;
likewise when there is thunder at twilight, a loud peal of thunder, an earthquake, or the falling of meteors.
One should avoid these aforementioned days prescribed by the Śruti;
[the rite] should instead be performed on the twelfth or even on the thirteenth day.

Where there is an injunction for the thirteenth lunar day, that refers to Viṣṇu, because it is recorded in the *Rāmārcanacandrikā*; and the thirteenth day is also praised along with the tenth as the "bestower of all desires," according to the words of Sanatkumāra.
Now follows the determination of the lunar mansions (nakṣatras): In Aśvinī one attains happiness; in Bharaṇī death is certain;
in Kṛttikā one becomes miserable; and in Rohiṇī one becomes a lord of speech.
In Mṛgaśīrṣa there is the attainment of happiness; in Ārdrā, the loss of kinsmen;
in Punarvasu, there shall be the acquisition of wealth; and in Puṣya, the destruction of enemies.
In Āśleṣā there will be death; in Maghā, liberation from suffering;
and in Pūrvaphalgunī, one attains beauty—of this there is no doubt.
Knowledge is attained under Uttaraphalgunī, and one becomes wealthy under Hasta;
success in knowledge occurs under Citrā, while the destruction of enemies occurs under Svātī.
In Viśākhā there is happiness, and in Anurādhā an increase of kinsmen;
in Jyeṣṭhā there will be loss of sons, while in the Mūla asterism there is an increase of fame.
Pūrvāṣāḍhā and Uttarāṣāḍhā shall be givers of fame;
in Śravaṇā there will be suffering, and in Dhaniṣṭhā there will be poverty.
Under Śatabhiṣā there is intelligence; under Pūrvabhādrapadā one becomes happy;
under Uttarabhādrapadā there is happiness; and under Revatī there is the increase of fame.
Now, regarding the determination of yogas in the Viśvasāra:
Śubha, Siddhi, Āyuṣmān, and thereafter Dhruva-yoga;
then Prīti, Saubhāgya-yoga, and thereafter Vṛddhi-yoga.
Likewise, the conjunction that brings joy is conducive to happiness in all tantras.
Now follows the determination of the Karaṇas:
Bava, Bālava, Kaulavān, and Taitila.
O beautiful lady, in all tantras, the instruments are indeed auspicious.

Now, the determination of the auspicious moment (lagna): One should undertake the commencement of initiation when the ascendant is Taurus, Leo, Virgo, Sagittarius, or Pisces, and provided there is favorability of the moon and the stars.
A fixed ascendant is recommended for the Viṣṇu-mantras, and likewise for the Śiva-mantras;
a dual-natured ascendant is praised for the Śakti-mantras.
Now, the determination of the lunar fortnight:
Initiation is auspicious during the bright fortnight, and likewise until the fifth day of the dark fortnight.
However, it is forbidden during prohibited months; there is a specific distinction based on the particular days.
In the *Āgamakalpadruma*: the sixth day of the month of Bhādrapada; the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Āśvina;
the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika; and the third day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa.
The ninth day of the bright fortnight of Pauṣa, the fourth of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa,
the ninth of the bright fortnight of Phālguna, and the fourteenth of the bright fortnight of Caitra are known as Kāmacaturdaśī.
In Vaiśākha, there is indeed the Akṣaya [tithi], and in Jyeṣṭha, the Daśaharā lunar day;
in Āṣāḍha, the fifth of the bright fortnight, and in Śrāvaṇa, the fifth of the dark fortnight.
On these festival days of the gods, one obtains the fruit of ten million sacred fords (*tīrtha*).
According to another tradition:
"The thirteenth day of the bright fortnight in Caitra, and that which is dear to Hari in Vaiśākha..."
The fourteenth day of the dark fortnight in Jyeṣṭha, Nāgapañcamī in Āṣāḍha,
the eleventh day in Śrāvaṇa, and the eighth day conjoined with Rohiṇī in Bhādrapada;
and in Āśvina, the highly meritorious Mahāṣṭamī which bestows success.
The determination of the times is as follows: the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, likewise the dark [ninth] of Mārgaśīrṣa, and the sixth day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna.
In the Yoginītantra: "O Goddess of the Gods,
on this [day], at the equinoxes, during the eclipses of the moon and sun,
on the day of the sun's transit (saṅkrānti), and on the first days of the Yugas."
In all the Manvantaras, as well as on the day of the Great Worship (Mahāpūjā),
there is nothing equal to the time of a solar eclipse upon the surface of the earth.
In that regard, whatever is performed there shall all result in infinite fruit;
on the occasion of a solar eclipse, there is no need for the calculation of weekdays, lunar days, months, and so forth.
Likewise, regarding an eclipse of the moon, it is stated in the Matsyasūkta:
"A practitioner should not perform a Śākta initiation during a solar parvan;
nor indeed should he perform a Vaiṣṇava initiation if there is an eclipse of the moon."
And this [rule] pertains to subjects other than the Śrīgopāla and Śrīvidyā [mantras]:
"The new moon on a Monday, the fourteenth on a Tuesday,
and the seventh on a Sunday are equal to hundreds of solar eclipses."
When a preceptor bestows [initiation] upon a disciple out of compassion,
one should not consider the astrological ascendant or other such factors in any way whatsoever.
All the lunar days, all the planets, all the constellations, and all the zodiac signs—
on whichever day the Guru is pleased, they all bring about auspiciousness.
In the *Yoginītantra*:
"Regarding the reception [of initiation] at a great sacred site (tīrtha), there is no determination of time;
[this applies] at Gayā, in the field of Bhāskara, at Virajā, and on Mount Candra."
O Pārvatī, one should not receive initiation at Catvara, Mataṅga, nor likewise in empty hermitages; one should not receive initiation at these sacred sites.
Thus concludes the determination of the time for initiation (*dīkṣā*).
Now follows the method of the ten purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) of mantras as taught in the *Śāradātilaka*:
first, birth (*janana*), then life-giving (*jīvana*), followed by striking (*tāḍana*), and likewise awakening (*bodhana*).
Then there is consecration, as well as purification and nourishment once again.
Satiating, kindling, and concealment—these ten are the purificatory rites of mantra.
The extraction of mantras from the midst of the Mātṛkā is known as their "birth.
A wise person should recite the syllables of the mantra with the Praṇava (Oṃ) interspersed between them.
Those proficient in mantra and tantra call this "living" (jīvana):
having inscribed the syllables of the mantra, one should strike them with sandalwood water.
The practitioner of mantras should strike each [syllable] with the wind [vowel *i*]; that is declared to be "striking" (*tāḍana*).
Having written the mantra, the practitioner [should worship it] with *karavīra* flowers.
The practitioner of mantra should perform the awakening with the letter *ra*,
equal in number to the syllables of that mantra, according to the procedure taught in the *Svacchanda-tantra*.
One should consecrate the mantra with the sprouts of the *aśvattha* tree for the sake of purification;
having contemplated the mantra mentally, one should burn it away with the light-mantra (*jyotirmantra*).
The practitioner of mantra purifies the three impurities through this mantra. The three impurities are as follows:
1) the innate (ānavya), 2) the illusory (māyika), and 3) the karmic (kārmaṇa).
The impurity arising from Māyā is the illusory one; that arising from Puruṣa is the Kārmaṇa impurity.
The mind is said to be unbound; that triad of impurities is forbidden.
The mantra of light (jyotirmanu) is remembered as consisting of *tāra*, *vyoma*, *ātman*, and the pair [of *indu* and *daṇḍin*].
*Tāra* is the *praṇava*, *oṃ*; *daṇḍī* is the *anusvāra*. *Vyoma* is the letter *ha*; *agni* is the letter *ra*; *manu* is the letter *au*. Thus, *oṃ hauṃ* is the *jyotirmantra*.
With this mantra recited over *kuśa* water, one should perform the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) syllable by syllable of the *mantra*.
By means of that mantra, this nourishment is considered to be performed according to the prescribed rule.
Satisfaction with water accompanied by mantra is known as *tarpaṇa* for the [Vedic] mantras;
for Śakti, it is with honey; and in the Śaiva tradition, it is with milk and clarified butter.

O Goddess of gods, the libation (tarpaṇa) for Vaiṣṇava likewise should be performed with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta). The practical application is: "I satisfy [the mantra] of such-and-such. The conjunction of the Tāra (om), Māyā (hrīṃ), and Ramā (śrīṃ) is called the illumination (dīpana) of the mantra.

Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ; then, regarding "one syllable of the mantra": the practical application is, "I confess the such-and-such syllable of the such-and-such mantra. As for "concealment of the mantra being recited," it means not making it public.
The ten consecrations are proclaimed; they are kept secret in all the tantras.
Thus concludes the method for the consecration of mantras.
Now, the series of mantras is written.
First therein are the mantras of Gaṇeśa: *vakratuṇḍāya hūṃ* (six times). The recitation (*japa*) is six hundred thousand times.

The bestower of six hundred thousandfold increase of wealth, the possessor of jewels and treasures, the slayer of Rākṣasas and destroyer of *balagas*, to Vakratuṇḍa, *huṃ*! (31) Worship, offerings, and so forth are as before.
Now follow the mantras of Ucchiṣṭagaṇapati.

We know Mahālakṣmī; we meditate upon Mahāśrī; may that Śrī inspire us. [The mantra] of Chinnamastā:
We know Vairocanī; we meditate upon Chinnamastā; may that Goddess inspire us. For Kālikā: We know Kālikā; we meditate upon the Dweller in the Cremation Ground; may that Goddess inspire us.
May she inspire us. (p. 35) Now, the meditation on Gāyatrī:
One should contemplate her as resembling the rising sun, holding a book and a rosary in her hands.
One should meditate upon Brāhmī, who wears a black antelope skin and whose garment is marked with stars.
At midday,
one should meditate on the goddess who is dark-complexioned, four-armed, with hands shining with the conch and discus,
holding a mace and a lotus, and seated upon the solar throne.
In the evening,
[one should meditate on] her who is white, clad in white garments, seated upon the bull, three-eyed,
and holding the gesture of granting boons, a noose, a trident, and a human skull.
One should practice while meditating on the Goddess as residing in the center of the solar disc.
Now follows the mantra of Svarṇākarṣaṇabhairava for the purpose of accomplishing the drawing of the yantra.
Oṃ aiṃ klīṃ klūṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ hūṃ saḥ haṃ!
For the uprooting of poverty, for him who is bound by the impurity of birth, for Lokeśvara, for Svarṇākarṣaṇabhairava, for the destruction of my poverty and enmity! Oṃ śrīṃ!

Salutation to Mahābhairava. For this mantra of Svarṇākarṣaṇabhairava, the sage is Caturmukha, the metre is Paṅkti, and the deity is Svarṇākarṣaṇabhairava; it is for recitation for the purpose of removing poverty.
The application (viniyoga) is: 9, 8, 12, 7, 10, 10. With these syllables, the placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) is performed.
Now, the meditation (dhyāna):
[She who] dwells in a ruby pavilion situated within the forest of Pārijāta trees...
One should meditate upon Bhairava, the bestower of gold, seated upon a lion-throne.

We take refuge in Bhairava, who holds in his hands the vessel of the Ganges, a hand-drum, a trident, and the gesture of granting boons; who has three eyes, is joined by the Goddess, possesses the hue of molten gold, and is of golden form.

One hundred thousand recitations [of the mantra] and an oblation of milk-rice (pāyasa) [should be performed]. On a Śaiva pedestal, one should worship with the [deities] beginning with Aṅgada, the world-protectors (dikpālas), and their weapons.
One should daily recite the perfected mantra three hundred times until the mandala is completed.
Having cast poverty far away, one becomes like the Giver of Wealth (Kubera).
"When the mind is perfected through recitation and other means, the stream of tantras shall attain success;
gold increases in the house, and there shall be no defeat for the practitioner.
(p. 36) Now follows the Hanuman-mālā-mantra.
Oṃ aiṃ śrīṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ hūṃ hsphreṃ khphreṃ hsrauṃ hskhphreṃ hsauṃ. Oṃ, salutations to Hanumat, whose prowess is manifest,
who has traversed the entire circle of the quarters, who has whitened the three worlds with the canopy of his fame, and who possesses a vajra-body.

O you whose body-hairs possess a radiance equal to ten million blazing suns and fires; O incarnation of Rudra; O burner of the city of Laṅkā; O one who crossed the ocean; O destroyer of the ten-headed Rāvaṇa’s heads; O consoler of Sītā; O son of the Wind-god born from the womb of Añjanī; O bringer of joy to Śrī Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa!

He who formed the rampart of the monkey army, the cause of friendship with Sugrīva, the cause of the slaying of Vālin, the uprooter of Mount Droṇa, the destroyer of the Aśoka grove, the cutter down of Akṣa Kumāra,
the shatterer of the host of forest-protectors, and the devourer of the Brahmāstra and the power of Brahmā.
The warding off of Lakṣmaṇa’s wound caused by Śakti, the bringing of the Viśalyā herb, the swallowing of the solar orb risen at dawn, the destruction of Meghanāda’s sacrifice,
the cause of Indrajit’s slaying, and the rending of the multitude of rākṣasīs who guarded Sītā.
Devoted to the slaying of Kumbhakarṇa and others, intent on devotion to Śrī Rāma,
possessing great power capable of leaping across the ocean, the sky, and mountains,
resplendent as a mass of great splendor, and having rendered assistance to Arjuna in battle by fulfilling his own word.
O Youthful Brahmacārin, you who are skilled in producing profound sounds, the sun in the southern quarter,

the one who worships the pedestal of Mount Meru, the teacher of all mantra-āgamas, the destroyer of all seizing spirits (grahas), the eradicator of all fevers, the destroyer of all poisons, and the repeller of all armies!
O destroyer of all evil ones! O warder-off of fear from all tigers and the like! O exterminator of all enemies!
Subjugate, subjugate all living beings—whether male, female, or neuter—comprising the three worlds;
bring them under my control, bring them under my control, making them obedient to my command, you who bear various names!

Make all the kings, together with their retinues, my servants; destroy, destroy all weapons, missiles, and poisons! Hrāṃ hrīṃ hūṃ hāṃ, come, come! Hsauṃ hskhphreṃ hsauṃ khphreṃ hsphreṃ, slay, slay all enemies!

Agitate, agitate the enemy forces, the hostile armies! Accomplish, accomplish all my undertakings! Nail down, nail down the mouths of all wicked and evil persons! Dhe 3 hā 3 huṃ 3 phaṭ 3 svāhā. (588) This is the garland-mantra of Śrī Hanumān.
Now follows the procedure for receiving the mantra.

First, having performed the recitation of auspiciousness (*svastivācana*), the disciple should make the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*). Taking three blades of *kuśa* grass, sesame seeds, barley, and water—

Oṃ. Today, in the month of [name], in the fortnight of [name], on the lunar day of [name], I, [name] Śarmā, residing here, for the sake of the destruction of all sins committed through knowledge or ignorance in previous births, preceded by— p. 37)—all...
With the desire for the delight of people, stainless intellect, sons, grandsons, wealth, grain, various kinds of auspicious poetic talent,

the understanding of all scriptures, happiness, mental well-being, and the attainment of one’s desired mantras, [I shall perform] the five [limbs] beginning with Gaṇapati, which constitute the constituent parts of the reception of the mantra of such-and-such a deity, O Illustrious One.
"I shall perform the installation of the water-pot (kalaśa), preceded by the worship of the deities, the guardians of the ten directions, and the nine planets.
Having made this formal resolve (saṅkalpa), one should place the auspicious pot upon a heap of grain on the altar, provided with five sprouts, five gems, and medicinal herbs.
In that regard, the five sprouts are those of the mango, the holy fig, the banyan, the udumbara, and the plakṣa.
The five jewels are—
Gold (1), diamond (2), sapphire (3), ruby (4), and pearl (5); and the seven types of earth:
from a stable for horses, from a stable for elephants, from an anthill, from a confluence of rivers, and from a lake.
Having brought earth from the king's gate and from a cow-pen, one should deposit it [into the pit].
The seven grains— rice (1), barley (2), wheat (3), black gram (4), mung bean (5), millet (6),
and the seventh is said to be *śyāmāka* (7)— thus is the group of seven grains described.
In that regard, these are the mantras for the ritual installation (*sthāpana*). First, the mantras for touching the ground (*bhūmisparśa*):
*oṃ bhūrasi bhūmirasyaditirasi viśvadhāyā viśvasya bhuvanasya dhatrīṃ pṛthivīṃ yaccha pṛthivīṃ dṛṃha pṛthivīmāhiṃsīḥ*.
Thus is the touching of the ground. Now follows the touching of the cow-dung:
Oṃ, may there be no harm to our offspring, no harm to our descendants, no harm to our life, no harm to our cows, and no harm to our horses.
"Do not harm us; do not slay our heroic sons, O Rudra, who are devoted to you. We, possessing oblations, shall ever invoke you for our great benefit.
This is the mantra for cow-dung.
"Oṃ, you are grain; satisfy the gods! For the sake of prāṇa (out-breath) I take you, for the sake of udāna (up-breath) I take you, for the sake of vyāna (diffused breath) I take you."

Having approached with the mantra: "Having measured out a long course for life, may the golden-handed god Savitṛ receive you with his flawless hand; for sight, you are the protector of the great ones," one should place the water-pot upon the heap of grain.
Now, the touching of the pitcher:
*Oṃ, smell the pitcher; may the drops enter you.
Return again with vigor; being auspicious, may you yield a thousandfold, broad-streamed, and abundant milk.*
"May wealth enter me again. Thus is the touching of the jar.
Then one should pour water into the jar:
"Oṃ, you are the support of Varuṇa; you are the two pillars set up by Varuṇa; [you belong] to Varuṇa..."
"You are the seat of *ṛta*, you are the seat of Varuṇa’s *ṛta*; sit upon the seat of Varuṇa’s *ṛta*. With these words, one should offer water.
Then follows the binding of cloth around the neck of the jar.
"You are the purifier of wealth, with a hundred streams; you are the purifier of wealth, with a thousand streams.
May the god Savitṛ purify you with the purifier of wealth, with its hundred streams. With this mantra, "O well-purified one, you have milked the wish-fulfilling cow," he should give the cloth.
Then one should offer a betel nut (*pūgīphala*).

"Oṃ! Those plants which bear fruit and those which are fruitless, those which are flowerless and those which are flowering—may they, impelled by Bṛhaspati, release us from sin. Thus ends the betel nut.
Now, the [mantra] for touch and so forth:
"Oṃ! Hiraṇyagarbha arose in the beginning; once born, he was the sole lord of all that exists.
He supported the earth and this sky—what god shall we worship with our oblation? Thus.
One should give gold and so forth.
Now, the five jewels: gold (1), diamond (2), sapphire (3), ruby (4), and pearl (5).
The wise one should place these five jewels into the vase.
(p. 39) With the mantra: *oṃ parivājapatiḥ kaviragnirhavyānyakramīt | dadhadratnāni dāśuṣe*, he should offer the five jewels.
Now, the offering of mango sprouts: *Oṃ aśvatthe vo niṣadanaṃ parṇe vo vasatiṣkṛtā | gobhāja itkilāsatha yatsanavatha pūruṣam | Oṃ ambe ambike ambālike namānayati.*
With the two mantras beginning with "kaścana" and "saśatyaśvakaḥ subhadrikāṃ kāṃpīlavāsinīm," one should offer a mango sprout. Next is the offering of all medicinal herbs (sarvauṣadhī).
Oṃ, those herbs which were born first, three ages before the gods, according to the mind of Manu, the great one—those whose abodes are a hundred and seven. Thus is the gift of all herbs.
Now follows the gift of the seven types of earth.
"O Earth, be pleasant to us, free from thorns, a place of rest; grant us wide-reaching protection. Thus are the seven types of earth.
Now follows the taking of *dūrvā* grass: "Growing up from joint to joint, from node to node."
"O Dūrvā, spread yourself with a thousand and a hundred shoots. Thus [is the mantra for] Dūrvā.
Then one should offer fragrance:
"Her whose door is fragrance, who is invincible, ever-nourishing, and productive."
"I invoke here Śrī, the sovereign of all beings. With these words, one should offer the fragrance (*gandha*).
Next is the placement of the vessel full of rice (*taṇḍula-pūrṇapātra*):
"O ladle, fly away full; fly back again well-filled. Bring us wealth as you trade."
"Carry hither food and strength, O Śatakratu!"—with these words, he should place the full vessel upon the pitcher.
Then he should set down the lamp:
"Om, Agni is light, light is Agni, Svāhā! Sūrya is light, light is Sūrya, Svāhā!"
"Agni is splendor, light is splendor, svāhā! Sūrya is splendor, light is splendor, svāhā!
Light is Sūrya, Sūrya is light, svāhā!"—with these words, one should place the *doṣa*. (p. 40) Now follows the consecration of the water-jar (*kalaśapratiṣṭhā*).
"Oṃ, may the inspiration of the mind enjoy the clarified butter; may Bṛhaspati extend this sacrifice;
may he establish the sacrifice as unimpaired. May all the gods rejoice here—Oṃ, be established!
Having thus performed the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of the vital breaths) of the water-pot (*kalaśa*), [one should perform the worship] in that pot with their respective mantras.

One should worship Gaṇeśa and Varuṇa. Then, having invoked Brahmā with the mantra "O Brahmā, come here; stay here," one should worship him with the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*). Then one should worship the Guru. After that, one should perform the installation of the conch (*śaṅkhasthāpana*).
That is as follows: having drawn a triangle on one's left side, [one recites] *oṃ hrīṃ*.

Having worshipped with "Obeisance to the Support-Power" (*ādhāra-śakti*), having placed the support-vessel (*ādhāra*) there, and having worshipped it with "Obeisance to Me," one sprinkles the triangle with pure water and worships the arghya vessel with sandalwood paste, flowers, and unbroken rice grains, saying: "Obeisance to the fire-mandala whose self is the subtle portion of the moon."
Having established it with the words, "I place the arghya vessel for the glorious [name] deity," and having worshipped it with "Oṃ,

obeisance to the arghya vessel, which is the orb of the sun, the self of twelve kalās," while reciting the root mantra and the *mātṛkā* in reverse order, [one recites]: *kṣaṃ haṃ saṃ ṣaṃ śaṃ vaṃ laṃ raṃ yaṃ*.
maṃ bhaṃ baṃ phaṃ paṃ naṃ dhaṃ daṃ thaṃ taṃ ṇaṃ ḍhaṃ ḍaṃ ṭhaṃ ṭaṃ ñaṃ jhaṃ jaṃ chaṃ caṃ ṅaṃ ghaṃ gaṃ khaṃ kaṃ aḥ aṃ auṃ oṃ aiṃ eṃ ḹṃ ḷṃ ṝṃ ṛṃ ūṃ uṃ īṃ iṃ āṃ aṃ

Having filled the arghya vessel with pure water, one should worship it with "Oṃ, salutation to the lunar disc consisting of sixteen kalās," and then, having invoked the sacred bathing places (tīrthas) with the mantra "Oṃ Gaṅge ca... and the syllable "Krom" while forming the goad mudrā, one should protect it with "Phaṭ."

Having veiled [the vessel] with "Hūṃ," displayed the conch-mudrā with "Śam," and the cow-mudrā with "Vam," and having covered it with the fish-mudrā, one should recite the root mantra eight times and sprinkle oneself and the articles of worship with that water. Then, having performed the *kuśakaṇḍikā* rite and performed the fire-oblation (*homa*), [one should proceed].
The disciple, having taken three blades of *kuśa* grass, barley grains, and water, should make this resolve:

"Oṃ! Today, [date], I, of such-and-such lineage, named so-and-so, for the sake of the destruction of all sins accumulated in previous births, and for the sake of a pure intellect that brings joy to all people, as well as sons, grandsons, and wealth..."

Having made the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) thus: "Desiring to attain the happiness and mental well-being that arise from the understanding of all scriptures and various kinds of auspicious poetry, I shall perform the reception of the mantra of such-and-such a deity," one should then perform the selection of the venerable Guru (*śrīguruvaraṇa*).

p. 41) "Today," and so forth: "I choose you, of such-and-such lineage and named such-and-such Śarman, a Brāhmaṇa, as my preceptor (guru) with these flowers, sandalwood paste, unbroken grains of rice, sacred thread, betel leaf, pair of garments, and ornaments."
"I am chosen" is the reply.
"Perform the rite as prescribed. "I shall do so."
Then, having placed a conch shell, dūrvā grass, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and sandalwood paste upon the head of the disciple,
and having performed the *mātṛkā-nyāsa*, one should sprinkle [the disciple] while mentally reciting the root mantra (*mūlamantra*).
Thereafter, the disciple, having performed the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and the *mātṛkā-nyāsa*...
Then the Guru should perform the ritual placement of the kalās (kalānyāsa) upon the body of the disciple as follows:
from the soles of the feet to the knees, *oṃ nivṛttyai namaḥ*; from the knees to the navel, *oṃ pratiṣṭhāyai namaḥ*; from the navel to the throat, *oṃ vidyāyai namaḥ*.

From the throat to the forehead: *oṃ śāntyai namaḥ*. From the forehead to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*): *oṃ śāntyatītāyai namaḥ*. Again, from the aperture of Brahmā to the forehead: *oṃ śāntyatītāyai namaḥ*. From the forehead to the throat: *oṃ śāntyai namaḥ*.
From the throat to the navel: *Oṃ vidyāyai namaḥ*. From the navel to the knees: *Oṃ pratiṣṭhāyai namaḥ*. From the knees to the feet: *Oṃ nivṛttyai namaḥ*.
Then the disciple, having recited the root mantra over his head, again places his hand upon the disciple’s head.
Having given [the mantra] and recited the mantra one hundred and eight times, he should give the mantra preceded by water [with the words]:
"May it yield equal fruit for both of us. Then the disciple should say, "Please grant it.
At that time, the Guru should give the mantra three times into the right ear of a male or the left ear of a female. Thereafter—

The disciple should recite the mantra either one hundred times or eight times. Contemplating the oneness of the guru, the mantra, and the deity, he should prostrate himself like a staff at the feet of the guru. Then the guru shall say:
"Arise, my child! You are liberated; become one who perfectly observes the conduct."
May fame, fortune, incomparable beauty, strength, and health be yours forever.
Thus the Guru should cause the disciple to rise. Then the disciple, taking water together with kuśa grass and sesame seeds, [should say]:
"Oṃ, for the sake of the consecration of this reception of the mantra named so-and-so performed today, this gold [is offered] to [the one] of such-and-such lineage, named so-and-so..."
"p. 42) 'I offer this sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to you, the Guru. One should dedicate one's body, wealth, and life-breaths—all of it—to him.
Then, one should give sacrificial fees to the Brahmins according to one's ability."
The procedure for receiving the mantra.
Then, on the night of the fourth day, one should perform the *caturthī-karma*. It is as follows:
there, the disciple, having performed the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), [should meditate] upon an eight-petaled lotus.
Having established the *kalaśa* and performed the worship of the five deities and Viṣṇu,

one should take three blades of *kuśa* grass, sesame seeds, and water, and make the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*): "Oṃ, on this day, etc., I, [Name], of such-and-such lineage, [Name] Śarman, [for the sake of] such-and-such deity and such-and-such mantra..."

Having performed the selection (*varaṇa*) with the words: "I choose you, O Brāhmaṇa of such-and-such lineage and such-and-such name, as the *Hotṛ* priest— with these materials consisting of flowers, sandalwood paste, betel, unbroken rice, sacrificial thread, and garments— for the performance of the rites of the *grahaṇa*, the *aṅga-homa*, and the inspection of what has been done and what has not been done," one should then perform the *homa*.
One should perform it as follows:
first, having prepared there either a fire-pit or a sacrificial mound measuring one cubit;
Having invoked one's chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā) into the jar placed in the northeast direction of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), one should worship it.

Then, having gazed upon the pit or the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) with the root mantra, struck it with "phaṭ," sprinkled it again with "phaṭ," and performed a ritual sprinkling with the syllable "huṃ. Thereafter, having uttered the root mantra—

Having worshipped with scents and flowers, saying "Salutation to the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa)" and "Salutation to the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila)," one should draw three lines on the altar for the fire-sacrifice (homavedī)—two pointing eastward and one pointing northward.
On the eastward-pointing lines, [one should offer salutations]: "Oṃ, salutation to Mukunda; Oṃ, salutation to Īśāna. Oṃ...

Salutation to Purandara. On the lines with their tips pointing north: *oṃ* salutation to Brahmā; *oṃ* salutation to Vaivasvata; *oṃ* salutation to Indu. Thus one should worship them in a clockwise direction with sandalwood paste and flowers. However, in the case of Tripurasundarī, [the mantra is]: *aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ*.
"OṂ AIṂ KLĪṂ SAUṂ, obeisance to Mukunda! OṂ AIṂ HRĪṂ ŚRĪṂ AIṂ KLĪṂ SAUṂ, obeisance to Īśāna!"—in this sequence, one should worship [the deities] upon the six lines.
Then, in the center of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or the fire-altar (sthaṇḍila), one should draw a triangle, and outside of that, a circle and an eight-petaled lotus.

Then, having drawn an earthen temple provided with four gates, one should offer a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) upon it with the root mantra. In the case of the *Sundarī* [mantra], one should offer the handful of flowers with "Aiṃ Klīṃ Sauṃ. Then, having sprinkled the sacrificial materials (*homadravya*) with the *praṇava* (Oṃ), [one should proceed].
One should worship the Vahniyoga-pīṭha. As follows: in the center of the yantra, "Oṃ, obeisance to Ādhāraśakti.
Likewise [one should worship] Prakṛti, Kūrma, Ananta, Pṛthivī, the Ocean of Milk, Śvetadvīpa, the Maṇimaṇḍapa, the Kalpavṛkṣa, and the Maṇivedikā.

To the Ratnasiṃhāsana (Jewel Lion Throne). Then, in the four corners starting from the southeast, one should worship Dharma, Jñāna, Vairāgya, and Aiśvarya. In the four directions starting from the east, one should worship Adharma, Ajñāna, Avairāgya, and Anaiśvarya, using the *praṇava* (oṃ) at the beginning and *namaḥ* at the end. In the center, [one worships] Aḥ.
To the infinite five-petaled lotus, *a*. Homage to the solar disc (*sūryamaṇḍala*) consisting of twelve digits (*kalā*).

*Oṃ*, homage to the lunar disc (*somamaṇḍala*) consisting of sixteen digits. *Maṃ*, homage to the fire disc (*vahnimaṇḍala*) consisting of ten digits. Then, upon the filaments starting from the east and in the center: *Oṃ* to Pītā; *Oṃ*.

One should worship with: *oṃ* to Śvetā; *oṃ* to Aruṇā; *oṃ* to Kṛṣṇā; *oṃ* to Dhūmrā; *oṃ* to Tīvrā; *oṃ* to Sphuliṅginī; *oṃ* to Rucirā; and *oṃ* to Jvālinī, [saying] "obeisance. In the center, one should worship with "to the Jewel-Throne. Then, one should meditate upon Vāgīśvarī.

Having meditated upon Vāgīśvarī, who has bathed after her menses and possesses eyes like blue lotuses, united with Vāgīśvara, one should worship her with the five offerings using the mantra: "Obeisance to Vāgīśvara and Vāgīśvarī. In the case of the Sundarī-pakṣa, however, one should meditate upon Kāmeśvarī.

One should worship. Then, having brought fire produced from a sun-crystal (sūryakānta) or from the house of a *śrotriya* (learned Vedic scholar), one should gaze upon the fire with the root mantra ending in *vaṣaṭ*. One should invoke it with the syllable *phaṭ*.
Then, having worshipped with "Oṃ, obeisance to the sacrificial pedestal (*yāgapīṭha*) of Fire," one [should worship] in the four directions with "Oṃ..."

One should worship with: "Oṃ, salutation to Vāmā; Oṃ, salutation to Jyeṣṭhā; Oṃ, salutation to Raudrī; Oṃ, salutation to Ambikā. Then, having uttered the name of the impurity (*mala*), one should worship with "Salutation to the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) of such-and-such deity" or "Salutation to the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*"), and [worship] Vāgīśvarī.

One should meditate on her as having the form of that respective deity, or, in the case of the *Sundarī* tradition, as Kāmeśvarī. Then, having uttered "Raṃ," and having drawn forth a small portion of fire from that [fire], one should offer it with the mantra: *Mūlaṃ hūṃ phaṭ kravyādibhyaḥ svāhā*. Thus, the raw-flesh eaters (*kravyāda*) are pacified. One should cast [the remainder] into the southwest corner (*nairṛtyakoṇa*). Then...

Having performed the inspection with the root mantra, one should perform the striking with "phaṭ," the sprinkling with "phaṭ," the consecration with the syllable "hūṃ," and the protection with the "phaṭ" syllable and the weapon-mudrā (astramudrā). Having veiled it with "hūṃ" and rendered it immortal by means of the cow-mudrā (dhenumudrā), [one prepares] the vessel for the fire.

Lifting [the vessel] with both arms, circling it three times above the pit, and touching the ground with his knees, he should pour [the contents] into the pit facing himself— the womb of the Goddess— with the thought that it is the seed of Śiva.
Then, having worshipped with "Hrīṃ, obeisance to the form of Fire," [he should worship again with] "Raṃ, obeisance to the consciousness of Fire."

Having united consciousness with the fire, one should kindle the fire with this mantra: *Oṃ cit piṅgala hana 2 daha 2 paca 2 parvajñājñāpaya svāhā*. Then, one should worship the blazing fire with the verse: "I bow to Agni, the Jātavedas, the consumer of oblations; he who is of golden hue and stainless."

One should worship the fire with the mantra: "Samiddhaṃ viśvatomukham" (The kindled one, facing all directions). Having performed the naming ceremony with the formula, "O Agni, you are the name of such-and-such deity," and having offered worship, one should recite: "Oṃ vaiśvānarajātaveda ihāvaha lohitākṣa sarvakarmāṇi sādhaya svāhā."

One should offer a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*). Then, these perfumes and flowers [are offered] with: *Oṃ, salutation to the seven tongues of Agni beginning with Hiraṇyā*. Likewise: *To Sahasrārcis, the heart, salutation*.
Thus: *Salutation to the six limbs of Agni*. *Oṃ, to Agni Jātavedas*.

Thus, one should worship with: "Salutation to the eight forms of Agni," likewise, "Salutation to the eight Śaktis beginning with Brahmī," likewise, "Salutation to the eight treasures beginning with Padma," likewise, "Salutation to the ten guardians of the directions beginning with Indra," and "Oṃ, salutation to the weapons beginning with the Vajra."
Then, having placed two *kuśa* blades, each a span (*prādeśa*) in length, into the midst of the clarified butter,
one should perform the oblation while meditating upon *iḍā*, *piṅgalā*, and *suṣumṇā* in the left, right, and middle portions [respectively].
Leaving six finger-breadths from the base and four finger-breadths as well,
one should cover the base of the forearm and wear it with the *śaṅkha-mudrā*.
The sacrificer indeed suffers loss from seeing the base of the *sruva* ladle;
therefore, one should conceal the base of the *sruva* at the time of the oblation.
It is said that [if held] at the tip it causes disease, at the middle it is considered to cause grief, and at the base it is said to cause loss; how then should one hold the *sruva*?
Leaving a space of four finger-breadths (vedāṅgula) at the front, and eight finger-breadths for the fire,
one should hold the conch-seal (śaṅkhamudrā) in the middle of that.
Then, having taken clarified butter from the southern portion with the *sruva* ladle, [one offers it] with "Oṃ agnaye svāhā."

Thus one should offer oblation into the right eye. Then, taking clarified butter from the left portion, one should offer it into the left eye with: *oṃ somāya svāhā*. Then, taking clarified butter from the middle portion, one should offer it upon the forehead with:
*oṃ agnisomābhyāṃ svāhā*. Again, [taking] ghee from the right side...
Having taken [the portion], one should offer it into the mouth of the fire with: *oṃ agnaye sviṣṭakṛte svāhā*. (p.
45) Then follows the *vyāhṛti-homa*: *oṃ bhūḥ svāhā*, *oṃ bhuvaḥ svāhā*, *oṃ svaḥ svāhā*. *Oṃ vaiśvānara jātaveda, bring hither [the gods]; O red-eyed one, [perform] all rites.*

One should offer oblations three times with the mantra: *sādhaya svāhā*.
