Then, in the fire, having worshipped with scents and flowers while reciting "Oṃ, obeisance to the deities of the seat (*pīṭha*)," one should offer oblations twenty-five times into the mouth of the deity using the root mantra (*mūlamantra*). Again, with the root mantra...
Having offered oblations eleven times, he should make the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*):

"Today, etc., I, of such-and-such lineage, the venerable Amukadevaśarman, desiring the propitiation of my chosen deity, shall perform the rite of one hundred and eight oblations with such-and-such substances by means of such-and-such a mantra."
"I shall perform it.

Then, having performed the fire-oblation (*homa*) according to the prescribed number, and having completed the oblation by reciting the root mantra followed by "svāhā," one should offer oblations to the deities of the enclosure (*āvaraṇadevatā*) and then the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the root mantra.

One should give [the fee]. Then, having brought the deity to one's own heart by means of the *saṃhāramudrā* (withdrawal gesture) and having dismissed them with "Forgive me," one should give the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*).
[The formula begins: "Today... and so forth, regarding this ritual of the *homa* which is a limb of the initiation (*dīkṣā*) for such-and-such a deity.

Having offered the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) with the words, "I relinquish this gold for the sake of the consecration to be given to my chosen deity," he should give it to the preceptor. Then, having poured curd in the northeastern direction, he should announce, "O Earth, be cool. Thereafter, [the remainder] clinging to the *sruva* ladle...
One should apply the ashes on the forehead and other parts of the body. Then follows the feeding of Brahmins.
One should satisfy one’s own guru with garments, ornaments, and so forth. Thus ends the method of the abbreviated initiation (*saṃkṣepadīkṣā*). May there be prosperity; may there be auspiciousness!
Now, the procedure for the consecration of the *dhāraṇā*-yantra:
having drawn the yantra with the materials specified in its respective ritual manual (*kalpa*), having wrapped it with silk thread or cotton thread,
and having washed it with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*).

One should perform a cleansing with scented water. Then, one should consecrate the yantra one hundred and eight times with the Gāyatrī mantra: "We know the King of Yantras; we meditate upon the Great Yantra; may that Yantra inspire us. Thereafter, the deity of the yantra [is to be worshipped] as the seat (*pīṭha*) within the yantra.

Having meditated [upon the deity], one should place [the substance] in a vessel, invoke one's chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā) upon it, worship it, and recite the root mantra one thousand and eight times, or one hundred and eight times. Then, having performed the fire sacrifice (homa), one should pour the clarified butter (ājya) remaining from the oblation onto the yantra; having completed the homa, one should give the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).

In the event that one is unable to perform the fire sacrifice (homa), one should perform twice as many recitations (japa) and so forth. Then, having fashioned the yantra out of gold or other materials on an auspicious day, one should perform the consecration of the vital breaths (prāṇapratiṣṭhā) over it using the mantra beginning with *āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ* and so on, and subsequently wear it upon the neck or other parts of the body.
The ritual procedure for the consecration of the yantra. Now, the purification of the rosary (mālā).
Its necessity is stated in the Yāmala:
The person who recites the mantra with a rosary that is not fixed should know that all of it is fruitless; the deity becomes angry.
O Sanatkumāra, the thread produced from cotton bestows dharma, kāma, artha, and mokṣa;
it should be beautifully fashioned by the daughters of the foremost among Brahmins.
And that [liquid] is red when it pertains to Śakti; yellow for Vaiṣṇava; and white is to be taken in the case of Śaiva. He states its function:
Having tripled the threefold [cord], the wise one should tie knots according to the treatises on craftsmanship (śilpaśāstra),
while muttering each single letter of the Mātṛkā preceded by the Tāra-mantra.
Having taken the gem, one should string it upon a thread, knotting it in the middle;
having thus fashioned a *brahmagranthi*, one should likewise attach the *meru* to the knot.
One should fashion a lotus shape using nine fresh leaves of the *aśvattha* tree;
in its center, one should place the rosary while reciting the root mantra of the *mātṛkā*.
One should wash [the image] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and fresh water;
one should rub it with sandalwood, agallochum, perfumes, and so forth, while reciting the Vāmadeva mantra.
One should fumigate it with the Aghora mantra, smear it with the Tatpuruṣa mantra,
and consecrate each [part] one hundred times with the fifth mantra alone.
Then, having first tripled [the thread] three times, one should string the rosary while reciting the *mātṛkā* syllables preceded by the *praṇava*. Taking the beads,
one should join the mouth of the second to the mouth of the first, and having placed the tail of the second against the tail of that [first], [one continues].

One should tie it with a nine-stranded cord. Having fashioned it in the shape of a cow’s tail or the form of a serpent, and having placed it upon a lotus made of nine *aśvattha* leaves, one should perform the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*). (p.
47) Oṃ, today, etc., [I], of such-and-such lineage, named so-and-so...
Desiring the accomplishment of my own chosen mantra, I shall perform the consecration of the rosary of [the deity] Amuka.
As a part of that, I shall perform the worship of Gaṇapati and the other deities.
Then, while reciting the Mātṛkā along with its root-mantra, [I shall place it] upon the rosary situated in the packet.

One should pour in the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) with the root mantra: *mūlam aṃ mūlam āmūlam*, and so forth. Then, one should wash it with clear water using the *Sadyojāta* mantra. The mantra is as follows: *oṃ sadyo jātaṃ prapadyāmi sadyojātāya vai namaḥ | bhave bhave nātibhave bhavasva māṃ* (I take refuge in Sadyojāta; salutations indeed to Sadyojāta! In every birth, do not lead me beyond existence; protect me.)
"Salutation to Bhavodbhava. Then, one should smear [the deity] with perfumes and other offerings using the Vāmadeva mantra.
The mantra is: *Oṃ vāmadevāya namaḥ, jyeṣṭhāya namaḥ, rudrāya namaḥ, kālāya namaḥ, kālavikaraṇāya namaḥ, balāya namaḥ, balapramathanāya namaḥ*.

"Salutations to the Subduer of all beings; salutations, salutations to the Transcendent (Unmanā); salutations. Then, one should fumigate them with the Aghora mantra. The mantra is as follows: "Oṃ, to the non-terrible ones and to the terrible ones, to those more terrible than the terrible, to all of them, to the all-encompassing ones—to you who possess the forms of Rudra, let there be salutation. Then...

One should smear it with the Tatpuruṣa mantra. The mantra is: *oṃ tatpuruṣāya vidmahe mahādevāya dhīmahi | tanno rudraḥ pracodayāt*. Then, one should consecrate each individual jewel one hundred times with the fifth mantra; one should also consecrate the Meru [jewel] in the same manner.

The fifth mantra, however, is: *oṃ īśānaḥ sarvavidyānāmīśvaraḥ sarvabhūtānāṃ brahmādhipatirbrahmā śivo me'stu sadā śivom*. This may be recited once for each [mantra], or alternatively, with reference to the entire garland of mantras as a whole.

One should perform the recitation (*japa*) one hundred times over the rosary with the fifth mantra. Then, having invoked the deity into the rosary preceded by the display of the eight mudrās of invocation, and having worshipped it with the root mantra, one should perform the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of the life-force) of the rosary. *Āṃ hrīṃ*.

KROṂ YA RAṂ LAṂ VAṂ ŚAṂ ṢAṂ SAṂ HRĪṂ OṂ KṢAṂ SAṂ HA SAḤ HRĪṂ OṂ HA SAḤ | The vital breaths (*prāṇa*) of the rosary of the deity [Name] are here, ĀM, etc., twenty times. All the sense-faculties (*sarvendriya*) of the rosary of the deity [Name], ĀM, etc., twenty times. Of the rosary of the deity [Name]...
"O speech, limbs, eyes, ears, nose, and vital breaths, having come here, may you remain happily for a long time;
svāhā! Oṃ kṣaṃ saṃ haṃ saḥ hrīṃ oṃ.
Having thus performed the consecration of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) with this mantra, [one should perform it] individually according to the reverse order.

Touching the jewel, one should recite the root mantra once; then one should recite each letter of the alphabet (mātṛkā) together with the nasal bindu. Thereafter, having performed a fire-offering (homa) in the consecrated fire consisting of one hundred and eight oblations, [one should proceed].

One should pour the ghee from the oblation into the rosary. If one is unable to perform the fire sacrifice (*homa*), one should perform two hundred and sixteen recitations (*japa*) with that rosary; having worshipped it with the root mantra, one should join the palms in *añjali* and recite the mantra.
"O Mālā, you are considered the bestower of all accomplishments for all the worlds;
by that truth, O Mother, grant me accomplishment—homage be to you!
Having thus prostrated, one should perform the dismissal of the deity (*devatā-visarjana*). Then, with musk, saffron, and so forth...
Having carefully fashioned a well-perfumed garland, one should preserve it with effort; such is the consecration of the garland.
Now follows the determination of rosaries. O Jāyā, listen as I describe those rosaries made from lotus seeds and other materials:
[rosaries] made of rudrākṣa, conch, lotus seeds, putranjīva, kama, and pearls.
The rosary of a householder may be made of crystal, precious gems, gold, coral, silver, or kusha grass roots.
Counting on the fingers, one [repetition] becomes eightfold;
with *putrañjīva* beads it is a hundredfold; with conch shells it is a thousandfold;
and with coral or precious gems, it is traditionally held to be ten thousandfold.
That same [number] is declared for crystal beads; for pearls, it is said to be one hundred thousand.
With lotus seeds, ten lakhs [of recitations] are accomplished; with golden beads, it is said to be ten million (koṭi);
with knots of kuśa grass, a hundred million; and with rudrākṣa beads, it becomes infinite.
A rosary fashioned from lotus seeds brings about the destruction of enemies;
a rosary made of knots of *kuśa* grass destroys all sins.
A garland fashioned from *putrañjīva* fruits brings about the attainment of sons; one made from sprouts bestows abundant wealth.

For the recitation of the Tripurā mantra and similar practices, a rosary made of red sandalwood seeds and the like is highly recommended; for the recitation of Gaṇeśa as well, a rosary of red sandalwood is praised.

A garland of *tulasī* is recommended for the worship of Viṣṇu; for Gaṇeśvara, one made of elephant tusks; and for the recitation of the *Tripurā* mantra, beads of *rudrākṣa* and sandalwood are praised.
The rosary is proclaimed to consist of the letters beginning with 'a' and ending with 'kṣa'.
One should arrange the letter 'kṣa' there as the summit of Mount Meru, in accordance with the consensus of the sages.
A rosary made of fifty gems is prescribed for all rites;
however, O beautiful one, if a rosary is unavailable, one may even hold a rosary made of desire-granting [gems] in the hand.
Now, the *karamālā* (finger rosary):
beginning with the middle finger and starting from the little finger,
one should perform the recitation over the ten joints up to the base of the index finger.
And this refers to the domain of cowherds. Now, the *karamālā* (finger rosary) of power:
by the successive rotation of the two joints of the ring finger, in due order.
One should bring together three joints of the middle finger and one joint of the index finger.
The Śaktimālā is fully proclaimed as the illuminator of all tantras;
this is the specific [instruction] regarding Śrīvidyā.
O Sovereign of the Gods, there are two joints each from the root and the tip of the ring finger and the middle finger,
and three joints of the little finger and the index finger.
O auspicious Tripurasundarī, one should perform the recitation by circling clockwise around both the ring finger and the middle finger, which constitute the Meru.
Thus it is stated in the *Yāmala*: "Whatever is recited with the fingertips, whatever is recited while bypassing the *meru*,
and whatever is recited at the joints of the fingers— all that becomes fruitless."
The number of recitations must indeed be performed; a wise person should not recite without counting.
For one who performs recitation without counting, that recitation becomes fruitless.
Placing the hand upon the heart and bending the fingers sideways,
one should always perform the recitation while covering the hand with a cloth using the right hand.
One should not release the fingers, nor even slightly contract them;
for through the separation of the fingers or a gap [in the hand], the recitation flows away.
When there is a difference in the desired objective, there is a restriction regarding the fingers:
the union of the index finger and the thumb causes the eradication of enemies;
through the union of the thumb and the middle finger, the accomplishment of the mantra becomes perfectly stable.
The union of the thumb and the ring finger is considered for expulsion and eradication;
the union of the index and little fingers is considered for the destruction of enemies.
When the thread has worn out, one should tie it again to a new thread and recite the mantra one hundred times.
If it falls from the hand through negligence, one should recite it one hundred and eight times.
If there is contact with forbidden things during recitation, one should wash [the hands] as is appropriate;
even when [the thread] is broken, there should be one hundred and eight recitations, because a broken [thread] and one that has fallen from the hand are equivalent.
Now follows the rule for the seat.
For the sake of fulfilling desires, a woolen blanket is excellent, as is a red woolen blanket;
through a black antelope skin, one attains the perfection of knowledge, while liberation and prosperity are gained through a tiger skin.
Success in mantra arises on a seat of kusha grass; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Misery arises from sitting on the bare ground, and misfortune results from a wooden seat.
On a bamboo seat there is poverty; on a stone seat, the affliction of disease;
on a grass seat, the loss of fame; and on a leaf seat, the delusion of the mind.
It causes the loss of recitation, meditation, and austerity, as well as damage to one's clothing and seat.

Here, "clothing and seat" (*vastrāsana*) refers specifically to the prohibition of using a mere cloth as a seat. This is because there is an injunction regarding the production of specific results, stating that "a cloth-seat removes disease," and also because of the Lord’s own statement: "With cloth, deerskin, and kusha grass placed in ascending order."

Thus ends the *Ṣaṭcakravivaraṇa* composed by the illustrious Maithila Jīvanātha, including the procedures for initiation (*dīkṣāvidhāna*), the collection of mantras (*mantrasaṃgrahamālā*), and the rites of purification (*saṃskārādividhāna*).
The five deities.

Gaṇeśa, Viṣṇu, Sūrya, Durgā, and Śiva; and the five world-protectors (lokapālas). Gaṇeśa, Ambikā, Vāyu, Ākāśa, and likewise the two Aśvins—these five world-protectors are proclaimed to be situated above the planets.
Indra, Agni, Yama, Nirṛti, Varuṇa,
Vāyu, Soma, Giriśa, and the serpent is remembered as the ninth.
Brahmā is proclaimed first, followed by all the guardians of the directions (dikpālas):
Vajra, Śakti, Daṇḍa, Khaḍga, Pāśa, Aṅkuśa, and Gada.
The wise know their weapons to be the trident, the lotus, and the discus. There are sixteen Mātṛkās:
Gaurī, Padmā, Śacī, Medhā, Sāvitrī, Vijayā, Jayā, Dedhasenā, Sudhā, Svāhā, and the Mothers who are the Mothers of the World.
Hṛṣṭi (13), Puṣṭi (14), Tuṣṭi (15), and likewise the tutelary deity of one's own family (16).
Now follows the procedure for the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*).
In the *Yoginīhṛdaya*:
Having received the command of the Guru, a person with a purified inner self,
desiring the accomplishment of the mantra, should begin the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa).
Just as a living being deprived of life is incapable of performing any actions,
so too is a mantra declared to be ineffective when it is devoid of the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa).
Therefore, at the outset, the wise person should perform [the rite] himself or have a guru perform it;
in the absence of a guru, he may have a brahmin who is devoted to the welfare of all living beings perform it.
And one should appoint a woman endowed with excellent qualities and having virtuous sons.
Then, during the northern course of the sun, in the bright fortnight, on a day favorable to the moon and the stars, one should consider the location for performing the preparatory rites.
A field of merit, the bank of a river, a cave, a mountain peak,
a sacred bathing place, a region of confluences of rivers, and a purifying forest.
A garden, a beautiful place, the foot of a bilva tree,
a mountain slope, a grove of tulasī, a cow-pen, a bull-pen, and a temple of Śiva.
The root of the *aśvattha* and *lakṣmaṇā* trees, a cowshed, the middle of water,
a temple, a seashore, and one's own home.
One should know that the merit is a hundredfold at home, a hundred-thousandfold in a cow-pen,
ten millionfold in a temple, and infinite in the presence of Śiva.
In a secluded, pure place, free from the fear and anxiety caused by barbarians, wicked beasts, and tigers, devoid of censure, and filled with devotion.
O beloved, an ascetic should dwell in his own country, in a righteous land that is well-supplied with food, free from calamities, beautiful, and inhabited by devoted people.

Resorting to any one of these places, one should perform the recitation (*japa*). In whatever village the practitioner of mantra (*mantrī*) recites, there he should meditate upon the Tortoise (*kūrma*).

Regarding the tortoise-posture (*kūrmasthāna*), it is stated in the *Gautamīya*: "Having divided the ground for the site of recitation (*japasthānabhūmi*) into nine parts, one should write the letters *ka, ca, ṭa, ta, pa, ya, śa, va* in the compartments starting from the east, and finally *la, kṣa, a, vi* [in the center]; then, the central compartment should also be divided into nine."

Having prepared that [grid], one should write pairs of vowels in the directions starting from the east. The square in which the first letter of the name of the field (kṣetra) is seen is the location of the lamp; the location for its absence is also right there. [This applies] on a mountain, by a riverbank, in a sacred forest, or on a river shore.
If one should perform the *puraścaraṇa* there, one need not consider the tortoise [as a site].
Also, in the *Devīyāmala*:
"At Kurukṣetra, at Prayāga, and at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean..."
(p. 53) One should not contemplate the location for the lamp in Mahākāla or in Kāśī;

rather, one should contemplate it in a village, or in a site, or in a house. Then, having examined the tortoise-diagram (*kūrmacakra*) within the center of the acquired field, [one should place it] in its mouth.
"Having constructed a recitation pavilion (japamaṇḍapa), one should perform the preparatory rite (puraścaraṇa).
Now, regarding the rules for what may and may not be eaten during the *puraścaraṇa*, the *Gautamīya-tantra* states:
"The practitioner of mantra performing the *puraścaraṇa* should carefully consider what is fit and unfit to be eaten."
Otherwise, O Goddess, the loss of accomplishment arises from eating.
Even while eating, he should consume only sacrificial food (haviṣya), vegetables, barley-gruel (yāvaka),
milk, roots, or fruits— whatever may be available at that time.

Regarding the sacrificial food (*haviṣya*), it is stated in the *Āgastya-saṃhitā*: "Curd, cow's milk, ghee, sugarcane products excluding jaggery, sesame seeds, white beans, and tubers excluding *kaimuka*."
The coconut fruit, the plantain, the kavalī, the mango, the āmalaka, the jackfruit, and the harītakī.
Furthermore, wise men consider sacrificial food (haviṣya) to be highly commended during the intervals between vows.
Regarding "another vow": it refers to the winter practice of not eating food that has been steamed with sugar, and so forth.
Now, the things to be avoided: one should avoid honey, alkaline substances, salt, and oil;
as well as betel-leaf, eating from a bronze vessel, and eating during the day.
Furthermore: alkaline substances, salt, meat, garlic, eating from a bronze vessel,
mung beans, adzukis, lentils, kodrava grain, and even chickpeas— [these should be avoided].
One should avoid crookedness, shaving, anointing with oil, eating food that has not been offered, performing tasks without proper engagement, and such things as massaging.
One should bathe with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) or with pure *āmalaka* fruit;
and one's bathing, sipping of water, and eating should be performed with food and drink over which mantras have been recited.
One should perform the worship of the deity three times a day according to the prescribed rule;
one should avoid hiccup, coughing, yawning, and sleep.
Now he states the rule for eating: One should fill half the stomach with food and one part with water;
one should leave the fourth part empty for the movement of the vital air.
Now, regarding the prohibition of another's food, the Kulārṇava states:
"If one whose body is nourished by another's food and drink performs an accumulation of merit, half of the fruit belongs to the giver of the food and half to the doer; of this there is no doubt."
Therefore, O Śāmbhavī, with every effort one should avoid the food of others during the period of *puraścaraṇa* and in all ritual acts.
The tongue is burned by the food of others, the hands are burned by receiving gifts, and the mind is burned by the wives of others; O fair-faced one, how then can there be spiritual success?
In this context, the eating of another's food refers to food obtained from sources other than [one's own family].
Now, the rule for recitation:
one should perform the recitation according to the stated number for the sake of accomplishing the *puraścaraṇa*.
Contemplating with one's intellect the identity of the deity, the guru, and the mantra.
One should recite with a one-pointed mind from the morning until midday;
whatever number has been undertaken, that must be performed day and night.
If one should perform it with deficiency or excess, that person becomes fallen from his vow.
Also in the Kulārṇava:
"Rites that are deficient or excessive never bear fruit;
for only those good deeds performed according to the rules indeed yield results."
Also in the Muṇḍamālā Tantra:
"One should recite daily the same number with which the practice was begun;
one should never perform less or more, but always recite until completion."
(p. 56) Now, regarding the twelve rules for recitation (*japa*), it is stated in the *Kulārṇava*:
"Sleeping on the ground, celibacy, silence, service to the teacher, daily worship, daily giving, and the praise and glorification of the deity."
Worship according to the specific signs, faith in the Guru and the Deity,
and steadfastness in recitation— these twelve are the duties that bestow success in mantra.

During the time of recitation (*japa*), one should avoid speaking with women, *śūdras*, outcasts (*patita*), those who have fallen from their caste (*brātya*), atheists, or those who have eaten the leftovers of others, as well as speaking untruths.
In the Yoginītantra: One should avoid false speech and crooked words;
one should not speak even the truth during recitation, fire-offerings, worship, and the like.
One should avoid listening to singing and instrumental music, watching dances,
as well as oil massages, the application of perfumes and ointments, and the wearing of flowers.
One should abandon bathing in hot water and the worship of other deities.
Also in that same context:
"One should not recite a mantra while wearing only a single garment, nor while crowded with many garments."
Upon seeing, speaking with, or hearing those who have fallen from their caste or those born of the lowest castes, [one must perform purification].
Upon sneezing, the passing of downward wind, or yawning, one should cease the recitation;
likewise, upon its occurrence during that [recitation], one should perform a six-limbed breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Having performed [the preliminary rites], one should recite the remainder correctly; or else, there should be the sight of the sun and so forth.
By the word "and so forth" (ādi), one should also look upon fire and a Brāhmaṇa.
Furthermore, in another tantra it is said:
"Withdrawal of the mind, purity, silence, reflection on the meaning of the mantra,
freedom from distraction, and lack of despondency are the causes for the successful accomplishment of japa."
Furthermore: One who wears a turban, one wearing a bodice, one who is naked, one with disheveled hair, one surrounded by a crowd,
one with unpurified hands, one who is impure, or one who is prattling— such a person should never recite [mantras].
Neither while sitting, nor lying down, nor walking, nor even while eating;
one should not recite [the mantra] on a road, in an inauspicious place, or in a place of darkness.
A cat, a cock, a dog, a curlew, a Śūdra, a donkey, and a monkey—
Having seen [an impurity], one should sip water and mutter [the mantra]; having touched the ear, bathing is prescribed.
This rule for muttering should be understood to apply everywhere; however, it does not constitute a fault in the case of mental recitation.
Now, regarding the mental recitation (*mānasajapa*), it is taught in that same [text] that there is no requirement for formal observances:
"Whether impure or pure, whether walking, standing, or even sleeping,
the wise person who has the mantra as his sole refuge should always practice thus with the mind alone."
There is no fault in mental recitation at any time or in any place;
the best of the twice-born, devoted to such recitation, obtains the fruit of all sacrifices.
However, regarding the recitation of mantras such as the Śrīvidyā, the specific requirements for each respective mantra should be understood.
Now he describes the fruit of recitation (*japa*): "O best among the foremost of the twice-born, one who is devoted to the recitation of all dharmas shall obtain the fruit of all sacrifices;
he indeed becomes one who yields great fruit for all sacrifices."
By constant recitation, the deity, being praised, becomes pleased;
being pleased, she grants abundant desires and eternal liberation.
[She also subdues] yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, planetary spirits, and terrifying serpents.
Terrified on all sides by fear, they do not approach the one who recites the mantra.
Whatever sacrificial rites there may be, and whatever purifying austerities,
they all do not equal even a sixteenth part of the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña).
This majesty of the sacrifice of recitation (vācika-japa-yajña) has been proclaimed;
therefore, the whispered (upāṃśu) is said to be a hundredfold more effective, and the mental (mānasa) a thousandfold.

For those desiring spiritual accomplishments (*siddhi*), mental recitation is prescribed; for those desiring nourishment (*puṣṭi*), whispered recitation; and for the purpose of killing (*māraṇa*), vocal recitation is said to be most excellent. Now, the characteristics of mental and other forms of recitation are described.
When one mentally utters, with the intellect, the sequence of syllables consisting of phonemes, vowels, and words,
directed toward the intended meaning, that is known as mental recitation (*mānasajapa*).
One whose mind is fixed on the deity should move the tongue and lips slightly;
that muttering which is barely audible to the ear is known as *upāṃśu* (whispered) recitation.
One should recite the mantra with speech; that is known as vocal recitation (*vācika*).
Also, in the *Viśuddheśvara-tantra*:
"That which is beyond the range of one's own ears is known as mental recitation (*mānasa*)."
The *upāṃśu* [recitation] is proclaimed to be within the range of one's own ear.
The vocal recitation known as *japa* is said by people to be of three kinds;
the whispered recitation (*upāṃśu*) is ten times more distinguished than the loud recitation (*uccair-japa*).
The mental recitation is said to be a thousand times more effective than the whispered recitation.
And in another Tantra: "Loud recitation is declared to be the lowest; the whispered recitation is considered middling."
O Goddess, the threefold recitation of the mind is said to be the most excellent.
One that is too short is a cause of disease; one that is too long causes the loss of wealth.
One should recite [the mantra] joined with the syllables and the non-syllable, like a string of pearls.
Whoever should remember the hymn only with the mind or mutter the mantra only with the voice—
both become fruitless, like water in a broken vessel.
Now, regarding the cause of a mantra’s sovereignty, it is said in the *Gautamīya*:
"Mantras existing in the state of the bound (paśu) are merely composed of phonemes;
when those mantras enter the path of the *suṣumnā*, they attain sovereignty through their recitation."
One should contemplate the syllables of the mantra as being proclaimed within the power of consciousness (cicchakti),
that very [power] which resides in the supreme void (paramavyoman) expanded by supreme bliss (paramānanda).
It reveals its own true existence even without worship, fire-offerings, and the like. (p.
59) However, there is a specific distinction regarding the *kulavarṇa*:
"The mind is in one place, Śiva is in another, Śakti is in another, and the vital breath (*māruta*) is in another."
O lady of excellent hips, it is not accomplished even in hundreds of millions of eons.
Now, regarding that very [topic], he states the two types of *sūtaka* for a mantra: "The birth-*sūtaka* occurs at the beginning, and the death-*sūtaka* occurs at the end.
A mantra joined with these two *sūtaka*s does not attain success."
O Supreme Goddess, having placed the seed-syllable of Brahmā at the beginning and end of the mantra,
one should recite the mantra seven times for liberation from the two types of birth-impurity.

The seed-syllable of Brahman is the syllable *oṃ*; having first recited the *praṇava* seven times, one should then recite the mantra, and at the end, one should again recite the *praṇava* seven times.
Now, another point: for one who does not know the meaning of the mantra, the consciousness of the mantra, and the *yonimudrā*,
no accomplishment arises even through a hundred million recitations.
O Dear One, those mantras whose seed-syllables are lost will not yield fruit;
however, mantras endowed with consciousness are said to grant all accomplishments.
Mantras are said to be devoid of consciousness; they are merely phonemes.
They do not bestow any fruit even in hundreds of millions of aeons.
Whatever nature first arises when a mantra is uttered— even if it is recited a hundred, a thousand, a hundred thousand, or ten million times— that result is not attained [otherwise].
The breaking of the knot in the heart, the expansion of all the limbs,
tears of bliss, horripilation, and the possession of the body— O Kuleśvarī!
And a sudden cessation of disease occurs; of this there is no doubt.
Even when a mantra endowed with consciousness is uttered but once, such a result follows.
Where conditions are seen in succession, that is called "paramparā" (succession).
Now, regarding the method for the offering of the mantra, it is stated in the *Gautamīya*:

"Having thus first performed the recitation (*japa*), one should offer [the mantra] in the form of light into the right hand of the deity, using *kuśa* grass, flowers, and water for the *argha* offering."
Having thus understood it to be fruitful, one should perform *prāṇāyāma*;
indeed, one should perform this triad both at the beginning and at the end of the recitation (*japa*).
In the Śakti-pakṣa, one should offer the recitation (japa) into the left hand.
Having thus first performed the recitation, the wise practitioner should offer the japa to the Goddess into Her left hand with scents, unbroken rice grains (akṣata), and water mixed with kuśa grass.
At the conclusion of the recitation (japa), the practitioner of mantra should perform a fire sacrifice (homa) every day with one-tenth of that number;

then, O Sage, he should perform libations (tarpaṇa) and ritual ablutions (abhiṣeka) with one-tenth of that amount. Furthermore, he should feed Brahmins every day to pacify any deficiencies or excesses in the rite.
Alternatively, when all [the preliminary rites] are complete, one should then perform the fire oblations (homa) and other rituals.
In the *Sanatkumārīya*, regarding the inability to perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) and so forth:
"If any limb [of the ritual] should be broken, the recitation (*japa*) shall be twice that number.
In the absence of the fire-oblation, the recitation must be performed; it shall be four times the number of the fire-oblations."
For Brahmins and Kshatriyas, it is traditionally taught that the quality [of the breath] is eightfold;
for Vaishyas, it is eightfold; and this same rule applies to their women.
In this matter as well, one who is incapable [should act accordingly].
That specific rule is stated in the *Yoginīhṛdaya*:
"For Brahmins who are unable to perform the rite of fire-offering (*homakarman*), the recitation (*japa*) shall be twofold;
for other castes, it shall be endowed with threefold [the standard number] and so forth."
By this, women and Śūdras have the entitlement to perform the *homa*; and that [entitlement] is only through the mediation of a Brāhmaṇa.
And likewise in another Tantra:
"By the utterance of the syllable *Oṃ*, by performing fire-sacrifices (*homa*), by worshipping the Śālagrāma stone,
and by having sexual intercourse with a Brāhmaṇa woman, even a Śūdra may attain the state of a Cāṇḍāla."

Thus, because of this explicit prohibition; likewise, it is said that "any mantra beginning with the *praṇava* (Om) is not recommended for women or Śūdras. Therefore, all women should be understood as equal to Śūdras.
Likewise, in the Agastya-saṃhitā: "If one is unable to perform the fire-oblation (homa), or the ritual worship (pūjā),
or even the libation (tarpaṇa), [one should accomplish it] by means of a recitation (japa) of that same number or by the propitiation of Brāhmaṇas."
In the rite of *puraścaraṇa*, it may be accomplished by means of these two limbs alone:
having given a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the guru, as well as food and clothing.
By the mere satisfaction of the guru, the accomplishment of mantra will certainly occur;
those who know the tantras say that all this has its root in the guru.
The Guru alone is the Supreme Brahman; therefore, one should worship him first.
At the conclusion of that, the best of practitioners should perform the great worship.
One should also adorn the married woman and the maiden with ornaments,
and feed them according to the prescribed rite with sweet foods, fruits, and roots.
Thus, the practitioner who has mastered the mantra shall accomplish all desired objects.
Now follows the procedure for the *puraścaraṇa* (preliminary rite) to be performed at the time of an eclipse.
In that very [text] it is said:
"Alternatively, the *puraścaraṇa* is desired to be performed in another manner."
During an eclipse of either the sun or the moon, one should first fast and remain pure.
Standing in a river flowing toward the ocean with water reaching up to his navel,
he should recite the mantra with one-pointed mind from the time of touch until liberation.
But in the absence of a river, it is stated in that very same [text]:
"Alternatively, having bathed in sacred water and being pure, having first fasted,
one should recite the mantra with a concentrated mind from the moment of [the moon's] eclipse until its release."
In the *Muṇḍamālā*:
"Having seen [it], one who has bathed and made a firm resolve should perform the recitation (*japa*) until liberation;
a pure man should likewise perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) and other rites until the end of the eclipse."

"Thus, through recitation, the perfection of the mantra will surely come to pass; of this there is no doubt. Thus [it is said]. He states the primacy of the preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*) during its performance: "If a person should abandon the recitation out of regard for a funeral feast (*śrāddha*) or similar occasions,"
He becomes an offender against the deities and leads seven generations of his ancestors to the netherworld.

He who abandons the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña) and performs the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña) becomes an offender against the deities; he leads seven generations of his ancestors to the nether regions.

(p. 62) According to the words of Sanatkumāra, the necessity of recitation (*japa*) is established; however, in reality, this refers specifically to the subject of the *puraścaraṇa* that has already been commenced.
For it is said: "If, when the *puraścaraṇa* has commenced, the [lunar] eclipse should occur, then one must not abandon the recitation (*japa*) out of regard for one's faith.
Now, he describes the *puraścaraṇa*.
Recitation, fire-offerings, libations, ritual ablution, and feeding of Brahmins—
this fivefold worship is recognized in the world as *puraścaraṇa*.

In the case of receiving [mantras] and so forth, however, *puraścaraṇa* consists of mere recitation (*japa*) alone. For this very reason, when *puraścaraṇa* in its five-limbed form has been performed, one possesses the qualification even for the primary ritual application (*mukhyaprayoga*). The essential point is that in the performance of ten-fold *puraścaraṇa*, which consists of mere recitation alone, there is no such qualification. Now:
The time for *puraścaraṇa* is stated in the *Vārāhī*:
"One should commence the *puraścaryā* when the moon and stars are favorable, during the bright fortnight on an auspicious day; however, one should not perform it while Hari is asleep."
And during the performance at a great sacred site (*mahātīrtha*), one need not observe a specific time restriction.
Now follows the procedure for the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*):
therein, having first taken possession of the ground, the person performing the *puraścaraṇa*—

On the third day prior [to the main event], having performed the shaving of the head and other rites, one should designate a square area extending one *krośa*, two *krośas*, or as far as desired in the four directions from the altar for the purpose of taking food and recreation; then, one should construct a pavilion in accordance with the *kūrmacakra*.
Having observed the practice of eating only once a day, one should then, on the following day, perform the ritual bath and other rites.

Being thus purified, one should take ten stakes, each measuring one *vitasti* in length, made from any one of the *aśvattha*, *udumbara*, or *plakṣa* trees, and consecrate them one hundred and eight times with the mantra: *Oṃ astrāya phaṭ*.

One should bury [the stakes] in the ten directions. *Oṃ tatsat*. Beginning with "Today," etc., for the sake of [myself], [Name] of such-and-such lineage and [Name] Śarmā, desiring the accomplishment of my own chosen mantra preceded by the eradication of all obstacles for this field, I perform the ritual of driving in the stakes in the ten directions, starting from the east.
And I shall perform the worship of Gaṇapati, Vāstupuruṣa, and Kṣetrapāla, without the syllable *hiṃ*.
As follows:
*Oṃ, and those who are here creators of obstacles, whether in heaven, on earth, or moving in the intermediate space.*
And those others who have become obstacles to the attainments of my mantra;
Having abandoned this field which has been staked out by me, let them all depart from afar; may there be success for me without obstacle.

Having buried [the weapons] therein with this [mantra], one should worship the Astra [weapon] with the mantra "Oṃ namaḥ sudarśanāya astrāya phaṭ," and then worship the world-protectors, Indra and the others, in order starting from the east.
For example: "Oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ, O world-protector Indra, come here!"—thus invoking [him].
Having worshipped with water for the feet and other offerings, one should worship the world-protectors, beginning with Agni, in their respective directions.
Then, having worshipped Kṣetrapāla and Vāstveśa in the central place, one should worship Gaṇapati for the sake of destroying all obstacles. As follows: Oṃ...

Having made the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) thus: "Today, I, [Name], of the [Gotra] lineage, [Name] Devaśarman, shall perform the worship of Gaṇeśa for the purpose of destroying all obstacles in the rite of *puraścaraṇa* consisting of the [Name] mantra to be performed by me," [he should do so] in the center of the altar.
One should worship Gaṇeśa with the five types of offerings (pañcopacāra).
And it is said:
"Furthermore, a place measuring one *krośa* from a village, or by a river and so forth, according to one's own desire."
Even within a city or similar place, [the distance] may be one *krośa*, or even two *krośas*.
One should traverse as much ground as is necessary for the purpose of procuring food and other such activities; or, one should designate a field, however large desired, for the purpose of habitation.
One should drive stakes made from milky trees, consecrated with weapon-mantras,
into the ten directions, and worship the Weapon-deity within them.
Furthermore, the wise one should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas) among them with perfumes and other offerings;
thereafter, he should duly worship Kṣetrapāla and the others there according to the prescribed rite.
One should worship Kṣetreśa, known by the name Vāstu, and Vighnarāja; then one should offer an oblation to the lords of the directions and subsequently enter the site.

Indra (1), Agni (2), Yama (3), Nirṛti (4), Varuṇa (5), Vāyu (6), Soma (7), Īśāna (8), Brahmā (9) above; Ananta (10) below. Between Indra and Īśāna is Brahmā; between the western and southwestern corners is Ananta.
Then, having worshipped with black gram (*māṣa*) rice and other offerings, one should present the sacrificial oblation (*bali*) to the deities:
Oṃ! Those who are fierce and performers of fierce deeds, who dwell in fierce abodes;
those who are even more terrible than Māra in form, and those who are the lords of the hosts (*gaṇādhipati*).
And those others who have become obstacles, dwelling in the cardinal and intermediate directions—
may they all, with joyful minds, accept this offering.

With this [verse], one should offer the *bali* to the spirits (*bhūta*) in the eight directions. Then follows the offering of the *bhūtabali*: "May those spirits who dwell here in this world, having accepted this *bali* offered according to the rite, seek their residence elsewhere; may they forgive us here. Homage be to them!"
Having recited this, one should offer the *bhūtabali* (oblation to the spirits). Then one should mutter the *gāyatrī*.
Having bathed in the morning, being self-restrained, one should mutter the *gāyatrī* a thousand times;
first and foremost, for the sake of destroying both known and unknown sin. Thus it is said.
The Vidyādhara-ācārya says:
"Having bathed in the morning, one who is self-restrained should recite the Sāvitrī ten thousand times."
That [vow], moreover, is undertaken out of apprehension of extreme sin. The formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) is as follows: *Oṃ, today... [etc.

I, of such-and-such lineage and named so-and-so, desiring the destruction of known and unknown sins, shall perform the recitation of the Gāyatrī one thousand and eight times. Thereafter, one should observe a fast or consume sacrificial food (*haviṣyānna*).* Then...

On the following day at dawn, having bathed and performed the *svastivācana* (invocation of auspiciousness), one should make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "Om tat sat! Today [etc., as appropriate], I, of such-and-such lineage and named so-and-so, for the sake of the attainment of the specific mantra of such-and-such deity, preceded by the destruction of all impurities that obstruct the attainment of that mantra—"

Having made the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*): "I shall perform the *puraścaraṇa* consisting of the recitation of such-and-such mantra for such-and-such a number of times at the appropriate time during the Kāmodyādi festival, followed by its one-tenth part as burnt offerings (*homa*), its one-tenth part as libations (*tarpaṇa*), its one-tenth part as ritual ablutions (*abhiṣeka*), and its one-tenth part as the feeding of Brahmins. Thus having resolved—

One should perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), and so forth. Having worshipped the deity according to the sequence prescribed in one's own specific manual (*paddhati*), and having placed the deity within the heart while the lamp is burning, one should perform the recitation (*japa*) starting from the morning until midday. Then...
Then one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*), then the libation (*tarpaṇa*), then the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), and then provide a meal for the Brahmins.
And it is said in the *Kulārṇava*:
"And then one should perform the libation with water from sacred bathing places mixed with moonlight."
Having invoked the deity Jala with the ritual services beginning with water for the feet (pādya), and so forth.
Having worshipped [the deity] together with his retinue according to the rules and with devotion,
one should satisfy the members of the retinue with water offered in individual handfuls.

Then, with a tenth part of the *homa*, one should satisfy the Supreme Deity. Furthermore, the formula for the libation (*tarpaṇa*) is as follows: "Root mantra, *namaḥ*, I satisfy [the deity] Amuka, *namaḥ*."

As for the words of consecration, the root mantra is: *Namaḥ [Name of Deity], I shall consecrate you.* Thus, one should consecrate [the disciple] on the head with the *kalaśa-mudrā*. Having recited the root mantra ending in *namaḥ*, one should then utter the name of the deity at its conclusion.
But afterwards, I consecrate with this [mantra] that which ends in the accusative case.
One should sprinkle one's own head with water from the pitcher using the *kumbha-mudrā*.

Regarding the case of those capable [of performing the rite], one should utter the name at the end of the mantra, followed by the words "I sprinkle, *namaḥ*," according to the *Nīlatantra*. Alternatively, the formula is: "Oṃ, [Root Mantra], I satiate such-and-such deity, *namaḥ*.
Then follows the feeding of Brahmins, and then the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). Today, this [rite] for such-and-such deity...

For the sake of accomplishing the completeness of the *puraścaraṇa* rite of such-and-such a tantra, I offer this gold, dedicated to the deity Agni, to you, the Guru, [named] so-and-so, belonging to the [gotra] so-and-so. In the absence of that [Guru], it should be given to his son or others.
Thereafter, one should observe the [auspicious] gaps.
Now follows the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) for the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) to be performed at the time of the eclipse:
"Today, etc., I, of such-and-such lineage and such-and-such name, while the sun or the moon is eclipsed by Rāhu..."

Or, having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "Desiring the accomplishment of the mantra of such-and-such a deity, I shall perform the preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*) consisting of recitation (*japa*), from the first morsel of food until liberation," one should then recite. Having performed the bath and other preliminary rites on that day or the following day, [one should say]: "Oṃ, today... [etc. ...of this such-and-such mantra, having performed this taking..."

"I shall perform the rites of reciting [the mantra] for such-and-such a number of times, followed by a fire-oblation (homa) consisting of one-tenth of that number, a libation (tarpaṇa) consisting of one-tenth of that, an ablution (abhiṣeka) consisting of one-tenth of that, and the feeding of Brahmins consisting of one-tenth of that.
Having thus made this formal resolve (saṃkalpa), he should perform the fire-oblation and the subsequent rites. As for the giving of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), it is as previously described.
Thus concludes the method for *puraścaraṇa* in the *Dīkṣāprakāśa*.

Now, if even after performing *puraścaraṇa* there is no attainment of the mantra (*mantrasiddhi*), then ten purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*) must be performed for the mantra. Even when that has been done, if there is still no attainment of the mantra—
Then one should perform the acts of liquefying and so forth.
As it is said in the Mahātantra:
"Liquefying, awakening, subduing, pressing, drying, and nourishing."
And the wise one should perform the burning rite; then the mantra becomes perfected.
Now, their application is as follows:
first, the application for liquefying. One should [recite] the root mantra strung together with the seed-syllable of Varuṇa, *vaṃ*, using camphor, saffron, *gorocana*, realgar, and *uśīra*.
Having drawn the wheel-shaped yantra in the center of a vessel, one should combine milk, ghee, honey, and water in that vessel, place the yantra therein,
and perform worship, japa, fire-offerings (homa), and so forth; thereafter, the mantra becomes perfected (siddha).
Now, the method of stringing [the mantra]:
One syllable of the mantra, then a syllable of the name, again a syllable of the mantra, and a syllable of the name; in this manner, the stringing is described.

Having done thus, one should perform the recitation (japa) one hundred and eight times; then one becomes accomplished. Now, the awakening: one should recite the root mantra encapsulated by the Vāgbhava seed-syllable, namely "Aiṃ. As follows:
Aiṃ rāṃ, salutation to Rāma; aiṃ. Thus is the awakening.
Now, the method for subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*):
having inscribed the root mantra upon birch bark (*bhūrjapatra*) with red sandalwood, *dāruharidrā*, musk (*kastūrī*), and realgar (*manaḥśilā*).
One should recite while holding [the rosary] at the throat.
Now, as for the pressing (*pīḍana*):
there, having recited the mantra-words and mantra-syllables in an inverted order, one should recite them.

Having meditated upon the deity in the manner of the lower and the upper, one should draw the yantra with the milk of the *arka* plant, step upon it with the foot, and perform the oblation (*homa*) while reciting the mantra in the reverse order (from bottom to top). Now follows the nourishment (*poṣaṇa*).
One should write the mantra encased by the third seed-syllable of the Child (Bāla), namely *sauḥ*, using honey and cow’s milk on birch bark or similar material, and then wear it. (p.
67) Now, the drying [of the body].

In that regard, one should write the root mantra interlaced with the seed-syllable of Vāyu (yaṃ) using sacrificial ashes and wear it on the neck. The method of interlacing (vidarbhaṇa) is as follows: yaṃ yaṃ rāṃ yaṃ yaṃ rāṃ yaṃ yaṃ mā yaṃ yaṃ yaṃ yaṃ yaṃ naṃ yaṃ yaṃ maḥ yaṃ yaṃ.
First, two pairs of mantra-syllables, then one syllable of the name;
thus it is repeatedly declared by the best of mantra-knowers as *vidarbha*.
Now, regarding the burning [of the mantra]:
having encapsulated each individual syllable of the mantra— enclosed within the seed-syllables of fire—
with the letters of the Mātṛkā, one should especially [perform this] for the mantra-vidyā.
First, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times for the sake of attaining success within the Kula;
having encased it with the Mātṛkā letters and placed the seed-syllable in the middle.
Then, one should perform the awakening of the mantra-syllables as prescribed for mantras; even a wicked mantra becomes effective when enclosed by the *tāra* (the syllable Om).
This is another method.
As it is stated in the Mahātantra:
"Melting, awakening, subjugation, piercing, nourishing, and drying."
And the wise one should perform the cremation; thereafter, the mantra becomes perfected.
Having written that mantra upon the yantra with stone-paste, camphor, and saffron, one should perform the liquefying and the knotting according to the sequence of the Varuṇa-bīja.
One should write the mantra joined with *uśīra* and *gorocanā*,
and place that written [mantra] in the midst of milk, clarified butter, honey, and water.
Through worship, recitation, and fire-offerings, the deity becomes melted and bestows the fruit [of practice].
Even if he is melted but not yet perfected, one should cause him to be awakened.
One should recite that [mantra] encapsulated by the third seed-syllable of Bālā;
thus one becomes a perfected Buddha, otherwise bring him under one's control.
p. 68) Likewise, with *kucandana*, *dāruharidrā*, *madana*, and *śilā*, the mantra should be written upon a very beautiful birch-bark leaf (*bhūrjapatra*).
If it is worn around the neck, one becomes a siddha; otherwise, perform the striking.
Having indeed recited the words in the form of upper and lower [positions], one should proceed.
In that same manner, one should meditate upon the deity who possesses both lower and higher forms.
Having written [the mantra] with the milk of the sun and having stepped upon it with the feet,
one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) day after day with the mantra in its established form.
If he is afflicted and overcome by shame, he will not indeed dry it up even if he has attained success.
One should hold the written mantra encased within the "Bāla" and the third seed-syllable in the midst of milk, or else one should perform the rite of drying.
And with two seed-syllables of Vāyu, one should write the mantra interlaced [with them];
the practitioner should then wear that around his neck, smeared with sacrificial ashes.
Or else, O Supreme Goddess, for the sake of accomplishment,
one should write the syllables of the mantra surrounded on the four sides by the fire-bīja using *pālāśa* oil; one should then wear it around the neck.
"The mantra will be effective; there is no doubt about this," so said Śaṅkara.
Thus ends the exposition on the attainment of one’s chosen mantra in the *Dīkṣāprakāśa* composed by the illustrious Maithila Jīvanātha. Now begins the worship of the five abodes (*pañcāyatanī pūjā*).
In the *Yāmala*: "When one worships Bhavānī in the center, one should worship Acyuta in the northeast,
Pañcavaktra in the southeast, and Gaṇanāyaka in the southwest."
And likewise, Tapani in the northwest; thus the sequence of worship has been declared. || 1 ||
When, however, one worships Govinda in the center, one should worship Śaṅkara in the northeast,
Gaṇanātha in the southeast, and likewise Tapanas in the southwest.
And in the northwest, Ambikā herself, the bestower of both enjoyment and liberation. || 2 ||
One should worship Śaṅkara in the center, Acyuta in the northeast,
Tapanas in the southeast, and Gaṇanāyaka in the southwest.
And in the northwest is Ambikā herself, the bestower of heaven and liberation.
When the sun is in the middle, one should worship Śaṅkara in the northeast,
and the goddess Ambikā— the ground for the means of attaining heaven— in the southeast.
When one worships Gaṇanātha in the center, one should worship Keśava in the northeast, Īśvara in the southeast, Tapanas in the southwest, and Pārvatī, the bestower of liberation, in the northwest.

In this context, the direction between the worshipper and the object of worship should be known as the East. The direction behind the deity is the West; to the right of the deity is the South; and to the left of the deity is the North.
The wise should understand that the direction between the worshipper and the object of worship is the East.
The western [direction] is behind the deity, and the southern would be to its right.
And the goddess Uttarā should be on the left of the deity, O Sovereign of the Gods.
Likewise, in the *Gaṇeśavimarśinī*:
"When Śambhu is in the center, [the deities] Hari, Naha, Hara, and Bhūdevī are in Hari; when Śaṅkara is in the center, [the deities] Śambhu, Hari, Naha, and Hara are in Śaṅkara."
In the Bhāṣya, the daughter of the Naga (Sarpa), Ravi, Hara, Gaṇeśa, Aja, and Ambikā are established.

In the Devī [chart], Viṣṇu, Hara, Ekadanta, Ravi, and Vaya [are placed] in Lambodara; in Ajeśvara, the women are from the portion of Śaṅkara and grant auspiciousness, while those arranged otherwise cause loss.
Now, the sixteen-fold, ten-fold, and five-fold modes of worship are as follows. First, the rule for the sixteen-fold worship:
the seat, welcome, water for the feet, the respectful offering (arghya), and water for sipping (ācamanīya).
The honey-mixture, the sipping of water, the bath, as well as garments and ornaments.
One should employ fragrant flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, and sandalwood in the worship; these are the sixteen services.
The rule for the sixteen modes of service (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*) in the *Kālikāpurāṇa*:
(p. 70) A seat, water for the feet, the respectful offering (*arghya*), and then water for sipping (*ācamanīya*);
honey-mixture (*madhuparka*), bathing water, clothing, sandalwood paste, and ornaments.
Flowers, incense, and a lamp; thereafter, collyrium for the eyes, as well as the food offering and water for sipping, followed by circumambulation and prostration.

These sixteen services (upacāra) have been previously specified. Now follows the rule for the ten services: water for the feet (pādya), water for the respectful offering (arghya), water for sipping (ācamanīya), fragrance, flowers, and incense.
They say that the lamp and the food offering are followed again by the water for sipping (ācamanīyaka).
And thereafter, one should always offer betel-leaf in every part of the worship.
Now, the five services (pañcopacāra):
the water for honor (arghya), fragrance, flowers, food offering (naivedya), and likewise the water for sipping (ācamana).
In the absence of material substances, one should perform everything with flowers twenty-one times.
Here, in the absence of the sixteen services (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*), there are ten services; in their absence, five services;
and in their absence, one should perform everything with flowers.
The procedure for offering flowers:
whether it be a flower, a leaf, or a fruit, that which has withered or is turned face-down [should not be offered].
This is declared to be the tooth of suffering; one should apply it exactly as it has arisen.
"Śambhu has stated that there is no fault in using a handful of flowers during worship.
Regarding the rules for the vessels for the *arghya* and other offerings, Gautama says:
"There should be three vessels for the *arghya*, and likewise three for the *pādya*."
In the same manner, the vessels for the water for sipping (ācamanīya) are also to be arranged separately.
Likewise, due to the weakness of the ritual implements, only one [type of arghya] is praised;
however, there is a necessity for both the general and the specific arghya.
And so it is said in another tantra:
One should not use a single bowl even if it belongs to Maheśvara himself;
otherwise, the mantras turn away and misfortunes arise at every step.
In this world he would be poor, and after death he would go to hell.
Now follows the necessity of offering the eight fragrances into the arghya water.
And it is said in the Śāradā:
"One should diligently offer this eightfold fragrance into the arghya vessel;
that eightfold fragrance is threefold, consisting of Śakti, Viṣṇu, and Śiva."
Sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, coraka, saffron, gorocana,
jaṭāmāṃsī, and kapi— these are known as the eight fragrances of Śakti.
Sandalwood, agallochum, hrīvera, kuṣṭha, saffron, sevyaka,
jaṭāmāṃsī, and surasī are known as the eight fragrances of Viṣṇu.
Sandalwood, agallochum, camphor,
tamāla, water, saffron, uśīra, and kuṣṭha— these they know as the eightfold fragrance of Śiva.
Then the preceptor should offer the *arghya* upon the head with the *śiras-mantra*,
and he should give the water for sipping (*ācamanīyaka*) with the *vāruṇa-mantra*.
Saying "svadhā," he should offer water for sipping three times into his lotus-like mouth;
saying "svadhā," he should offer the honey-mixture (madhuparka), and again water for sipping.
Now he describes the six-component incense (*ṣaḍaṅgadhūpa*).
In another tantra:
"Guggulu, agallochum, and sandalwood, mixed with white sugar, clarified butter, and honey."
This six-ingredient incense is always beloved by all the gods.
Now, the ten-ingredient incense: honey, musta, clarified butter, fragrance, guggulu, agallochum, realgar,
sarala resin, simha, and siddhārtha— this is desired as the ten-ingredient incense.
Now, the method for offering incense, flowers, ornaments, and lamps in the *yāmala* [tradition]:
One should present the incense, flowers, and ornaments in front;
one should offer the lamp to the right or in front, but never behind.
The incense, however, should be on the left side, either in front or not on the right;
the food offering (naivedya) should be on the right side, either in front or never behind.
In this context, the left and right sides belong to the deity and not to the practitioner;
for it is observed that one should offer incense, lamps, and excellent food before the deity.

p. 72) Now, [the lamp] mixed with ghee is for the right side, while that mixed with oil is for the left. Likewise, a white wick is excellent for the right, and a red one for the left. Thus it is stated in the *Yāmala*:
A lamp filled with ghee should be placed on the right, and one filled with oil on the left.
On the right is a white wick, and on the left is a red wick.
The established rule regarding food offerings is that they must be distinguished as either cooked or uncooked;
however, in certain cases, there is no such restriction for lamps or food offerings.

One should place the cooked milk on the left side of the deity, and the uncooked raw food on the right. Then, one should prostrate like a staff. Now, the Vedic-style mantras for the sixteen services (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*) are as follows; first, the mantra for the seat (*āsana*):
O Bhavānī, Great Goddess, bestower of all prosperity,
please accept this seat adorned with many jewels.
Now, regarding the water for washing the feet: it is very beautiful, cool, divine, and endowed with various fragrances.
Accept [this], O Goddess of the gods, Great Goddess; salutations be unto you!
Now, for the *arghya*:
"O beloved of Śiva, O highly fortunate one, O you who speak words dear to Śaṅkara!
Accept this *arghya*, O auspicious one, O Supreme Goddess, out of your compassion."
Then follows the mantra for sipping water:
"O noble and sinless lady, accompanied by Hara, please sip this pure water brought and placed in a golden pitcher."
Now, the mantra for bathing:
"O Goddess, you have been bathed by me with the waters of the Gaṅgā, Sarasvatī, Revā, Kāverī, and Narmadā; likewise, grant me peace."
Alternatively, regarding the garments:
"O you who are superior to all beings, delightful, and a shield against worldly shame—
please accept these two robes offered by me."
(p. 73) Now, regarding sandalwood:
"May this sandalwood, ground with camphor and agallochum, combined with saffron and other substances, and joined with musk, be accepted."
Now, the mantra for the unbroken grains (akṣata):
"O Goddess Pārvatī, these most beautiful unbroken grains have been colored by a profusion of flowers; through the offering of them, be gracious to me."
Now, the mantra for the ornaments:
"O bestower of all desires, please accept with supreme affection these various ornaments made of jewels and pearls."

Now, O Sovereign of the World, I worship you with flowers— sanmallikā, bakula, campaka, pāṭala, lotus, punnāga, jāti, karavīra, and mango blossoms— as well as with bilva sprouts and various pure mālatī flowers.
Be gracious to me.
Now, the incense mantra:
"O Bhavānī, this incense produced from the sap of celestial trees and endowed with black aloe-wood has been brought by me; please accept it."
Now, for the lamp:
"You are the light of all the gods, the supreme splendor among all splendors;
you are the self-luminous, supreme abode—may this lamp be accepted."
The mantra for the gift of collyrium:
"O Great Goddess, adorn both eyes with unguent and black collyrium;
O Supreme Sovereign, ocean of compassion for gods and asuras, protect me!"
Now, regarding the food offering (naivedya): May this food offering— consisting of various kinds of delicious food endowed with the six tastes, and comprising both hard and soft foods— be accepted.
Then, the water for sipping (ācamanīya) is offered as before. (p.
74) Now follows the mantra for the betel leaf:
"Combined with camphor, cardamom, cloves, and other ingredients, together with betel leaves..."
Please accept this betel nut and the betel leaf as well.
Then one should offer the *ārārtika* (the waving of lights):
"O Moon and Sun, Earth, Lightning, and likewise Fire—
you who are the very essence of all splendors— please accept this *ārārtika*."
Thus end the sixteen traditional services (*paurāṇika-ṣoḍaśopacāra*). Now follows the rule for the sixteen Tantric services (*tāntrika-ṣoḍaśopacāra*). Therein, first is the word of welcome:
"I have achieved my purpose; I am favored; my life has become fruitful."
O Goddess of the gods, you have arrived; this is your welcome once again.
Now, for the water for washing the feet (pādya): one should cast śyāmāka, viṣṇukrāntā, lotus, and dūrvā grass into the water for the feet.
One should offer this pādya at the lotus-feet with the root verses and the *namaḥ* mantras.
To those lotus feet of yours, from contact with even a fragment of whose devotion the arising of supreme bliss occurs, I offer water for the feet.
Now, regarding the sipping of water (ācamana): having placed cloves, nutmeg, and betel nut therein, one should place it in the mouth.
The mantra is:
"To the one who is the Veda even of the Vedas, the divine self of the gods..."
O Sovereign, I prepare this rinsing-water for the sake of the purification of the pure.

Then, having placed dūrvā grass, sesame seeds, darbha grass, mustard seeds, unbroken rice grains (akṣata), and flowers into the arghya vessel, one should offer the arghya water upon the head. The mantra is as follows:
"The divine [water], which removes the threefold suffering and is characterized by supreme bliss..."
I offer this arghya to you, which is completely free from the three kinds of suffering.
Now, the mantra for the honey-mixture (madhuparka):
"O Goddess, who art free from all impurity and whose nature is perfect bliss, I offer this honey-mixture to you; be gracious unto me."
(p. 75) The mantra for sipping water again:
"To him by whose mere remembrance one becomes pure even if defiled or impure—to him, [O Lord], be this water for sipping again."
It is prescribed that [the name of the deity] should be remembered at the conclusion of the bath, the garments, and the sacred thread, as well as at the end of the food offering (naivedya).
However, in the absence of substances such as water for the feet (pādya) and so forth, one should remember [the deity] and scatter unbroken grains of rice (akṣata).
Now, the mantra for the offering of fragrant oil:
"O Goddess worshipped by gods and asuras, accept this oil with affection; O bestower of the fulfillment of the aims of devotees, I offer this supreme oil."
Now, the bath:
O Ocean of Supreme Bliss and Awareness, O Goddess worshipped by the gods, O Beloved of Hara, I offer this bath along with its primary and secondary limbs upon you who are moistened [by the water].
Then, while reciting the mantra, one should sprinkle the Goddess with water mixed with fragrances using a vessel with a thousand openings, or a hundred, or even according to one's capacity. Then:
Having recited the root mantra, one should then offer two verses along with a garment and a sacred thread—
one variegated with many colors and adorned with pearls and gems.
I provide for you a dwelling of unobstructed consciousness,
depending upon which Mahāmāyā, the perpetual deluder of the world, resides.
To you, who possess supreme sovereignty, I offer this upper garment.
Now, the mantra for the ornaments:
O Goddess, refuge of manifold powers, O fair-limbed Queen of the Gods!
I fashion various ornaments for you, O one worshipped by the immortals.
Now, the mantra for incense: One should offer the incense placed in the vessel with the little finger, reciting this:
"O you who completely fill the quarters of space with the fragrance of supreme bliss!"
O Supreme Goddess, out of compassion, please accept this supreme fragrance.

"This fragrance is for [Name] Devatā; obeisance. Then, one should display the fragrance mudrā with the little finger and the thumb. Next is the flower mantra: having recited the root mantra and taken up the flowers.
"Let this wonderful flower be taken— it is born from the fourth forest, enchanting with its manifold qualities, and possesses intense fragrance."
"Vauṣaṭ to such-and-such deity for these flowers.
Then, one should display the flower-mudrā with the index finger and thumb. Now, a special rule:
a wise person should not offer unhusked rice, the *arka* plant, or the *dhattūra* plant to Viṣṇu.
Bandhūka, ketakī, kunda, kesara, kuṭaja, and japā;
A wise man should not offer *mālatī* or even *yūthikā* to Śaṅkara;
nor should he offer *dūrvā*, arka, mandāra, *mālūra*, or *antagara* to the Sun, even if he is able to do so.
A wise person should never offer *tulasī* to Vināyaka.

Having thus performed the worship with flowers, one should perform the worship of the deities of the enclosure (*āvaraṇadevatā*). Then, one should offer the worship of the deities of the enclosure with this [mantra]:
"O You who are affectionate toward those who have come for refuge, grant me the fulfillment of my desired goal;
with devotion, I offer this worship of the enclosures unto You."

Then, having washed one's hand, one should arrange the subsequent offerings. Then, one should place the incense burner on the left side of the deity. Then, having washed the incense burner with "phaṭ" and offered a flower with "namaḥ," one should touch it with the left index finger while reciting the root mantra and the verse.
This divine incense, the essence of the forest-king, rich in fragrance and the most excellent scent, fit to be smelled by all the gods— may it be accepted.

Having recited this, saying "I offer incense to my chosen deity, together with her limbs, aspects, and retinue; *namaḥ*," one should pour the water from the conch onto the ground and display the incense mudrā by joining the index finger and the thumb.

With the mantra "Jayadhvani," and having worshipped the bell with "Mātaḥ svāhā," while ringing it with the left hand and proclaiming the qualities of the deity, one should fumigate the deity from the region of the navel with the right hand.
Now, the procedure for the lamp:

A ghee lamp should be placed on the right side of the deity, and an oil lamp should be placed on the left side of the deity. Then, having consecrated the lamp vessel with "phaṭ" and offered a flower with "namaḥ," [one should proceed].
Touching it with the left middle finger and reciting the root mantra:
"This great lamp, self-luminous, dispelling darkness everywhere,
the light that shines both outside and within— may this lamp be accepted."
"To [Name] Devatā, together with the limbs and the retinue, I offer a lamp; homage!

Having poured the water from the conch onto the ground and displayed the lamp-mudrā by joining the middle finger and the thumb, while sounding the bell as before, [one should worship] from the eyes down to the feet.
One should display a lamp.
Now, regarding the offering of the food oblation (naivedya):

having placed the naivedya in a vessel, sprinkled it with water while reciting the root mantra, and protected it with the *cakramudrā*, one should [sprinkle it] twelve times with water consecrated by the seed-syllable of air (*vāyubīja*).

Having sprinkled [the offering] with water and dried up its defects by means of the air arising therefrom, one should contemplate the fire-seed syllable (*vahnibīja*) on the palm of the right hand; then,

placing the palm of the left hand against the back of the right, one should burn away the defects of the food offering (*naivedya*) with the fire arising therefrom, and meditate upon nectar (*amṛta*) on the back of the left hand.
Having taken the right hand and displayed it, having meditated upon all that as being of the nature of nectar,
having touched it and recited the root mantra eight times, having displayed the *dhenumudrā*,
having worshipped with water, fragrance, and flowers, and having offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) to the deity;

Having meditated that light has issued forth from his mouth, and having touched the vessel of the food offering with the left thumb and grasped it with the right hand, one should recite the root mantra:
"The excellent vessel contains the perfected, well-prepared oblation, a variety of foods to be consumed."
"I offer this, O Queen of Gods; you, together with your attendants, accept it.

Having recited this verse, one should offer the food offering (naivedya) with the words: "I offer this food offering to the venerable [Name] Deity, along with her limbs (aṅga), retinue, and entourage; obeisance! Then, having sprinkled water, one should [offer it] with the thumb and ring finger.
One should display the *naivedya-mudrā*.

Then, one should offer water into the hand of the Goddess with the mantra: "Oṃ amṛtopastaraṇam asi svāhā. Thereafter, having displayed the *grāsa-mudrā*, which resembles a full-blown blue lotus, with the left hand, [one should proceed] with the right hand.

One should display the mudrās for the vital breaths and so forth, accompanied by their mantras. For example: *oṃ prāṇāya svāhā*, with the thumb, little finger, and ring finger; *oṃ apānāya svāhā*, with the thumb, index finger, and middle finger; *oṃ vyānāya svāhā*.
With the ring finger, middle finger, and thumb: *oṃ vyānāya svāhā*. With the ring finger, middle finger, and thumb: *oṃ udānāya svāhā*.
With the thumb, index finger, middle finger, and ring finger: *oṃ samānāya svāhā*.

"By all of them" means: then, one should meditate upon the Goddess, who is praised by Brahmā, Īśa, and the others, fanned with chowries by celestial maidens like the moon, and making the hosts of enjoyers laugh— at this juncture.

One should perform the *pūjāṅgahoma* (the fire-offering as an auxiliary to worship). Now, regarding the obligatory nature of the *homa*, it is stated in the *Somabhujagāvalī*: "A mantra is not perfected if it is not recited; it does not bestow fruit if it is not offered in sacrifice; it does not grant desired objects if it is not worshipped [with fire]; therefore, one should honor these three."
Through worship, worship is obtained; through recitation, accomplishment is attained without a doubt.
Through the fire-ritual, divine power is gained; all accomplishments are achieved without a doubt.
As it has been said:
"Having established the fire upon the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila), one should perform the Vaiśvadeva rite;
having inspected it with the Mūla-mantra and performed sprinkling and striking with the Astra-mantra."
Having sprinkled that pure armor with *kuśa* grass as before, one should establish it;
then, having worshipped it with its own mantra, one should invoke the chosen deity there.
Then one should worship her with perfumes and flowers,
having offered four oblations with the Great Vyāhṛtis, both individually and collectively.
One should offer oblations with food and the root mantra twenty-five times;
having offered again with the vyāhṛtis, one should then unite the Goddess with the image.
"Having cast the fire [into the hearth], one should offer water for sipping (ācamanīyaka) to the deity.

Then, having prepared there a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) measuring the span of one's own right hand and four fingers high, one should gaze upon it with the root mantra, sprinkle it with "phaṭ," and strike it with those same kuśa grasses.

Having sprinkled [the fire] with the *hum* mantra, having taken up the fire with the root mantra and grasped a portion of it, one should cast it into the southwest corner, saying: *oṃ kravyādebhyo namaḥ*. Then, having established the fire with the root mantra, having rendered it nectarine with *vam*, having veiled it with *hum*, and having protected it with *phaṭ*: *oṃ*...
Having worshipped the fire with the mantra: "O Vaiśvānara Jātavedas, bring [the deity] here; O red-eyed one, accomplish all rites, svāhā!
he should then invoke his chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) there, worship it with clarified butter, and offer oblations with:
*oṃ bhūḥ svāhā*; *oṃ bhuvaḥ svāhā*; *oṃ svaḥ svāhā*; *oṃ bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svaḥ*.

"svāhā! Having thus offered oblations, having offered twenty-five times with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*), and having again offered with the *vyāhṛtis*, one should unite the deity with the image and dismiss the fire.
O Fire, O you of great power, accomplisher of all rites!
"Even when another task arises, please remain present with respect."

Having performed the dismissal (*visarjana*) and offered water for sipping (*ācamana*) to the deity, one should contemplate that the splendor which had entered the deity’s mouth has now emerged from it once more; then, having offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) and prostrated, one should perform the recitation (*japa*).
It is as follows: having performed the ritual placement of the seers and so forth (*ṛṣyādinyāsa*), one should contemplate the *kula-kā* [syllable] upon the head.
Having recited [the mantra] ten times and performed worship, one should take the rosary and sprinkle it with *arghya* water in a vessel,
[reciting]: "O *mālā*, O *mālā*, O great *mālā*, you whose nature is all powers!"
"The fourfold aim has been entrusted to you; therefore, grant me success."

Having worshipped [the rosary] with incense and other offerings, and having grasped it with the right hand while reciting the mantra "O Rosary, grant me freedom from obstacles," one should bring the rosary near the heart while meditating on the Guru at the head and one's chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā) in the heart,
and place it upon the middle joint of the middle finger of the right hand.
Having placed [the rosary] and uttered the *praṇava*, one should recite the *mālā-mantra*. Then, having completed the recitation by uttering "Oṃ" once more:
"O Rosary, you are considered the bestower of delight and the giver of auspiciousness to all the gods."
"O auspicious lady, always perform what is beneficial for me, as well as that which brings fame and valor."

Having placed the rosary on one's own head with the mantra "Hrīṃ Siddhyai Namaḥ," and having again performed three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma) and the sixfold ritual placement (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) beginning with the seer (ṛṣi), [one should place it] in the left hand of the Goddess with water for the offering (arghya).
"You are the guardian of the secret, more secret than the secret; accept this recitation performed by us.
O Great Goddess, may accomplishment be mine through your grace."
