Having offered the recitation (*japa*) before the Goddess, one should scatter a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*). Then, one should set aside the rosary. Thereafter, having recited the armor-verse (*kavaca*) and other hymns and offered a handful of flowers, one should say:
"Whatever has been done and whatever has been spoken prior to this, may all that be an offering to Brahman for the sake of the deity [named] so-and-so."

Then, having performed the recitation for peace (śāntipāṭha), one should worship with the remains of the offering (nirmālya) placed on the left side; having applied the paste from the yantra to the head, one may discard the remains of the offering.
Thus ends the section on the sixteen modes of service (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*) in the *Dīkṣāprakāśa* composed by Śrī Jīvanātha.
(p. 80) Now, concerning Kulukā:
the Śrīdevī said:
"O Deva, what is Kukulā like? And O Nātha, what is the Setu like?"
What is the Great Bridge like, and what is even Nirvana like?
"Or whatever else has been spoken, O God—tell me what that was like, O Lord.
The Lord said: "O Goddess, this which is more secret than the most secret is being told out of affection for you."
O Great Goddess, without which recitation and other practices become fruitless.
The *kulukā* of Tārā, O Goddess, is Mahānīlasarasvatī;
the five-syllabled mantra of Kālikā is declared to be her *kulukā*.
O Parameśvarī, the mantra of Kālīkūrca consists of *vadhū* and *māyā*, ending with *phaṭ*. O Supreme Goddess, for Chinnā, the *kulukā* becomes three syllables.
And at the end of Vajravairocanī, one should proclaim the armor-mantra (varman);
it is considered the *kulukā* of Bhairavī, the first [deity] who bestows prosperity (*sampat*).
The twelve-syllable Kulukā mantra of the illustrious Tripurasundarī consists of the Vāgbhava seed-syllable as the first, followed by the Kāmarāja.
After that, the seed-syllable of Laṅjā (hrīṃ), then Tripureśī, and thereafter the word "Bhagavatī"; at the end, one should utter the two ṭha-syllables (ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ).
But for others, O Great Goddess, the *kulukā* is considered to consist of three syllables;
having uttered the *tāra* and the *kūrca*, one should then utter the *nārasiṃha*.
Thus, O Goddess, this Kulukā has been described by me in brief.
O Goddess, that lowest of men who recites the mantra without knowing the Kulukā [is lost].
One quickly meets with death and the loss of spiritual accomplishment occurs;
the mantras turn away and the failure of the mantra arises.
In that case, all [practices] such as recitation (japa) and so forth are fruitless; there is no doubt about this.
Therefore, with every effort, one should recite Kullakā upon the head.
O Supreme Goddess, his mantra-siddhi shall be swift; it is not otherwise. [The mantras are:
Hrīṃ strīṃ hūṃ for Tārā; Krīṃ haṃ strīṃ hrīṃ phaṭ for Kālikā; Oṃ hūṃ kṣrauṃ for Chinnamastā; and [the mantra] for Tripurabhairavī.

Vajravairocanīye hūṃ! Śrītripurasundaryāḥ aiṃ klīṃ hrīṃ tripureśi bhagavati svāhā! For other vidyās, the *kuluka* is to be known as *oṃ hraṃ kṣrauṃ*. The *praṇava* alone is the bridge for all vidyās and is to be meditated upon in the heart.
The Great Bridge (*mahāsetu*) is the root mantra (*mūlamantra*). It should be recited in the region of the throat. As for the Nirvāṇa [mantra]:
*oṃ aṃ mūlaṃ aiṃ aṃ āṃ iṃ īṃ uṃ ūṃ ṛṃ ṝṃ ḷṃ ḹṃ eṃ aiṃ oṃ auṃ aṃ aḥ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ ṭaṃ*.
Ṭhaṃ, ḍaṃ, ḍhaṃ, ṇaṃ, taṃ, thaṃ, daṃ, dhaṃ, naṃ, paṃ, phaṃ, baṃ, bhaṃ, maṃ, yaṃ, raṃ, laṃ, vaṃ, śaṃ, ṣaṃ, saṃ, haṃ, jñaṃ, kṣaṃ, oṃ— thus, Nirvāṇa is to be contemplated at the region of the navel.
And it is said in the Mahātantra:
"Oṃ is the bridge of all vidyās, the great bridge, and the root.
Having first extracted the Praṇava, immediately thereafter [comes] that which begins with a vowel."
O Goddess, O Sovereign of the Gods, one should then contemplate the Vāgbhava, followed by the Mātṛkā, and then Nirvāṇa within the Oṃkāra mantra.
O Goddess of the Gods, having recited the *setu* at the heart,
one should then contemplate the *mahāsetu* at the region of the throat, and subsequently *nirvāṇa* at the navel.
Then, having performed the six-limbed placement (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) and meditated, one should recite the mantra;
O Goddess of the Gods, when this is done, the perfection of the mantra arises.
Thus ends the section on the secret method in the *Śrī-Dīkṣāprakāśa*.
Now follows the method for the *śivābali* offering.
And so it is stated in the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*:
One must certainly and invariably satisfy Śivā with the gift of food,
just as one performs the daily śrāddha, the twilight rites, the application of sandalwood paste, and the libations for the ancestors.
In the same way, the worship of the family deities is a constant duty during the family ritual;
he who does not worship the goddess Paśupāśivā in a secluded place [is at fault].
By the howling of jackals, all of that— whatever meritorious deeds have been performed through the practice of recitation and worship— will certainly perish instantly.
Having seized him and delivered a curse, Śivā weeps in solitude;
for if she is enjoyed by only one Śivā there, O Bhairavī.
At that very time, when one is beset by fear of kingship and the like, or by fear of foreign lands and so forth, the favor of all the Śaktis is exceedingly difficult to obtain.
Having reflected upon auspicious and inauspicious actions,
one should offer the bali-oblation at the root of a bilva tree, in a wilderness, in a cremation ground, or outside the city.
One should offer the principal oblation of meat at the time of twilight;
for while one should say "Kālī, Kālī," there Umā is present in the form of Śiva.
She proceeds in the form of a beast together with her retinue of attendants.
Then, facing north, he should make this formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*): "Oṃ, at this twilight, I, belonging to such-and-such a lineage (*gotra*..."

Having made the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*)— "I shall perform the offering to the Śivās for the sake of [the success or failure of] such-and-such a glorious undertaking"— and having performed breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), the ritual placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*), and established the water for libation (*arghya*),
he should take food fit for consumption and, with his hair loose, slowly invoke the Śivās.
With the mantra "Kālikāli," one then says:
"O Goddess, O highly fortunate Śivā, whose form is the fire of time (kālāgni), accept this;
reveal clearly the fruit of good and evil, and accept your offering."
Having thus offered the arghya water and then stepped back slightly while the auspicious [beings] are eating:
Oṃ, salutation to Saṃhārabhairava 1. Oṃ, salutation to the Baṭukas 2. Oṃ, salutation to the Vināyakas 3. Oṃ, salutation to the Mothers 4. Oṃ Kṣauṃ.
"Salutation to the guardians of the field (kṣetrapālas) 5; Oṃ, salutation to the yoginīs 6; Oṃ, salutation to the ḍākinīs 7;

Oṃ, salutation to the messengers of Śiva (śivadūtīs) 8. Having thus offered these eight oblations (balis), and taking handfuls of fragrant flowers, he should rise with his hair loose and naked, with eyes closed.
One should recite the hymn of praise:
"O Goddess who bears the form of Śivā, O Guhyakālī, obeisance be to you! O Ulkāmukhī, with your lolling tongue and terrible roar, O Śṛgālinī!"
O dweller in the cremation ground, O ghost, O you who delight in the flesh of corpses, O sinless one!
O blameless one who wanders in the forest, O auspicious one in the form of a jackal,
salutations to you, O Mahāmāyā, O Kālikā, savior of the world!
O Mātaṅgī, O Kukkuṭī, O Raudrī, O Mahākālī, homage be to you! O bestower of all accomplishments, O terrible one, O inspirer of fear, O remover of fear!
Be gracious, O Goddess of gods, toward me, your devotee, O Caṇḍikā;
victory to you, who are intent on ferrying beings across the ocean of worldly existence and who bring about all that is auspicious!
O fierce Cāmuṇḍā with disheveled hair, garlanded with severed heads,
wrathful bringer of destruction, grant me all spiritual accomplishments!
O Durgā, Kirātī, Śabarī, seated upon a corpse and free from fear, grant me your grace always; look upon me with compassion.
O Vikaṭā, grant me sovereignty, wealth, long life, sons, and a wife;
O Īśvarī, may you become gracious through this offering of the Śivā-bali.
"Salutations to you, salutations to you, salutations to you, salutations be to you!
Having recited this, one should bury the remnants of the food and the vessel in the ground.
Furthermore, at the time of eating, the auspicious or inauspicious results should be understood according to the sounds of the jackal (*śivā*).
It is stated in that very same work:

"If, after eating, one raises the face toward the northeast and cries out in a loud voice, one should know that at that very moment there is auspiciousness; otherwise, there is no worship of the Kula."
When an object is not being enjoyed, it cannot be auspicious;
if it were auspicious there, it would be enjoyed in its entirety.
In this matter, a virtuous brahmin should offer a bean-cake (*māṣavaṭaka*) in place of meat;
for it is said that a virtuous person should never, under any circumstances, cause the killing of a living being.
Then, having entered the house, one should worship the Goddess.
Now, the substances for the secondary ritual (anukalpa) are as stated in the Śaktisaṅgamatantra:
"One should regard the kūṣmāṇḍa fruit as a buffalo and the karkaṭī fruit as a goat."
One should give a *vṛntāka* gourd as a cock, a *tumbikā* as a ram,
a *panasa* fruit as a human, a sugarcane stalk as a fish,
a *śūraṇa* root as a donkey, and a *kośaka* as a deer.
One must offer milk-rice (pāyasa) for the state of being an elephant, horse-gram (kulutthaka) for the state of being a cat,
patola for the state of being a boar, and likewise sugar for the state of being a sand-creature.
O Great Goddess, when he is a rhinoceros, [the offering is] a sword; when a fish, a plantain fruit;
when a mouse, a radish; and when a crane, a *kaliṅgaka* fruit.
For the state of a parrot, a coconut is used; for the state of a fish, a plantain;
and for all types of bali offerings, black gram and kṛśara rice are likewise prescribed.
Thus ends the section on the method of the Śivābali in the *Dīkṣāprakāśa* composed by the venerable Jīvanātha.
Now follows the method for the sixteen Vedic services (*upacāra*) for Viṣṇu.
Therein, first is the mantra for the seat (*āsana*):

Oṃ. The Puruṣa has a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, and a thousand feet. Having pervaded the earth on all sides, he transcends it by ten fingers' breadth. This is the mantra for sitting down. The Puruṣa alone is all this—whatever has been and whatever is to be. Moreover, he is the Lord of immortality, which surpasses that which grows through food.
Now the mantra for the water for the feet (*pādya*):
*oṃ etāvānasya mahimāto jyāyāṃśca puruṣaḥ | pādo 'sya viśvā bhūtāni tripādasyāmṛtaṃ divi ||*
The Arghya Mantra:
The Puruṣa rose up, three-quarters of him being above; one-quarter of him came to be here again. From there he strode out in all directions, toward that which eats and that which does not eat.
The mantra for sipping water (*ācamana*):
"From that, Virāj was born; from Virāj, Puruṣa was born as its lord. Once born, he extended beyond [the world], behind the earth and also before it."
The bathing mantra:
"From that sacrifice in which everything was offered, the speckled butter was gathered."
He made the domestic animals [his] sacrificial fees: those belonging to Vāyu, those belonging to the forest, and those that are domestic.
(p. 85) Now follows the mantra for covering:
From that sacrifice in which everything was offered, the *ṛg* verses and the *sāman* chants were born; the meters were born.
From that the Yajus was born;
from that the mantra for the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) was born. From that horses were born, and whatever animals have two rows of teeth; from that cows were indeed born.
From him were born goats and sheep.
The mantra for the fragrant offering:
"Upon the sacrificial grass at the sacrifice, they sprinkled the Puruṣa who was born first; by him the gods..."
The Sādhyas and the Ṛṣis performed the sacrifice. Now, the mantra for the flower:
"When they divided Puruṣa, into how many parts did they arrange him? [What was] his mouth?"
What was his mouth? What were his arms? What were his thighs? His feet are now being described. [The incantation for the incense:
"The Brāhmaṇa was his mouth; his arms were made into the Rājanya; his thighs were..."
From his feet, the Vaiśya and the Śūdra were born.
Now, the mantra for the lamp:
From [his] mind the moon was born; from [his] eye the sun was born; and from [his] ear, the wind.
And from his breath, fire was born from his mouth.
The mantra for the food offering:
From his navel the intermediate space arose; from his head the sky evolved; from his feet...
From his ear, they fashioned the earth, the directions, and likewise the worlds.
This is the mantra for joining the palms in reverence:
"When the gods performed the sacrifice with the Puruṣa as the oblation, the spring was its clarified butter."
Summer is the fuel, autumn is the oblation.
Now follows the mantra for circumambulation:
"Seven were your enclosing-sticks; thrice seven were the fuel-sticks prepared. O gods..."
When they bound the Puruṣa as the sacrificial animal with the sacrificial cord, then follows the mantra for the dismissal:
"By means of sacrifice the gods sacrificed to the sacrifice; those were the first ordinances."
Their glories abide where the ancient Sādhyas, the gods, dwell.
Thus ends the method for the sixteen-fold service (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*) of Viṣṇu in the *Dīkṣāprakāśa*.
Now, he describes the procedure for reciting the *Saptaśatī* in the *Vāsavītantra*:
Having established the support, one should then recite the book;
for, O Goddess, by merely holding it in the hand, half the fruit is obtained.
One should not cease reciting until the chapter is completed;
however, O beloved, if an interruption occurs in the middle of a chapter due to negligence, one must stop.
One should begin again from the beginning and recite everything repeatedly;
O Goddess, one should recite in proper sequence and avoid shaking the head and other such gestures.
Furthermore, elsewhere it is said:
"Having first uttered the *praṇava*, one should recite either a hymn or a *saṃhitā*;
and at the end, one should place the *praṇava*—so spoke the Primordial Being."

One should not recite a hymn mentally; rather, the oral recitation is praised. One should not recite a hymn written by oneself, nor one written by a non-Brāhmaṇa, nor a hymn composed by oneself, nor one composed by another.
For that which is praised by the sages in the Kali age, and that which is contemplated by them;
Furthermore:
Whatever is written by oneself, whatever is written by another scholar,
and whatever is written by one who is not a Brahmin— all that shall be fruitless.
"The wise man, having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the seer (*ṛṣi*), the meter (*chandas*), the deity (*devatā*), and so forth, should recite the hymn.
However, in the *Kīlaka-grantha*, it says:
"On the eighth or the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, being well-composed..."
"He gives and he receives; otherwise, she is not pleased."
"Thus, by means of this wedge (kīla) of Mahādeva, [the door] is pinned shut.
Having first recited the bolt (argala) and the wedge (kīlaka), one should recite the armor (kavaca).
"Then one should recite the Saptashati; this is the sequence declared by Śiva.

Oṃ. Of this first chapter, Brahmā is the seer (ṛṣi), Gāyatrī is the meter (chandas), Mahākālī is the deity (devatā), Nandajā is the power (śakti), Raktadantikā is the seed-syllable (bīja), and Fire is the principle (tattva).

"May this be applied to the recitation for the pleasure of Mahākālī. Having said this, one should recite the first chapter. Then: "Oṃ; for the middle narrative, Viṣṇu is the seer (*ṛṣi*), the *uṣṇik* meter (*chanda*), Lakṣmī is the deity (*devatā*), Śākambharī is the power (*śakti*), Durgā is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), and Vāyu is the principle (*tattva*). [This is] for the sake of pleasing Mahālakṣmī."

"Jape viniyogaḥ. Having recited this, one should recite the second chapter, the third chapter, and the fourth chapter. Then, for the subsequent section (*uttaracaritra*), the seer is Rudra, the meter is *triṣṭubh*, the deity is Mahāsarasvatī, the seed-syllable is *klīṃ*, and the principle is *ravi*; [this is used] for the sake of pleasing Mahāsarasvatī.
This is the application for the recitation (*japa*).
And it has been said:
"In the first chapter of the *Saptasatī-caritra*, the sage Padmabhū—"
The meter is declared to be Gāyatrī, and Mahākālī is the deity.
The seed-syllable of speech (vāk) is the element of fire (pāvaka), which is applied for the sake of dharma and artha;
the seed-syllable of speech is "ai," and the fire is "ram.
Regarding the middle conduct, however, the sage Vaṣṇu has been proclaimed.
The meter is Uṣṇik, the deity is Mahālakṣmī, and the seed-syllable is Bhadrikā.
The element is air (vāyu), and its application is declared to be for the attainment of wealth;
the seed-syllables are *adrijā*, *hrīṃ*, and the air-seed *yaṃ*.
For the *uttaracaritra*, Śaṅkara is declared to be the seer (*ṛṣi*);
the meter (*chandas*) is *uṣṇih*; the deity (*devatā*) is Mahāsarasvatī;
the seed-syllable (*bīja*) is *kāma*; the principle (*tattva*) is the Sun; and its application (*viniyoga*) is for the attainment of desire.
"Kāma" is *klīm*; "Ravi" is the seed-syllable *praṇava*—so say those who know the mantras.
Having thus recollected the sages and others, and having meditated upon them according to the previously mentioned method,
one should recite the Caṇḍī-stava with clear syllables while keeping its meaning in mind.
At the conclusion, however, having meditated upon Mahālakṣmī and performed the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*),
one should recite the root mantra one hundred and eight times and offer it to the deity.
At the beginning, one should also recite the root mantra one hundred and eight times; here, however, the root mantra is: *aiṃ hrīṃ klīṃ cāmuṇḍāyai vicce*. In the Rudrayāmala it is said:
"The first deed is proclaimed as the slaying of Madhu and Kaiṭabha."
Know that the second deed was the slaying of the demon Mahiṣāsura.
The subsequent life-story, including the slaying of the Daitya Śumbha, should be known;
one should recite these three life-stories along with their secret portions without sloth.
Elsewhere it is also said:
"One should recite the nine-syllable mantra a hundred times at the beginning and a hundred times at the end;
this is declared to be the 'encasement' (sampuṭa) within the Caṇḍīsaptaśatī."
The *sampuṭa* [mantra] should be recited for one who has desires; for one without desires, it should be recited without the *sampuṭa*.
Now, in the Mārīca-kalpa, the sequence is as follows: one should first recite the Rātrisūkta, in the middle the Saptaśatī-stava,
and at the end the Devīsūkta should indeed be recited.

Thus, this combined hymn bestows the accomplishment of all desires and purposes. Now, as for the *Rātrisūkta* and the *Devīsūkta*, which are Vedic, authoritative scholars maintain that they are in fact included within the *Saptaśatī* hymn itself. Furthermore, there is the hymn composed by Brahmā.

The *Viśveśvarī-sūkta* is designated as the *Rātri-sūkta*. Then, beginning with "Obeisance to the Goddess, to the Great Goddess, to Śivā, constant obeisance," and ending with "all calamities [are warded off] by those whose forms are bowed in devotion," is the *Devī-sūkta*. Śakra and the other hosts of gods...
Beginning with "Thus [I praise] our [Lord]" and ending with "Obeisance to You, O Lord, who caused the enemies of the gods to become intoxicated," this is the Lakṣmīsūkta.

Beginning with "When that great lord of the asuras was slain by the Goddess" and ending with "O You who are praised by the inhabitants of the three worlds, be the bestower of boons upon the worlds," this is the Sarasvatīsūkta.
Now, in the Vārāhītantra:
Having consecrated the ground and established the jar, having filled it with water from a sacred ford and containing gold within, one should then cast the eight types of earth into it.
One desiring Dharma should cast gold; one desiring wealth, a pearl;
one desiring prosperity, a lotus; and one desiring love, one should cast yellow orpiment.
One who desires liberation should place the jewel, and one who desires the fruit of recitation should place Aparājitā.
One should use the root of the tigress plant for the purpose of eradication, and the root of the peacock plant for the purpose of subjugation.
For the purpose of killing, one should place *marīca* (black pepper) inside the jar; for delusion, *ketakī*; and for attraction, one should cast *dhattūra*.
O Maheśānī, listen as I speak; recite the mantra beginning from the very start. The sequence of emanation (sṛṣṭikrama) is described here.
The sequence of recitation begins from Indra and extends up to the slaying of the demon Śumbha;
this is declared to be the order of the manifestation (sthiti-krama) from the beginning to the end, starting with Indra.

Beginning from the remainder [of the sequence] up to the beginning and end, the process of withdrawal (saṃhāra) has been described. For all ritual activities, the recitation follows the order of maintenance (sthiti); however, for one who desires liberation, there is no withdrawal.
The sequence of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*) is proclaimed for one desiring prosperity (*śrī*) and for one desiring nourishment (*puṣṭi*).

The reading beginning with "Sāvarṇi, the son of the Sun" and ending with "Sāvarṇi shall be the Manu" constitutes the sequence of emanation. Having recited the nine chapters beginning with "In ancient times, O Śumbha... [and so forth].
The established order of recitation is that one should recite up to the end of the chapter on Śakra.

Thus, having obtained the boon from the Goddess, and so forth, the order of dissolution (saṃhārakrama) consists of reciting up to the verse ending with "Sāvarṇi, the son of the Sun. This is the recitation.
"In times of distress, [the fire] is praised"—so say the Southerners.
Now he states the specific rule: "One should offer oblations to Kāma first among Dharma, Artha, Kāma, and Mokṣa."
For the rites of enchantment and killing, one should perform the oblation facing the southern direction.
For the rite of eradication (*uccāṭana*), one should face north; such is the arrangement of the directions.
For the complete attainment of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, one should offer milk-rice (*pāyasa*) into the fire.
For the rites of killing, liberation, and likewise for the rite of eradication, one should offer black gram smeared with the three sweets; for the rite of delusion, honeyed milk-rice.
For the rite of immobilization (*stambhana*), one uses the *māttulaphala* fruit; for subjugation (*vaśya*), white mustard seeds.
Furthermore, in the *Devīprayogasāra*:
"Whenever a crisis has arrived, or when there is constant fear that is difficult to cure..."
When the lineage is destroyed, the family is severed, and the destruction of one's lifespan has arrived.
In the increase of enemies, in the increase of disease, likewise in the loss of wealth and in decline;
likewise in the occurrence of the three kinds of portents, and also in the case of a great transgression.
One should perform this with effort one hundred times; from that, auspiciousness is attained.
His misfortunes perish, and in the end, he goes to the supreme state.
There is an increase of prosperity through a hundredfold repetition, and likewise a supreme increase of sovereignty;
O Goddess, whatever is conceived in the mind, one hundred and eight [recitations] bring it to fulfillment.
O lady of virtuous vows, one obtains the fruit of a hundred horse-sacrifices;
by reciting it a thousand times, Lakṣmī herself always attends upon one.
Having attained the desires residing within the mind, a person may obtain liberation,
just as the Aśvamedha is among sacrifices or as Hari is among the gods.
Among all hymns of praise, the Saptashati hymn is likewise supreme;
for those men who recite it with pure accuracy, worldly enjoyment and liberation are not far off.
O lady of beautiful countenance, there is no hymn of praise superior to this.
Now follows the procedure for the Navarātra.
Hereafter, I shall fully explain the ritual of the Navarātra:
one should perform the recitation with an increase of one [mantra] per day for nine days.
Having worshipped according to the ritual of the nine-syllabled mantra, the wise one should recite the mantra a thousand times every day in accordance with the prescribed rules.
Having performed the fire-oblation (homa) there with a tenth part [of the total recitation], one shall attain success.
Furthermore: Seated at the root of a bilva tree, the wise person should perform japa for one month.
The practitioner [should worship] with bilva leaves combined with the three sweets (madhuratraya).
Or one may perform it for a month according to the rules of the fire-oblation, or for a tenth part of that time;
by offering lotuses mixed with milk, the attainment of Lakṣmī is certain, without a doubt.

(p. 91) However, the traditional teaching (sampradāya) is that the fire-oblation (homa) should be performed here with exactly one-tenth [of the total] using the mantras beginning with *namo devyai*. Regarding the payment of fees (*dakṣiṇā*) for the officiating Brahmins, the rule is stated in that very same place:
"In the case of five repetitions, one gold coin; in the case of three repetitions, half of that."
"A wise man should give one quarter [of the fee] for a single performance, or according to his capacity."
The Gāyatrī as it appears in the Yajurveda: "We know Kātyāyanī; we meditate upon the maiden Kumārī; may that Durgā inspire us."

Now, another ritual application from the Kātyāyanī-tantra: Having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in the forenoon measuring sixteen finger-breadths in length and four finger-breadths in height,
one should [place] thirteen Rudra-wicks in a single vessel there with pure cow’s ghee.
Having lit the lamps, one should invoke the deity of the first chapter into the first lamp, perform worship beginning with the seat and water for the feet and ending with the offering of fragrance,
and at the time of offering flowers, [recite] the nine verses to be mentioned hereafter.

Having offered a handful of flowers, presented incense and lamps, and performed the lustration ceremony (*nīrājana*), one should feed a single Brāhmaṇa, a young girl, and a married woman, or alternatively, make a formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*). In this manner, for each chapter, the ritual begins with the invocation of the deity of that chapter and concludes with the feeding of the Brāhmaṇas.

One should perform [the rite]. At the conclusion, a great worship (mahāpūjā) with abundant offerings of food (naivedya) and other articles should be performed. In the case of favoring (anugraha), the completion occurs in the forenoon;
in the case of subjugating (nigraha), the completion occurs in the afternoon. As for the verses: "To Viśveśvarī, the sustainer of the world...
praised by the gods in the past as the refuge of desired goals... she who now..."

And that which is remembered as "coddhata" destroys us at that very moment. "The pacifier of all afflictions"—here, in the phrase "the destroyer of enemies," one should understand it to mean "the destroyer of diseases";
the same applies to the phrase "by those tormented by the Daityas. [She who is] "the most auspicious among all auspicious things" regarding creation, maintenance, and destruction.
7. To the one who has gone for refuge, the wretched and the afflicted; 8. O you whose nature is all, the Lord of all; 9. These nine verses are for the purpose of grace (*anugraha*).

However, there is a specific distinction regarding subjugation (*vaśya*): *oṃ hrīṃ raktacāmuṇḍe turu turu amukaṃ me vaśamānaya svāhā*. By means of this [mantra], worship is performed at the beginning and end of each chapter, and at the conclusion of all [chapters].
There should be ten thousand recitations of the mantra and ten thousand fire-oblations.
One should offer red sandalwood and black mustard seeds with pungent oil;
by merely performing one thousand oblations, one shall bring a king under one's control.
Having offered honey and *aśoka* flowers at night as before,
one will certainly become a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) through the power of the Caṇḍī mantra.
At the conclusion, one hundred Brahmins and maidens should be fed.
For the sake of wealth, worship with bilva leaves; for the sake of subjugation, with karavīra flowers.
For the sake of obtaining a son, one should worship with hibiscus flowers (*japākusuma*) or *tulasī* leaves; for the sake of satisfaction, with lotuses (*paṅkaja*);

but in the ritual application (*prayoga*) for a great undertaking, having fashioned a golden image weighing sixteen *māṣas* and having performed the installation of the water-pot (*kalaśasthāpana*), [one should perform the rite] before that, either in a jar-and-barrier device (*ghaṭārgalayantra*) or in a hexagonal device (*ṣaṭkoṇayantra*).

One should establish a lamp. For a great undertaking, it should be maintained for forty-nine days; for a middling one, twenty-four days; and for a small one, twelve days—which is half of that. In the same manner, the quantity of gold for the image should also be understood accordingly. For a great undertaking, three Brahmins [should be employed].

The performers of the ritual practice: there is only one for minor [rites]. However, regarding the subjugation [rite], after saying "the pacification of all afflictions," one should recite "having arisen" (*samutpatya*). In this ritual practice, one should also perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*). There are thirteen vessels.
Having filled [the vessel] with milk and offered a handful of flowers at the beginning and the end, one should perform the libation for each verse using the formula:
"I satiate the deity of the first chapter. Likewise, having invoked and worshipped the deities of those respective chapters in order within the thirteen fires, one should proceed.

With the mantra "Oṃ, obeisance to the deity of the first chapter, svāhā," one should offer oblations of milk-rice (*pāyasa*) for each chapter, or one may simply recite [the chapter]. It is taught that this should be performed before lamps, heaps of unbroken rice (*akṣata*), water-vessels, fires, or young maidens. Now, regarding the recitation of this hymn:
The ritual procedure for the encapsulation (*sampuṭīkaraṇa*) of the nine-syllable mantra as taught in the *Ḍāmarakalpa*. First, its extraction (*uddhāra*):
*aiṃ*, the seed-syllable whose radiance is equal to the first moon; *hrīṃ*, the second [syllable], possessing the brilliance of the sun’s splendor.
Furthermore, the third syllable *klīṃ*, which has a form equal to Vaiśvānara (Fire), should be meditated upon for the sake of infinite bliss;
and the fifth syllable *muṃ*, possessing the luster of pure Jāmbūnada gold and resembling the sun, should be fashioned as the most excellent of praises.
The sixth is Ḍāṃ, which removes fierce suffering and is deep blue; the seventh is Yai, which is very black and destroys enemies.
The eighth is pale-white, established from the beginning; the ninth is smoke-colored and extensive.

Aiṃ Hrīṃ Klīṃ Cāmuṇḍāyai Vicce. This is the nine-syllable mantra. Its application is as follows: by reciting it one thousand times while standing in water reaching the navel, one attains the perfection of poetic composition (*kavitā*). By reciting it ten thousand times, one is liberated from imprisonment, royal peril, and other such calamities.
In this mantra of nine syllables, Mahālakṣmī is established;
therefore, it is perfectly accomplished for all and is a lamp in every direction.
By this, it is indicated that for this [mantra], there is no purification of the *siddhādicakra*.
The seers (*ṛṣi*) of the nine-syllable [mantra] are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara;
the meters (*chandas*) declared by the sages are Gāyatrī, Uṣṇih, and Anuṣṭubh.
The goddesses of this Manu are said to be Mahākālī, Mahālakṣmī, and Mahāsarasvatī;
Nandā, Śākambharī, and Bhīmā are recorded as his Śaktis.
These are Raktadantikā, Durgā, Bhrāmī, and Bījasañcayā;
their essence consists of Agni, Vāyu, and Bhaga, and their fruit arises from the three Vedas.
The application (*viniyoga*) is declared for the sake of accomplishing all desired aims.
Now, the ritual procedure (*prayoga*):
For this glorious nine-syllable mantra, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara are the seers (*ṛṣis*).
The meters are Gāyatrī, Uṣṇih, and Anuṣṭubh;
the deities are Mahākālī, Mahālakṣmī, and Mahāsarasvatī;
the powers (śaktis) are Nandā, Śākambharī, and Bhīmā; [the attendants] are Raktadantikā, Durgā, and Bhrāmari.
The seed-syllables are fire, wind, and the earth element; the application (viniyoga) is for the sake of attaining all desired goals during recitation.

Thereafter, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the seers and so forth, as follows: "Salutation to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara" on the head; "Salutation to the Gāyatrī, Uṣṇih, and Anuṣṭubh meters" at the heart.
Salutation to Nandā, Śākambharī, Bhīmā, and Śakti on the right breast; salutation to Śrī, Raktadantikā, Durgā, Bhrāmarī, and Bīja on the left breast;
salutation to the principles of Fire, Wind, and Sun at the heart.
And it is said:
One should place the sages, meters, and deities on the head, face, and heart;
the seed-syllables of the powers (śaktis) on the two breasts; and the principles (tattvas) again in the heart.
Now he states the distinction:
"The foliage of mantras is their clothing; the head of mantras is the foliage.
A mantra endowed with both head and foliage accomplishes nourishment and other such aims."
Accompanied by the sprout of the syllable *huṃ*, it is used for killing— except for a Brahmin—
and for tasks such as breaking mechanical devices and destroying most terrible fears.
One should employ a mantra ending in *vaṣaṭ* to destroy the afflictions caused by planetary influences;
however, for the purpose of eradication (*uccāṭana*), the mantra is said to be provided with the sprout of *phaṭ*.
These introductory verses (*pallava*) should be employed at the beginning of each respective ritual action, even during the recitation of the *Caṇḍī*. Likewise:
"One who is devoid of the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) becomes mute; one without the head [of the mantra] would be as if dead;
one who has cast off his garment is naked; and one without a seat is as if asleep."
A mantra without a guru is in vain; even with correct recitation, it is empty.
One given by a wicked person is devoid of power, while one with the wrong seed-syllable is paralyzed.

*Duṣṭadattaḥ* means that which has been given to a wicked person. He who is devoid of the *devachanda-ṛṣi* is like a sleeping serpent. Mantras such as those beginning with *mūka* are to be avoided. In the Vedic tradition, there is no consideration of *pallava* and so forth. *Hrīṃ*.
With the mantra "To Caṇḍikā," one performs the six-limbed ritual placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) for this mantra and hymn.

The sequence is as follows: "Salutation to the heart" (*hṛdayāya namaḥ*), "Svāhā to the head" (*śirase svāhā*), "Vaṣaṭ to the tuft of hair" (*śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*), "Hum to the armor" (*kavacāya huṃ*), "Vauṣaṭ to the three eyes" (*netratrayāya vauṣaṭ*), and "Phaṭ to the weapon" (*astrāya phaṭ*). It should be understood that the weapon-mantra is to be applied in all directions.

At the end of the nine-syllable mantra, the libation (tarpaṇa) is performed with the mantra: "May Caṇḍikā be satisfied. This should be understood to apply likewise to the fire-offering (homa) and other rites.
Now, he describes the yantra.
One should draw an eight-petaled lotus with saffron, agallochum, and sandalwood;
thereafter, a twenty-four-petaled lotus provided with anklets.
One should draw a six-pointed wheel consisting of Caṇḍikā in the center of the lotus;
one should place the three primordial seed-syllables situated in the middle of that six-pointed wheel.

Therein, in the central seed-syllable (bīja), is Mahālakṣmī; to her right is Mahākālī, and to her left is Sarasvatī. One should place the other seed-syllables in the six corners starting from the east. This is the worship diagram (pūjā-yantra). Any one of the seats, such as the lotus seat (padmāsana) and others, [should be used]. Likewise...

The ritual placement (*nyāsa*) is performed with the verses of the *Saptaśatī*. Having recited the five verses beginning with "Khaḍginī, Śūlinī," one should meditate upon the first seed-syllable, which is extremely black, and perform the placement upon all the limbs.
Regarding "the first is the single self":
having recited the four verses beginning with "O Goddess, protect us with the trident," one should place the second [mandala], which resembles the sun, everywhere.
The second is *grīṃ*. Having recited again the pentad of verses beginning with "sarvasvarūpa," one should place the third, which has the luster of crystal, on all sides; the third is *klīṃ*.
It is also stated in some places that the placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) is performed using those same verses in two repetitions.
Then one should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) using the divided letters of the root mantra:
with one, one, one, four, and a pair [respectively].
The wise practitioner should perform the six limb-assignments (aṅga-nyāsa) with the entire mantra.
Having thus completed the rite of assignment (nyāsa), he should display the mudrā of emanation (sṛṣṭimudrā).
Then, having sprinkled water for the sake of worship with the nine seed-syllables,
one should form the *talapṛṣṭha* mudrā and veil [the offerings] with the *astra-mantra*.
Having established the argha vessel, one should fill it with auspicious water;
O son of a king, having placed therein perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains of rice.
Having meditated upon all the sacred fords (tīrthas) and placed his hands [in water], he should consecrate them with mantras;
for the sake of protection, the Cakra-mudrā together with the Astra [mantra] should be performed.
The consecration of the offering materials with *arghya* water is as before.
Now, the meditation on the triad of deities beginning with Mahākālī:
[she holds] a sword, a discus, a mace, arrows, a bow, a bludgeon, a trident, a *bhuśuṇḍī*, and a head.
I worship Mahākālī, who holds a conch with her hands, possesses three eyes, is adorned with ornaments on every limb,
has the luster of a blue sapphire, and has ten faces and ten feet— she whom the lotus-born Brahmā sought out when he entered the cave to slay Madhu and Kaiṭabha.
Holding in her hands a rosary, an axe, a mace, an arrow, a thunderbolt, a lotus, a bow, a water-pot, a staff, a spear, a sword, a shield, a lily, a bell, a vessel of wine,
a trident, a noose, and the Sudarśana discus— she who possesses the luster of coral.
One should worship Mahālakṣmī here, the slayer of the buffalo demon, seated upon a lotus.
Holding a bell, a trident, a plow, a conch, a mace, a bow, and an arrow in her lotus-like hands; possessing a luster like the cool-rayed moon shimmering amidst thick clouds;
born from the body of Gaurī; the great foundation of the three worlds.
First, one should worship Sarasvatī here, the destroyer of the Daityas such as Śumbha.

(p. 96) Then, having performed the worship with the previously mentioned mantras using the five-fold offerings (pañcopacāra), one should recite [the mantra] four hundred thousand times. One should offer oblations into the fire with milk-rice (pāyasa) in the tenth part of that number. Once she has been worshipped...
In the case of the *hemareta* [mantra], this alone is its preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*):
by reciting daily the *Caṇḍīstava* as described in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*,
and interweaving it with the recitation of the root mantra (*mūlamantra*), one attains one's desired object.
Now follows the procedure for the Śatacaṇḍī rite:
near the temple of Śaṅkara or Bhavānī,
one should construct an auspicious pavilion, richly provided with gate-altars and adorned with beautiful banners and archways.
There, one should construct a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) either to the west or in the center;
having bathed and performed the daily rites, one should feed ten Brahmins.

[He should appoint] Vāḍava Brāhmaṇas who have conquered their senses, who follow right conduct, who are of noble birth, who speak the truth, who are highly learned, devoted to the recitation of the Caṇḍikā [hymn], and possessed of modesty and compassion.

According to the procedure for the madhuparka offering, one should give gold, garments, and other gifts; furthermore, one should provide them with a seat, a rosary for the purpose of recitation, and food.
Eating sacrificial food with their minds fixed on the meaning of the mantras,
lying upon the ground, they should each individually recite the hymn of praise to Caṇḍikā.
Those of pure mind should recite ten times the Navārṇa Caṇḍikā mantra as declared in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa, and they should separately chant it ten thousand times.
The ellipsis [to be supplied] is "from the separate encapsulation and recitation. A recitation of ten thousand [times] for each [mantra] should be performed by Brāhmaṇas.
Now, on the eighth, ninth, fourteenth, and full-moon days, as follows:

The traditionalists maintain that the commencement should be performed in such a way that the completion occurs on the hundredth repetition. Furthermore, the patron (yajamāna) should worship a group of nine auspicious maidens; he should fully honor those virgins who are between two and ten years of age.
Because there is an absence of affection for one-year-old [girls], those aged one year are excluded; rather, they are [to be worshipped] up to eleven years of age.

Their names in order are: Kumārī (1), Trimūrti (2), Kalyāṇī (3), Rohiṇī (4), Kālikā (5), Caṇḍikā (6), Śāmbhavī (7), and Durgā (8). (p. 97) [Note: The numbering in the source text appears to be inconsistent; the list provided here follows the sequence of names given.]
Subhadrā 9|10: The worship of these [goddesses] is performed with these very name-mantras.
The mantra for their invocation, as proclaimed by Śaṅkara, is stated as follows:
"I invoke the maiden who is composed of the syllables of mantra, who assumes the form of the Mothers, and who is the manifest embodiment of the nine Durgās.
Having invoked her thus, one should worship her. The mantra is as follows:
O you who are worshiped by the world, adored by the world, whose very nature is all-powerful energy;
accept this worship, O Kaumārī, Mother of the World! Salutations to you! (1)
I worship Tripurā, the support of the three cities, whose form is the knowledge of the three aims of life, the Goddess praised throughout the three worlds, the embodiment of the triple manifestation.
I worship the auspicious Goddess, the mother of all well-being, who consists of the creative powers (kalās) yet transcends them, whose heart is compassion, and who is ever-blessed. 3.

I worship Lakṣmī, who is the support of the powers such as atomization (aṇimā) and others, whose essence consists of the letters beginning with 'A', who possesses infinite power, and who is Rohiṇī. || 4 ||
I worship Kālikā, who moves at will, who is auspicious and beloved, whose nature is that of the Wheel of Time, who grants all desires, and who is noble with compassion.
I always worship the goddess Caṇḍikā, who possesses fierce valor, who is of fierce illusion, and who is the destroyer of Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa.
I worship Lakṣmī, the consort of Śambhu, who bestows eternal bliss, who is peaceful, who is saluted by all the gods, and who is the self of all beings.
I always worship with devotion Durgā, the destroyer of the suffering of worldly existence, who is difficult to reach, difficult to cross, and formidable, yet the destroyer of the pain of distress.
I worship the goddess Subhadrā, who is beautiful, possesses a golden complexion, bestows happiness and good fortune, and is the mother of Subhadra.
One should worship each respective maiden with these mantras spoken in the Purāṇas.

In this regard, those who have deficient or excessive limbs, those afflicted with leprosy or ulcers, the blind, the one-eyed, the deformed, the squinting, those whose bodies are covered in hair, those born of slave-women, and those who are diseased— such as these are to be avoided.

One should sacrifice with a Brahmin woman for the accomplishment of all desired goals, with one born of a Kṣatriya for fame, with one born of a Vaiśya for the acquisition of wealth, and with one born of a Śūdra for the attainment of sons.
One should worship with perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and various kinds of food, as well as with garments and ornaments according to one's ability.
Now follows the method of worship.
Having placed a water-pot according to the prescribed rite upon a beautiful Sarvatobhadra mandala prepared on the altar, one should invoke and worship Śivā there.
In front of that, one should also worship the maidens and the Brāhmaṇas with various types of offerings,
as well as those of the nine syllables.
In that regard—
one should worship Oṃkārapīṭha as the first, Pūrṇapīṭha immediately thereafter, and Kāmapīṭha as the third, according to the oral tradition.
In the directions starting from the east, there is the quartet beginning with Gaṇeśa on the pedestal;
furthermore, Gaṇeśa and Kṣetrapāla, the two sandals, and the three Vaṭukas.
Having worshipped the four goddesses— Jayā, Vijayā, Jayantī, and Aparājitā— in the four directions beginning with the southeast (āgneya), [one should proceed].
In the previously mentioned yantra, Brahmā accompanied by Sarasvatī is in the eastern corner; Viṣṇu accompanied by Śrī is in the southwest; Śiva accompanied by Umā is in the northwest;
Mahālakṣmī is at the central seed-syllable situated in the middle of the six-cornered wheel; and Mahākālī is to its south.
To her left is Mahāsarasvatī; to the north, a lion; and to the south, a buffalo. In the six-cornered wheels are Nandajā (1), Raktadantikā (2), Śākambharī (3), Durgā (4), Bhīmā (5), and Bhrāmarī (6).
These [deities] are preceded by the Tārā-mantra and enriched with the first letter of their names accompanied by the *bindu*.
The name-mantras for the worship and other rites should be understood as follows: the practical application is "Oṃ, obeisance to Nandajā.
In the eight [directions] beyond these are Brahmāṇī (1), Māheśvarī (2), Kaumārī (3), Vaiṣṇavī (4), Vārāhī (5), Nārasiṃhī (6), Indrāṇī (7), and Cāmuṇḍā (8).
(p. 99) They are to be worshipped with the name-mantras according to the method described above. The formula is: *oṃ braṃ brahmāṇyai namaḥ*, and so forth.
Then, the twenty-four deities beginning with Viṣṇumāyā are [placed] upon the twenty-four petals.

They are to be worshipped with their respective name-mantras in the sequence beginning from the east. And they are: Viṣṇumāyā (1), Cetanā (2), Buddhi (3), Nidrā (4), Kṣudhā (5), Chāyā (6), Śakti (7), Tṛṣṇā (8), Kṣānti (9), Jāti (10), Lajjā (11), Śānti (12), Śraddhā (13), Kīrti (14), Lakṣmī (15), Dhṛti (16), and Vṛtti (17).
17 Śruti, 18 Smṛti, 19 Dayā, 20 Tuṣṭi, 21 Puṣṭi, 22 Mātā, 23 Bhrānti.
At the base of the lotus stalks are: 1 Ādhāra, 2 Kūrma, 3 Śeṣa, 4 Pṛthvī. In the corners of the outer square (bhūpura) are:
1 Gaṇeśa, 2 Kṣetrapāla, 3 Vaṭuka, 4 Yoginī. These are to be worshipped.

In the directions starting from the east, in order, are Indra and the others: 1. Indra, 2. Agni, 3. Yama, 4. Nirṛti, 5. Varuṇa, 6. Vāyu, 7. Saumya (Soma), 8. Īśāna, 9. Ananta, 10. Brahmā. Following these are the weapons starting with the thunderbolt: 1. Vajra, 2. Śakti, 3. Daṇḍa, 4. Khaḍga, 5. Pāśa, 6. Aṅkuśa.

The mace (gadā), the trident (triśūla), the discus (cakra), and the lotus (padma) are to be worshipped. Having performed this for four days, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) on the fifth day.
Therein, on the first day there is one round; on the second day, two; on the third, three; and on the fourth—
There are four [offerings], one for each Brāhmaṇa. The materials for the oblation are:
milk-rice (pāyasa) soaked in the three sweets (trimadhu), grapes, mangoes, and other fruits; citrons, sugarcane stalks, coconuts, dates, and sesame seeds.
One should perform oblations with nutmegs, mangoes, and other sweet substances,
offering them for each mantra ten times over the course of seven hundred repetitions.
And having performed ten thousand oblations with the nine-syllable mantra according to the prescribed rite in the established fire,
one should perform the fire-offering for the presiding deities using their respective name-mantras.
Having properly performed the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) and having bid farewell to the divine fire,
the assembly of brahmins should consecrate the sacrificer with the waters from the ritual jars.
One should bestow a gold coin or a piece of gold as a sacrificial fee for each,
and one should feed a hundred Brahmins with various kinds of foods and delicacies.
Having given sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) even to them, one should then receive their blessings.
When this is done, the entire world becomes submissive and all calamities perish.
One should perform this ritual ten times over for the *Caṇḍīsāhasraka*;
one should select one hundred Brahmins who are learned in the Vedas and of virtuous conduct.
Each of them should perform the recitation of the Caṇḍikā; I shall instruct them.
The remainder is that they should do so according to the aforementioned method over four days.
Each of them should mutter the nine-syllable mantra ten thousand times.
The auspicious maidens previously mentioned should be worshipped a hundred times with the aforementioned mantras;
having thus completed the fourfold [recitation], they should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with great care.
By reciting the Saptaśatī one hundred times according to the prescribed rite for each mantra,
with the previously mentioned collections of substances and a total count of one hundred thousand syllables;
Having given the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Hotṛ priests, one should feed the previously mentioned twice-born ones—
virtuous men, numbering a thousand, who are intent upon the propitiation of the Goddess.
When the ritual of Caṇḍī has been performed in this manner a thousand times by men,
everything desired is accomplished and the flood of suffering is destroyed.
Mara, famine, disease, and other such multitudes of calamities perish.
This procedure is tenfold for the Ayuta-chaṇḍī rite, and ten times that again for the Lakṣa-chaṇḍī rite, or it may be performed by a hundred Brahmins alone.

The *Ayutacaṇḍī* rite should be performed over forty days. In that regard, it should be understood as follows: in the first decade, one recitation; in the second decade, two; in the third, three; and in the fourth, four, and so forth. Furthermore, regarding the fire-offering (*homa*) during the recitation of the *Caṇḍī*, there is a prohibition against performing the *homa* with the *Kavaca-mantra*.
And the great Daitya Andhaka, who was devoted to the oblations for Durgā,
was struck down by Maheśa with a single oblation of armor.

In that regard, the armor (*kavaca*) consists of the four verses beginning with "Protect [me] with the trident" (*śūlena pāhi*). Regarding this, the learned authorities maintain that there is only one oblation for these four verses, namely: "To Mahālakṣmī, svāhā!
Now follows the sequence of the ritual application (*prayoga*).

Having constructed a pavilion in a temple of Śiva according to the procedure taught in the Tantras, and having fashioned an altar in its center— or having prepared it within a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) to the west— one should perform the daily rites,
recite the benediction (svastivācana), and then make the formal resolve (saṅkalpa) as follows: *Oṃ tatsat*.
Today, for me, [named] so-and-so, of such-and-such a lineage (*gotra*), together with my retinue—

preceded by the pacification of all afflictions and the absence of fear caused by enemies, thieves, kings, weapons, fire, and other such causes— the pacification of the three types of calamities, and the possession of wealth, grain, and sons, and freedom from fear... [all] this...

Desiring the attainment of freedom from distress, strength, nourishment, increase of wealth, happiness, mental well-being, and health, I shall perform the Śatacaṇḍī rite today [or at the appropriate time]. Having thus made this formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*),
and having performed the installation of the Mātṛkās and the *nāndī-śrāddha*, [one should worship] ten [deities] possessing the previously mentioned characteristics.

One should honor the Brahmins with honey-mixture (madhuparka), garments, gold, and other offerings. Seated upon the seats provided by the patron and adorned with the garlands given by him, they— possessing composed minds and recollecting the Blessed Lady— should [perform the rite] upon the altar marked with the Sarvatobhadra diagram using the root mantra of the Saptashati.

Having placed a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, or any other [precious metal], and having invoked Durgā therein and worshipped her with the sixteen types of offerings (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*), they should recite the *Saptaśatī* ten times for each verse and the nine-syllable mantra (*navārṇa*) ten thousand times before her. [They should observe] a diet of sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) and celibacy (*brahmacarya*).

They should observe rules such as sleeping on the ground and avoiding contact with those who are untouchable. The patron (yajamāna) should provide gifts of clothing, ornaments, and various kinds of cooked food. Having invited the maidens, he should worship them with their respective mantras beginning with "Jagatpūjyā" (Worshipful of the World). In this manner, [the rite continues] for four days.

Having completed the recitation (*japa*) and the worship of the maiden (*kumārī-pūjā*), on the fifth day, one should establish the sacred fire in a pit (*kuṇḍa*) or on a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) according to the procedure taught in the Āgamas, and offer oblations of milk-rice (*pāyasa*) and other prescribed substances. [This should be done] for every verse of the *Saptaśatī*.

When ten times ten thousand oblations have been offered with the nine-syllable mantra, each twice-born [priest] shall offer one thousand oblations for every verse of the *Saptashatī* using the root mantra; then,
they shall offer one oblation each to the deities of the enclosures (*āvaraṇadevatā*) using their respective name-mantras, beginning with *Tārā* and ending with *svāhā*.

Having given [the offerings], worshipped the Goddess residing in the jar, and performed the ritual offering of the *bali*, one should give one *niṣka* of gold to each of the officiating priests (*hotṛs*); in case of inability, one should give gold measured at one *suvarṇa*. This is the procedure for the *Śatacaṇḍī* rite.
Now follows the procedure for the Sahasra-caṇḍī rite.

As follows: therein, there is the selection of one hundred Brahmins. These one hundred Brahmins shall each individually recite the *Saptashatī* ten times each; and they shall perform the recitation of the nine-syllable mantra (*navārṇa*) ten thousand times each.
One hundred virgins should be fed and honored. Thus, when the ten days have concluded,
on the eleventh day,
one should perform a homa with the nine-syllable mantra (*navārṇa*) one hundred thousand times, reciting the *Saptaśatī* one hundred times for each verse.

The remainder is as before. Thus concludes the procedure for Sahasra-Caṇḍī. In this manner, the procedure for Ayuta-Caṇḍī is ten times that of Sahasra-Caṇḍī; the procedure for Lakṣa-Caṇḍī is ten times that [of Ayuta-Caṇḍī]. [This applies] to the recitation (japa), the fire-oblation (homa), the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), and the feeding of virgins (kumārī-bhojana).
And by feeding Brahmins, there is a tenfold increase [of merit].
Now, other applications mentioned in the Kātyāyanītantra:
one should mutter the *praṇava* (oṃ) at the beginning and end of each mantra; thus there is the accomplishment (*siddhi*) of the mantra. This applies everywhere hereafter.
The term "verse-quarter" (*ślokapada*) is an indicator for the mantra.

By performing this for each verse—placing the three *vyāhṛtis* preceded by the *praṇava* at the beginning and in reverse order at the end—if one recites it one hundred times, success is achieved very swiftly. || 1 ||
If one recites the verse beginning with "jātavedase" at the start of every śloka, there shall be the fulfillment of all desires.

A single *ṛc* is also written here: "To Jātavedas we press the Soma; he burns away the wealth of those who act with enmity. May he carry us across all difficulties, as Agni, like a boat, carries us beyond all misfortunes across the river.
This is the *ṛc*. To ward off untimely death, one should recite the *Tryambaka* mantra a hundred times at the beginning and at the end. (4)
The recitation of that mantra for every verse is another [method]. || 5 ||
If one recites the verse concerning those who have come for refuge and the distressed at every stanza, there shall be success in all undertakings.
"May that Sovereign Lady, the cause of our auspiciousness, grant [this] for every verse"—by reciting this half-verse, one attains all desires. || 7 ||
For the sake of obtaining one's own desired boon, one should recite this verse—"Thus having obtained the boon from the Goddess"—at every subsequent verse. || 8 ||
For the purpose of warding off all calamities, one should recite the words "Durge, thou art remembered" at the end of every verse.

Even for this single verse alone, the recitation (japa) should be performed one hundred thousand times, ten thousand times, one thousand times, or one hundred times, according to the requirements of the task. || 10 ||
By reciting "sarvā bādha" one hundred thousand times, the fruit described in the verse is obtained. || 11 ||
When this verse beginning with "itthaṃ yadā yadā" is recited one hundred thousand times, there is the pacification of the great pestilence (mahāmārī). || 12 ||
Then, by reciting this mantra one hundred thousand times, King Vabhru regained his kingdom. || 13 ||
By the mantra "hinasti daityatejāṃsi," there is the pacification of the Bālagrahas through the offering of a lamp and oblation (bali) and the tying of a bell. || 14 ||
Having recited the first rotation in direct order, then having performed the second in reverse order, and again in direct order— by means of these three rotations in the aforementioned manner,
there is the swift accomplishment of the task. || 15 ||

For the warding off of all calamities, one should recite the half-verse: "When remembered in a difficult place... Then, at the end [of that], one should recite the *ṛc*: "Whatever fear one encounters here, whether near or far, O Pavamāna, drive it away," and likewise the half-verse:
"...from poverty and suffering. In this manner, according to the specific purpose, one should perform [the recitation] a hundred thousand, ten thousand, or a thousand times.
Or one hundred recitations. || 16 ||

"I am Kāṃsā; I invoke here Śrī, who has a golden rampart, who is moist, blazing, satisfied, and satisfying, who dwells upon a lotus, and who is lotus-colored"—one should recite this Ṛgvedic verse with each stanza for the attainment of Lakṣmī. || 17 ||
Reciting the mantra "I am free from debt toward him verse by verse," one should offer a firm circumambulation. || 18 ||
Having spoken thus for the purpose of slaying, one should fly up and recite [the mantra] verse by verse. || 19 ||
The accomplishment of the fruit occurs through the modes of activity described for the rite of killing. || 20 ||
It is established by experience that the immediate delusion [of enemies] occurs merely by the recitation of the verse beginning with "jñānināmapi cetāṃsi. || 21 ||
In the recitation of each mantra, that verse must necessarily be included for the sake of deluding [the enemy].
By reciting this verse in response to the verse beginning with "rogānaśeṣān," there is the destruction of all diseases. || 23 ||
Even in the mere recitation of those [mantras], he [attains that result]. || 24 ||
Thus addressed, that goddess [spoke]; by reciting a response-verse (*pratiśloka*) to the verse beginning with "gambhīrā," or by chanting it separately, the attainment of the *vidyā* occurs. || 25 ||
And there is the destruction of vocal defects. || 26 ||
The mantra of one hundred and twelve syllables beginning with "bhagavatyā kṛtaṃ sarvam" grants all desires and wards off all calamities. || 27 ||

O Goddess, by reciting the verse beginning with "O Goddess who removes the distress of those who have sought refuge" one hundred thousand, ten thousand, one thousand, or even a hundred times according to the specific purpose, or by reading it for each individual verse, there is the cessation of all calamities and the attainment of all desires. || 28 ||
In these applications, success is achieved through a mere salutation with a lamp for each verse. || 29 ||
By reciting each verse encapsulated by the seed-syllable of Kāma for forty-one days with three repetitions, all desires are accomplished. || 30 ||
(104) By reciting [the mantra] twelve times daily for twenty-one days according to the aforementioned method, subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*) is achieved;

by reciting it thirteen times for seven days while it is encapsulated by the *māyā* seed-syllable and accompanied by the *kūṭapallava*, the accomplishment of eradication (*uccāṭana*) is attained. || 32 ||
By reciting each verse fifteen times, encapsulated by the *śrī* seed-syllable (*śrī-bīja*), for a period of forty-nine days, the attainment of Lakṣmī occurs. || 33 ||
Now, the classification of meditative absorption (dhyāna) according to the specific desires [to be accomplished]: for subjugation (vaśya), it is red; for nourishment (pauṣṭika), it is variegated;

for eradication (uccāṭana), it is smoky-grey; for killing (māraṇa), it is black; and for the sake of progeny, it is dark like the petal of a blue lotus. Meditation on the form of a jewel grants all desires in battle.

In times of fear of water accompanied by great drought, one should meditate on [the deity] as being like the fire of time (kālāgni); in times of fear from poison and the like, one should meditate on him as being like the full moon accompanied by a rain of nectar (pīyūṣa).
Thus ends the procedure for the recitation of the *Saptaśatī* in the *Dīkṣāprakāśa* composed by Śrī Jīvanātha.
Now follows the method for the worship of the earthen linga (*pārthivapūjā*).
Oṃ, I take refuge in Sadyojāta; salutations indeed to Sadyojāta. Bhave...

"Bhava, O Over-Bhava, salutations again and again to me, the source of existence. With this mantra, the taking of the clay is performed. "Oṃ, salutations to Vāmadeva; salutations to the Eldest; salutations to the Most Excellent;
salutations to Rudra; salutations to Kāla; salutations to the Maker of Time; salutations to the Maker of Strength."

"Obeisance to Bala, obeisance to the Subduer of Bala, obeisance to the Tamer of all beings, obeisance to Manonmana, obeisance! With this mantra, one should sprinkle water. Then: "Oṃ, obeisance be to you, to the non-terrible ones, to the terrible ones, to those more terrible than the terrible, to all, and to all of the all."
"To those who have the form of Rudra.
Thus is the ritual for the *liṅga*.
Oṃ, we know that Tatpuruṣa; we meditate upon Mahādeva; may that Rudra [grant us] that.

One should fashion the *bāṇa* with the mantra "pracodayāt. Having joined the *bāṇa* to the pedestal with the mantra: "Oṃ, may Īśāna, the Lord of all sciences, the Sovereign of all beings, the Overlord of Brahman, the Overlord of the Veda, the Brahman, the Auspicious One, ever be mine—Śivom," one should meditate upon it.
It is as follows: "Oṃ, one should constantly meditate upon Maheśa, who resembles a mountain of silver, adorned with a beautiful crescent moon,
his limbs radiant with jewel ornaments, holding in his hands an axe, a deer, the gesture of granting boons, and the gesture of fearlessness, and who is gracious."

Seated upon a lotus, praised on all sides by hosts of immortals, wearing a tiger skin, the primordial source of the universe, the seed of the universe, the remover of all fears, five-faced, and three-eyed.
I bow to Bhava, who is white as camphor, the incarnation of compassion, the essence of worldly existence, who wears a necklace of lordly serpents,
and who eternally delights in the lotus of his heart together with Bhavānī.
One should meditate upon Him who is seated in the center of the Kailāsa throne, being worshipped by His devotees such as Nandin and others;
who is the forest fire that consumes the suffering of His devotees, who is immeasurable, embraced by Umā, and adorned with the moon.
Having meditated thus, one should take a bilva leaf along with fragrant flowers and unbroken rice grains (akṣata), and perform the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) with the mantra "oṃ manojyotiḥ.
The mantra is as follows:
Oṃ, may the mind-light enjoy the clarified butter; may Bṛhaspati extend this sacrifice;
may he establish this sacrifice as unimpaired; may all the gods rejoice here; Oṃ, be established!
Then one should recite this:
O Lord, Sovereign of the entire world, until the conclusion of the worship,
please remain present within this *liṅga* with a spirit of affection.
Then the water for the feet:

*Oṃ*, we meditate upon Bhava, the destroyer of worldly existence, upon Mahādeva; upon Ugra, the destroyer of the fierce, upon Śarva, the moon-crested one—salutation! This is the water for the feet for Śiva. *Oṃ*.
Salutations to Sāmbaśiva. This is the *arghya*, svāhā. This is the water for sipping (*ācamanīya*), svadhā.
This is the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*), svadhā. This is the unguent. These are the flowers. Om, to Sāmbaśiva, vauṣaṭ. Having offered the *bilva* leaves: Om, to Śarva, whose form is the earth...

Homage! To Bhava, whose form is water, in the northeast; Oṃ, homage to Rudra, whose form is fire, in the east; Oṃ, homage to Ugra, whose form is wind, in the southeast; Oṃ, homage to Bhīma, whose form is space, in the south; Oṃ, [homage] in the southwest... [Oṃ].

"Oṃ, salutation to Paśupati, whose form is the sacrificer; [in the west]. Oṃ, salutation to Mahādeva, whose form is the Moon; [in the northwest]. Oṃ, salutation to Īśāna, whose form is the Sun; [in the north].
One should offer a handful of flowers with the mantra: 'Oṃ, salutation to Śiva. This..."
Incense, obeisance! This lamp, obeisance! These food offerings, I present. This betel-leaf, obeisance! Then: Obeisance!
Obeisance to the one whose form is the syllable *Oṃ*, who bears a body consisting of the imperishable syllable.
Salutations to you, whose self is the *nāda*; salutations to you, whose self is the *bindu* and the *kalā*.
Salutations to you who possess both the form of the unmanifest (*aliṅga*) and the manifest (*liṅga*), and who transcend all forms.
You are the mother of all worlds; you alone are the father of the universe.

You are my brother, you are my well-wisher and friend; you are the beloved one who assumes the form of what is dear. You are the teacher, you are the goal, you are the manifest witness; you are my father and you are my grandfather.
Salutations to you, O Blessed Rudra, the sun of immeasurable splendor;
salutations to Bhava and Rudra, together with Umā.
Salutation to the protector of all the earth, who always slays the Asuras; and salutation to the Lord of creatures, whose splendor is like that of fire and is immeasurable.
Salutations to you, the formidable one, whose form is space and who consists of sound alone;
salutations again and again to Mahādeva, to Soma, to the Immortal.
Salutations to you, the fierce one, for the sake of the sacrificer; salutations to you, the practitioner of yoga.

Om, salutations to Hara. Om, salutations to Maheśvara. Om, salutations to the Trident-bearer. [This is] the taking of the clay. One should perform the fashioning [of the image]. [This is] the consecration of the vital breaths (prāṇapratiṣṭhā). Om, O Trident-bearer, here...

"Be well-established. One should recite: "Oṃ, the light of the mind... Oṃ, obeisance to the wielder of the Pināka bow; Oṃ, obeisance to Paśupati; Oṃ, obeisance to Śiva. [With the words] "Invocation: come here," one should perform the bathing.
[Then] the worship: Oṃ, obeisance to Mahādeva. [Finally] the dismissal.
And by this worship of the earthen linga which has been performed by me,
may the Blessed Lord Rudra grant my desired object.
Having thus prostrated, one should dismiss the *liṅgas* with the following:
"Salutations again and again to Bhava, to Rudra, and to Śiva;
salutations again and again to Īśāna, to the bull-bannered one, and to Bhīma and Ugra."
Salutation to Mahādeva, the protector, the beloved of Vāsudeva;
salutation to Vāsudeva, the peaceful one, and likewise to Umāpati.
Salutations to you, the blue-throated one; salutations to you, the dark-throated one.
Salutations to Gopati, to Śaṅkara himself, and to the one who is eternally composed of all things.
Having worshipped in the morning and likewise in the evening, that best of men who stands with palms joined in reverence recites these nineteen names.
He is liberated from all sins and is honored by the gods in heaven;
by reciting this hymn, he burns away his evil and shall go to Śiva.

One should prostrate again and again. One should perform circumambulation in the shape of a half-moon. "Go, go, O Supreme Lord, to the supreme bath, to your own abode, and for the sake of returning once more at the time of worship and propitiation."
"Oṃ, O Śambhu, you have been worshipped; be gracious, O Śiva, and go to your own abode"—thus one should say. Now follows the procedure for worship during the four watches of the night on Śivarātri:
"Not by bathing, nor by clothing, nor by incense, nor by [ordinary] worship [is he pleased]."
I am not so pleased with flowers as I am by fasting during the night.
Then, during the night, those intent on pleasing Śiva should perform bathing and especially worship at every watch.
In this context, it is understood through repetition that worship is to be performed during all four watches of the day.
As stated in the *Narasiṃhacaryā*:
"Whether one be a Śaiva or a Vaiṣṇava, if they should be a worshiper of another [deity]..."
One who turns away from Śivarātri destroys the entire fruit of all worship.
In the *Saṃvatsarapradīpa*:
"First, the bath is with milk; in the second [month], with curd;
in the third likewise with clarified butter; and in the fourth likewise with honey."
In the Īśānasaṃhitā: "O Goddess, when the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Phālguna falls on a Sunday or even a Tuesday, this supreme vow should be observed."
Through the yoga of Śiva-yoga, that becomes the most excellent of the excellent;
it is known as the Śivarātri vow, which destroys all sins.
It bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon all human beings, down to the very outcastes (caṇḍālas).
In the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*:
"By the power of fasting, and even by force through keeping a vigil..."
Likewise, by worshipping that linga on the occasion of Śivarātri, [one attains the same fruit].
One obtains inexhaustible desires and attains union with Śiva.
In the Padma Purāṇa: "Year after year, O Great Goddess, a man or a woman devoted to her husband should worship Mahādeva on Śivarātri with fervent devotion."
In the Īśānasaṃhitā:
"The observer of the vow should perform the vow in this very manner every year;
for it lasts either fourteen years or likewise twenty-four years."
One obtains all desires and is liberated from all sins. Now follows the ritual application:
in the morning, facing north, having uttered "Oṃ tatsat" and recited "Sūryasoma," [one should proceed].
Taking water and other materials, [one should say]: "O Lord of the World, by your grace, may this Śivarātri vow— which yields great fruit— be performed by me without obstacles."

With this, one should undertake the observance of the vows and restraints. Then, taking water again, one should say: "Oṃ, desiring the attainment of all enjoyments such as good fortune, as well as liberation, I shall perform the Śivarātri vow."
Then one should recite the mantra:
"Having fasted on the fourteenth day, O Śambhu, I shall eat on the following day for the sake of enjoyment and liberation; O Lord, be my refuge."

Then, when the first watch of the night has passed, whether the *liṅga* has been installed or not, one should perform the installation and then the worship. Having cleared away the earth with three kicks while reciting "Haḥ! To the weapon, Phaṭ!", one should likewise [ward off obstacles] with three claps of the hands using the fingertips.

Having performed the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*) and the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), and so forth, [one recites]: *hāṃ* to the heart, *namaḥ*; *hīṃ* to the head, *svāhā*;
*hrūṃ* to the crest-lock (*śikhā*), *vaṣaṭ*; *hauṃ* to the armor (*kavaca*), *huṃ*; *hauṃ* to the three eyes, *vauṣaṭ*; *haḥ*.

Reciting "Astrāya Phaṭ," perform the triple *tāla* gesture; having performed the binding of the ten directions with the *chotikā* snap, perform breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with the mantra "Hauṃ. Then, one should worship Śiva in the earthen *liṅga* according to the prescribed rite. In this regard, the specific detail is as follows: "Hauṃ, obeisance to Īśāna."
Having bathed [the deity] with milk during the first watch of the night, one should bathe him again with water.
Then:
"O Lord, devoted to the worship and recitation of mantras, [I observe] the Śivarātri vow."
I perform this offering according to the prescribed rite; accept this arghya, O Maheśvara.

Having offered the *arghya* in this manner, having worshipped with perfumes and other offerings, and having prostrated, one should pass the watch of the night through singing, instrumental music, reciting hymns, listening to his life stories, and so forth.
[As it is said: "Meditation upon him, chanting his name, bathing, and listening to his life stories and the like..."
For these virtues resulting from fasting have been proclaimed by the ancients.
Then, during the second watch: *Hauṃ Oṃ Aghorāya Namaḥ*. Thus is the bath with fragrant substances (*gandhasnāna*).
Then: Oṃ, salutations to Śiva, the peaceful one, the remover of all sins;
on this Śivarātri, I offer this arghya; be gracious along with Umā.

Having thus offered the *arghya* and performed the worship (*pūjā*) and other rites as before, then, during the third watch (*prahara*): "Oṃ hauṃ, obeisance to Sadyojāta. With this, the bath is performed with clarified butter (*ghṛta*). The *arghya* mantra, however, is:
"O beloved of Pārvatī, I am consumed by suffering, poverty, and grief."
On this Śivarātri, I offer this arghya; O beloved of Umā, be gracious to me.
One should perform the other [rites] as in the first watch. In the fourth watch: *oṃ hauṃ tatpuruṣāya namaḥ*. Thus is the bath with honey.
The mantra for the *arghya* offering is as follows:
O Śaṅkara, take away the many sins committed by me;
O beloved of Umā, I offer this arghya on Śivarātri—please accept it from me.
The rest is as before. Then, having recited the root mantra *oṃ namaḥ śivāya*, one should recite the mantra beginning with *avighnena*.
The mantra is as follows:
Oṃ! By your grace, O Lord, this vow has been completed without obstacle;
forgive me, O Protector of the worlds, O Hara, Sovereign of the three realms.
Whatever merit has been earned by me here, that too is offered to you;
through your grace, O Mahādeva, this vow is today completed.
Be gracious to me, O God; grant me a good rebirth, O Śaṅkara!
By the mere sight of you, I am purified—of this there is no doubt.
Then, on the following day, having fed the Brahmins, one should recite the mantra as follows:
"O Śaṅkara, for me who am consumed by the afflictions of saṃsāra, through this vow..."
Be gracious; becoming well-disposed, grant the vision of knowledge.
Having spoken thus, one should perform the recollection (*smaraṇa*).
Thus concludes the procedure for the worship of Śivarātri.
Now follows the specific details regarding the worship of Śiva.
At night one should perform worship facing north, and during the day facing east;
likewise, being pure, one should always perform the worship of Śiva facing north.
"Always" means day and night.
The reason for this is shown in the Rudrayāmala: "One should not [offer] to the east of Śambhu, nor to the north, where the Śakti resides."

The sacrificer should not resort to the western direction, since his back would be toward it; rather, he should take recourse in the southern direction. Standing facing the east, the sacrificer should not perform the sacrifice before Śambhu, because that would mean being face-to-face with Śambhu, the destroyer of the world—this being according to the view that [Śiva] has five faces.
The principal face is situated facing the east. Regarding the form of the single-faced [deity], the Āditya Purāṇa states:
"He has a gentle [face], a crown, eyes like moonbeams, one face, and four arms."
Holding a trident and a lotus in his hands, with his two other hands granting boons and fearlessness.
One should fashion an irreproachable image of Śiva in one’s house or temple— one with long eyes, worthy of worship by the gods, and adorned with all ornaments.

Because worship before [an image] is prohibited; this is not the subject of the statement, "The east is declared by the best of gurus to be both in front of the deity and in front of oneself," but rather the well-known east according to common usage and the like that should be taken as the primary direction. It is precisely in accordance with this that the worship described hereafter proceeds from the east to the southeast.
Wherever the sun rises in the sky, those who know the Vedas call that direction "Prācī" (the East);
and beyond that, those who know the scriptures always declare it to be the direction between the worshipper and the deity.
Thus it is stated. Now, the *Liṅgapurāṇa* shows the specific [requirement]:
"Without the triple mark of ashes (*bhasmatripuṇḍra*) and without a rosary of Rudrākṣa beads..."
Even if Śambhu is always worshipped, he will not be the bestower of fruit for him.
Therefore, even with clay, the *tripuṇḍra* should be made on the forehead; thus it is stated in the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
"Thirty-two Rudrākṣas should be worn on the neck, forty on the head, six on each ear, and twelve on each of the two wrists."
(114) On the two arms, sixteen [beads] for each by the digits of the moon (16); and on the topknot-thread, one—such a person is a human being.
He who places one hundred and eight on the chest is himself Nīlakaṇṭha.
In the *Saṃvatsarapradīpa*:
"At the time of the destruction of Tripura, those drops of tears that fell from the eyes of Rudra became the rudrākṣas upon the earth."
One, two, three, four, six, seven, eight,
nine, ten, eleven, twelve, thirteen, and fourteen.
O God, Śaṅkara, tell us truly according to the facts about these faces, for you are their deity— the secret, even more secret [of all].
Śrī Śaṅkara said:
Listen, O Ṣaṇmukha, to the truth according to the sequence for each face:
Śiva with one face directly removes the sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa.
The God of gods has two faces and is the destroyer of sins such as cow-slaughter;
he who has three faces is the Fire-god himself and removes even the sin of killing an embryo.
Brahmā himself, with four faces, removes the sin of killing a human being;
