Rudra himself, with five faces, is known by the name Kālāgni.
Even for the sin of approaching those who should not be approached and for the consumption of what should not be eaten,
one is liberated from all evils by wearing the five-faced [liṅga].
Kārttikeya with six faces should be held in the right arm;
one is liberated from sins such as the killing of a Brahmin—of this there is no doubt.
The seven-faced Mahāsena is the king of serpents named Ananta;
one is liberated from sins such as violating the guru’s bed—of this there is no doubt.
The eight-faced Mahāsena is the god Vināyaka himself;
he would even touch the wife of his guru with the water on his back.
Indeed, all such evils and even the most heinous sins are entirely destroyed by him;
freed from obstacles, he goes to the supreme goal.
These qualities arise from the wearing of this eight-faced [amulet].
Bhairava Navāsya himself should wear it on the left arm.
Kāpila is the direct bestower of liberation; one who performs this obtains a fruit equal to my own.
Even he who commits thousands of millions of crores of Brahman-murders [attains this].
All that is quickly consumed by the recitation of the Navavaktra [mantra];
the ten-faced Mahāsena is the Lord Janārdana himself.
Planets, piśācas and the like, vetālas, brahmarākṣasas,
and all serpents perish through the wearing of the ten-faced [Liṅga].
The eleven Rudras of those who have eleven faces are remembered as the eleven Rudras;
one should always wear them upon the crest-lock—listen now to the fruit of that merit.
Whatever fruit results from a thousand horse-sacrifices, a hundred Vājapeya sacrifices, and a hundred thousand cows with golden horns given as a proper gift; [that fruit one obtains by this].
One attains that fruit by wearing the face of Rudra;
one should wear a twelve-faced rudrākṣa on the region of the neck.
The Sun is eternally pleased when established as twelve Arka-s;
likewise, he is pleased when having thirteen faces and fourteen mouths.
These two bestow infinite fruit; it is impossible to describe their merit.
A wise person should likewise install an image with fourteen faces upon a stone slab.
That man on earth who wears a rudrākṣa without the mantra goes to a terrible hell for as long as the fourteen Indras endure.
For the consecration of a rudrākṣa, the five-syllabled mantra is prescribed;
one should especially employ either the "Oṃ Tryambakam" mantra or the Aghora mantra.
At the time of bathing, one should apply the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
And even by a small mantra, O best of the twice-born, [the merit] of the rudrākṣa [is attained].
One should perform the consecration according to the prescribed rules; thereby one obtains even greater fruit.
Then, endowed with devotion, one should wear it as instructed by Sumantu.
Now, the mantra for this is as follows:
1. Oṃ oṃ bhṛ śa namaḥ 2. Oṃ oṃ namaḥ 3. Oṃ hrīṃ namaḥ 4. Oṃ hraṃ namaḥ

p. 116) Oṃ huṃ namaḥ (5) | Oṃ oṃ huḥ huṃ namaḥ (6) | Oṃ sa hraṃ namaḥ (7) | Oṃ haṃ namaḥ (8) | Oṃ hrīṃ namaḥ (9) | Oṃ śrīṃ namaḥ (10) | Oṃ hrīṃ hūṃ namaḥ (11) | Oṃ kṣāṃ kṣauṃ namaḥ (12) | Oṃ namaḥ (13) | Oṃ namo namaḥ (14) |
Now, the mantras stated according to another method: oṃ aiṃ 1, oṃ śrīṃ 2, oṃ kūṃ 3, oṃ draḥ 4, oṃ hrīṃ 5, oṃ hrīṃ 6,
oṃ hrīṃ 7, oṃ brūṃ rāṃ 8, oṃ hrāṃ 9, oṃ hrīṃ 10, oṃ hrīṃ 11, oṃ.

KṢAUṂ STRĪṂ (12), OṂ UMĀM (13), OṂ NAMO NAMAḤ (14). Although there are specific fruits and mantras for rudrākṣas with one to fourteen faces, one should nevertheless wear the five-faced rudrākṣa according to the prescribed rules because it is easily available.

"Rudra himself is five-faced, known by the name Kālāgni. By merely coming [into contact with this] and by the recitation [of its name], even in the case of approaching those who should not be approached and eating what should not be eaten, one is liberated from all sins through the wearing of the Five-Faced [Amulet]. Thus it is said.
Oṃ. Having recited "huṃ namaḥ" one hundred and eight times for each [mantra], one should wash it with water and wear it.
As stated in the *Liṅgapurāṇa*:
He who worships the earthen linga shall obtain longevity, strength, glory, sons, wealth, and wisdom, as well as his desired boon.
Therefore, that earthen linga should be known as the means for accomplishing all goals;
the wooden one is known to bestow wealth, and the crystal one grants all desires.
The Narmada stone is the most excellent, as is any other mountain-born stone resembling a *liṅga* here.
In the *Kālakaumudī*:
"A man should never [worship] a *liṅga* anywhere that is smaller than an *akṣa* in size."
One should make it shorter than the thumb; one should never rely upon [a length] equal to it.
An *akṣa* consists of eighty *raktikās*. In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"As long as the *argha* offering has not been presented to the Sun-god, one should not worship Viṣṇu, Śaṅkara, or Maheśvarī."
Everywhere, the lotus is praised, except for the worship of Śiva and Sūrya.
(p. 117) "Abja" means a conch shell.
In that [conch] vessel, the practitioner of mantras should worship all the deities individually.
In the Devīpurāṇa: "The fetching of clay, the kneading, the consecration, the invocation, as well as the bathing, the worship, and thereafter the dismissal."
Hara, Maheśvara, Śūlapāṇi, Pinākadhṛk,
Śiva, Paśupati, and Mahādeva— in this order.

In this context, regarding the seven rites previously mentioned, having designated the specific nature of each action by means of the seven names stated in the words of others, the respective effects are to be performed accordingly; however,

when the sequence of meaning is impossible for two rites intended for unseen results (*adṛṣṭārtha*), the order follows the sequence of the recitation itself, [beginning] from the invocation (*āvāhana*) onwards.

The installation (*pratiṣṭhā*) is performed there in the same manner as the offering of a *kuśa*-grass seat during a *śrāddha* ceremony. For example: "Oṃ, obeisance to Hara"—thus the fetching of the clay; "Oṃ, obeisance to Maheśvara"—thus the kneading;
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śūlapāṇi"—thus the installation of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*).
Then, regarding meditation:

"One should constantly meditate upon Maheśa," and so forth. Then, having invoked [the deity] with "Oṃ, obeisance to the wielder of the Pināka bow," and having performed the ritual bathing with "Oṃ, obeisance to Paśupati," [one offers] "Oṃ, obeisance to Śiva."

Thus one should worship. Prior to the ritual dismissal (*visarjana*), one should worship in the eight directions beginning with the east and northeast, proceeding counter-clockwise (*vāmāvartena*): 1. *Oṃ śarvāya kṣitimūrtaye namaḥ* (Salutation to Śarva, the earth-form), in the east. 2. *Oṃ bhavāya jalamūrtaye namaḥ* (Salutation to Bhava, the water-form), in the northeast. 3. *Oṃ rudrāyāgnimūrtaye namaḥ* (Salutation to Rudra, the fire-form), in the north.

Oṃ, obeisance to Ugra, the form of Vāyu; in the northwest (4). Oṃ, obeisance to Bhīma, the form of Ākāśa; in the west (5). Oṃ, obeisance to Paśupati, the form of the Sacrificer; in the southwest (6). Oṃ, obeisance to Mahādeva, the form of Soma.
Salutation to the South (7). Oṃ, salutation to Īśāna, the solar form, in the southeast.
These eight forms of Śiva are to be employed in order starting from the East and ending with the southeast; one should worship Śiva on the altar and in the *liṅga*.
In the Nāndīpurāṇa: One should offer oblations of cows, land, clothing, gold, and the like, as well as flowers and food.
The mantra "Namaḥ Śivāya" should be known as the accomplisher of all aims.
p. 118) And this six-syllabled mantra, beginning with *oṃ*, is superior to all mantras.
In the *Bhaviṣyapurāṇa*, after introducing the five-syllabled [mantra]: "Whether impure or pure, or even having reached any state whatsoever..."
Even one who is burdened with great sins [is purified] likewise by the recitation of this mantra.
"Everyone shall be an eligible candidate," thus spoke the Lord Śiva.
Likewise:
"Among all worthy recipients, there is none higher than Maheśvara in this regard."
Because it supports one who is falling into the exceedingly deep ocean of hell,
that which is given with Śiva in mind is the cause of all causes.
What wonder is there that the giver of this obtains infinite fruit in this world? As stated in the *Śivadharmottara*:
"Therefore, whatever fruit [is obtained] from flowers, fruits, water, or even leaves..."
That should be known as the final fruit; devotion alone is the cause in this matter.
In the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa: "Anointing the Liṅga should be performed with fragrant substances possessing divine scents;
[the devotee] is glorified in the world of Śiva for a hundred million divine years."
In the Skanda Purāṇa: "Even dried leaves of the Śrīvṛkṣa (bilva tree) should always be offered with devotion by men who desire devotion to Śiva."
In the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa: "Whoever constantly worships Śiva even once with *dhattūra* flowers attains the fruit of giving a hundred thousand cows and is glorified in the world of Śiva."
Whoever worships the Liṅga even once with Bilva leaves and Anarta flowers is liberated from all sins and is glorified in the world of Śiva.
And as it is said:
"The bilva fruit grants all desires and destroys great poverty."
There is nothing superior to the bilva leaf by which Śaṅkara is pleased;
[leaves] infested with hair or insects, those offered at night, and those that have become stale.
One should discard flowers that have fallen on their own, even if they are otherwise unblemished.
By offering deodar wood, along with all varieties of *śrīvāsa* and *kunduru*,
as well as *śrīphala* mixed with clarified butter, one attains the supreme goal.
Sarja, śālarasa, kunduru, and śaileya—
from these, the saugandhika incense is six thousand times superior;
aguru is a hundred thousand times superior, and black aguru is twice that.
Śaṅkara directly accepts guggulu mixed with ghee;
indeed, a man may also offer it with oil in the absence of ghee.
By that gift of a lamp, one shines in heaven like Śiva.
In the Nandikeśvara Purāṇa: "One should prepare well-prepared food from a prastha measure of śāli rice."
One should offer a sacrificial oblation (caru) dedicated to Śiva, especially on the fourteenth day of the lunar fortnight.
And in the Śivasarvasva it is said:
"He who offers even a single ripe mango fruit to Śiva sports with enjoyments in the abode of Śiva for ten thousand years."
Whoever offers a single ripe plantain fruit to Śiva is honored in the world of Śiva with great enjoyments for a hundred thousand years.
A person should offer as a food offering (naivedya) that which is mixed with ghee and cooked in honey;
such a human being obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
In the *Śivadharmottara*: "The pedestal of the *liṅga* is the Goddess, and the *liṅga* itself is Maheśvara manifest.
By worshipping those two, both the Goddess and the God are worshipped."
In the Devīpurāṇa:
"One should then offer the oblation with the right hand (dakṣiṇa), and one must not cross over the water-channel;
thus, one who performs three circumambulations should treat Rudra as being unified [with the deity]."
In an instant, liberation shall be his, and for him there will be no rebirth. As it says in the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa: "The wise man, with both knees, both hands, and his head..."
Having offered salutation to the Lord of Gods, one shall obtain all desires.
In the Mahābhārata:
"Even one devoid of all auspicious marks, or even one joined with all sins..."
One crosses over all that evil by bowing one's head to Bhava.

Then, having bowed down again and again with the mantra "Oṃ vāmadevāya namaḥ," he should dismiss [the deity] with the *saṃhāramudrā*. Having worshipped Caṇḍograpāṇi with the remnants of that offering,
he should carry upon his head the remains of Śiva’s offerings together with the remains of Viṣṇu’s offerings.
"Leaves, flowers, fruits, and water offered to Śiva are not to be taken [by others];
yet, through the touch of the Śālāgrāma stone, everything becomes pure."
Now, the method for the special worship of earthen lingas,
as stated in the *Śrīmantramahārṇava*:
"The practitioner, having bathed and performed his daily rites, goes to a pure place."
Having removed the top layer of earth, consecrated it with the mantra "HŪṂ, obeisance to Earth," taken the earth,
and inspected it for palm trees, he should remove any pebbles and place it in a pure vessel for the purpose of the daily Śiva-pūjā. Then, on an auspicious day...

For the sake of accomplishing worship, one should receive from a true guru the mantras of Bāla Gaṇeśa and Kumāra, as well as the seven mantras beginning with Hara. *Hrīṃ gaṃ glauṃ gaṇapataye glauṃ gaṃ hrīṃ* is the Kumāra-tantra. *Aiṃ kṣuṃ kṣuṃ klīṃ*.

"Kumārāya namaḥ"—this is the mantra of Kumāra. Having also collected these seven mantras: "Oṃ namo harāya maheśvarāya," "Oṃ namaḥ śūlapāṇaye," "Oṃ namaḥ pinākine," "Oṃ namaḥ paśupataye," "Oṃ namaḥ śivāya," and "Oṃ namo mahādevāya."

On an auspicious day, for the sake of accomplishing one’s desired goal, one should begin the worship of Śiva. It is as follows: having performed the daily obligatory rites (*nityakriyā*) and having offered the *arghya* libation to the Sun, one should take earth, sprinkle it with water consecrated by the syllable *vaṃ*, and fashion an image of the desired dimensions.
Having placed that [substance] in the vessel, one should perform the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*).
It is as follows: "For the sake of accomplishing the desired undertaking of mine, [namely] so-and-so Śarmā of such-and-such lineage..."
Having made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa): "I shall perform the worship of as many earthen liṅgas as there are," one should take lumps of clay and earth,
fashion the youthful Gaṇeśa— whose lotus-hands shine with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness— by means of the Gaṇapati mantra, and install him upon the pedestal.
Having worshipped with one's own mantra and with the *haramantra*,

namely the mantra "Oṃ namo harāya," and having taken up more than a hundred measures of clay, one should fashion a beautiful *liṅga*— measuring from no less than a thumb up to a span— with the mantra "Oṃ namo maheśvarāya."

One should fashion [the image] with equal proportions and equal form. Then, with the mantra "Oṃ namaḥ śūlapāṇaye," one should install the *liṅga* upon the pedestal. Then, having fashioned a Kumāra from the remaining clay using the Kumāra-mantra and having installed him at the end of the row of *liṅgas*, one should worship him with his own mantra. Then—
Having invoked Hara, who resides within his own characteristic marks, with the mantra "Oṃ namaḥ pinākine," one should meditate upon him as follows:
With his right hand, he touches the lordly elephant-headed one seated on his right side; with another, he embraces Guha, who sits upon the lap of the Daughter of the Mountain on his left thigh;
and with his other two hands, which grant boons and dispel fear, he holds the moon-like splendor—
The blue-throated, three-eyed one, who humbles the three worlds when seized by Rāhu.
Having meditated thus, one should bathe Śiva with the mantra: *oṃ namaḥ paśupataye*.

Then, having offered perfumes and other articles with the mantra *oṃ namaḥ śivāya*, one should worship Śarva and the others in the ten directions, beginning from the east and proceeding counter-clockwise. It is as follows: *oṃ*...

Salutation to Śarva, whose form is the earth, in the east; Oṃ, salutation to Bhava, whose form is water, in the northeast; Oṃ, salutation to Rudra, whose form is fire, in the north; Oṃ, salutation to Ugra, whose form is wind, in the northwest; Oṃ, salutation to Bhīma, whose form is space.
In the west: *Oṃ paśupataye yajamānamūrtaye namaḥ*. In the southwest:

*Oṃ mahādevāya somamūrtaye namaḥ*. In the south: *Oṃ īśānāya sūryamūrtaye namaḥ*. In the southeast corner: [offerings]. Then, [one should worship] Indra and the others, as well as the vajra and the other weapons, starting from the east and proceeding clockwise toward the south.

One should worship. Then, having offered incense, a lamp, and food offerings, and having bowed down again and again, one should perform circumambulation in the shape of a half-moon, recite the mantra (p. 122), chant hymns and so forth, and dismiss [the deity] with the *saṃhāramudrā*.
One should also dismiss Gaṇeśa and Kārttikeya. Now, the visualization (dhyāna) is described according to the distinction of one's desires. In that very same [text]:
"Those who desire wealth, sons, and so forth, should worship Śiva as described by the aforementioned characteristics."
Those desiring knowledge should meditate upon the Supreme One, who holds an axe and a deer,
bears the gesture of wisdom (jñānamudrā) in his hands, and is seated at the foot of a banyan tree.
Now follows the meditation for the purpose of effecting a reconciliation:
"In order to reconcile two men who are at odds, the practitioner should fashion their images;
he should worship them with clay brought from the banks of a river."
There, Hari-Hara is to be meditated upon, bearing the conch, the lotus, the serpent, and the trident;
resembling a sapphire and the autumnal moon, and adorned with a multitude of ornaments.
Now, he describes the meditation for the purpose of pacifying the discord between the couple:
To signify the non-opposition between the two [Śiva and Śakti], he is remembered as Ardhanārīśvara;
he holds a jar filled with nectar, as well as a noose and a goad.
Now, the meditation for the purpose of eradication, killing, and inciting enmity:
For eradication, killing, and enmity, one should again meditate upon him in this manner—
as a mass of radiance impaled on a trident, supported by the lotus-hand of Kālī.
His neck was adorned with a shimmering garland of severed heads, and his roar terrified all beings.
Now, he states the method of practice according to the specific purpose:
"One should perform worship according to the requirement, from a thousand up to a hundred thousand;
by worshipping one hundred thousand earthen liṅgas, one becomes a partaker of devotion and liberation."
By worshipping one hundred thousand *guṇaliṅgas*, a king shall become [a sovereign];
and whichever virtuous woman (*satī*) worships a thousand *guṇaliṅgas* [shall likewise attain her goal].
Having attained unbroken happiness from her husband, she shall become Pārvatī in the end;
by worshipping the lingas made of fresh butter, one shall obtain the highest attainment.
Every morning, one should constantly worship lingas made of cow-dung and cloths.
One should offer an oblation of jaggery using the leaves of the *vṛhatī* and *bilva* plants.
The attainment of desired fruits [is achieved] even by means of ashes, cow dung, or likewise by a young girl.
Children play on the ground, having fashioned a linga out of dust.
Even they, by honoring him with diversion, shall become lords of the earth.
Doing this for three months, one obtains no small amount of wealth;
one should worship exactly eleven lingas made from cow dung.
If one practices thus every day— at dawn, at midday, in the evening, and at midnight— one shall attain all prosperity within six months.
He who constantly worships eleven lingas made of rice-flour for the duration of a single month shall burn away his accumulation of sins;
a crystal linga, when worshipped, destroys the multitude of mental afflictions.
That which originates from the Udumbara tree bestows all desires upon men.
The stone from the middle of the Revā river bestows all perfections and destroys suffering.
In whatever manner the worship of the Liṅga is performed constantly, it grants one's desired objects.
He who, meditating on the wrathful Maheśvara, worships Śiva born of cow-dung with leaves derived from the *picumanda* tree, conquers his enemies.
Whoever, devoted to the worship of Śiva, constantly worships the Liṅga,
even a heap of sins as vast as Mount Meru shall quickly go to its dissolution for him.
Between one who would give cows that yield milk, horses, or grain to a reciter of the Vedas,
and one who would worship a Linga made of earth, the worshiper of the Linga is superior.
On the fourteenth, as well as the eighth, the full moon, and the new moon, one should bathe the Lord with milk; one shall attain the fruit of the gift of the earth.
Having performed the worship of the Liṅga, one should then recite either a hymn or the Śatarudriya with a focused mind; having done so, one should offer oneself to Śiva.
One should perform a fire-oblation (homa) with a number equal to that of the liṅgas worshipped,
using sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter, or ghee, or milk-rice (pāyasa), in the fire.
At its conclusion, one should also feed the Brāhmaṇas with the Śiva-mantra;
when this is done, the accomplishment of all desired goals will certainly come to pass.
(p. 124) Now, the consecration of the worship-diagram (*pūjāyantra*).
In the *Vāmakeśvaratantra*:
Bhairavī said:
O Mahādeva, by your grace I have heard the classification of the wheels;
now I desire to hear the determination of the ritual of installation (pratiṣṭhā).
Śrī Śaṅkara said:
Listen, O illustrious Goddess, O Kaulinī who creates the universe;
the concluding rite (udyāpana) of the yantra must be performed, which determines the success of all ritual actions.
Having bathed, the practitioner of mantra, performing the worship of the Guru, should make a formal resolve (saṃkalpa);
then, having prepared the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), he should consecrate it with the Śiva-mantra.
The mantra-practitioner should cast that wheel, thoroughly permeated by the *praṇava* (OM);
then, having lifted that wheel, he should place it in a golden vessel.
With the five nectars, with milk, and with cool water;
with fragrant sandalwood, musk, and saffron.
One should again perform the rite of the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) in sequence with milk, curd, ghee, honey, sugar, and so forth, interspersed with water and incense.
One should cause the supreme bathing of the Goddess to be performed with eight golden jars filled with water, or with those filled with decoction-water (kaṣāya).
Having completed the bath, one should place that goddess upon a golden vessel;
having touched the vessel with the tip of a *kuśa* blade, one should consecrate it with the *Gāyatrī*.
O Goddess, for the sake of attaining the state of identity with the deity, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times;
then, having performed the purification of the self, one should perform worship with the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga).
There, having invoked the Great Goddess, one should perform the placement of the vital breath (jīvanyāsa),
always with the sixteen services and the great mudrās and so forth.
One should worship the Goddess there with fruits, betel leaves, and food offerings;
one should also present silken threads and the like, as well as garments and ornaments.
O Maheśvarī, one who is intent on their own welfare should diligently offer a mirror, a fly-whisk, and a bell, as appropriate, for all of these.
Then one should recite it a thousand times for the sake of accomplishing all desired goals.
Then one should perform the offering of the *bali* and prostrate before the King of Mandalas (*cakrarāja*).
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations, one should pour the residual clarified butter (*sampātājya*) [into the fire].
If one is unable to perform the rite of *homa*, one should perform twice as much recitation (*japa*).
Having brought a single cow adorned with golden horns and other ornaments, one should give it as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor; thereafter follows the dismissal of the Goddess.
Now follows the method for the consecration of the worship yantra.
Having performed the daily obligatory rites and recited the benediction (svastivācana), one should make the formal resolve (saṃkalpa):
"Today, etc., I, of such-and-such lineage and such-and-such name, [for the sake] of such-and-such deity..."

Having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) thus: "I shall perform the consecration of the [specific] yantra for the purpose of worship," one should bring the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), empower it one hundred and eight times with the mantra *haum*, and place the yantra into the *pañcagavya* while reciting the *praṇava* (OM). Having lifted it out from there, one should place it upon another leaf. Then:

Having bathed [the deity] with cold water, saffron, and musk, one should offer incense. Likewise, one should bathe [him] with curd, ghee, honey, and sugar. Then, one should bathe [him] with eight jars.
One should bathe [him] with waters mixed with saffron, yellow pigment (rocanā), and sandalwood. In every instance, however, the bathing is as follows:

With the root mantra, one should then lift up the yantra, touch the yantra with the tip of a blade of kuśa grass, and consecrate it one hundred and eight times while reciting: "Oṃ, let us know the King of Yantras; let us meditate upon the Great Mantra; may that Yantra inspire us. Then, one should perform the rite of infusing life (prāṇapratiṣṭhā).

Of this Prāṇapratiṣṭhā mantra, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara are the seers (ṛṣis); the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas are the meters (chandās); Consciousness is the deity; its application (viniyoga) is in the ritual of the installation of life-force (prāṇapratiṣṭhā). Oṃ.
Hrīṃ krauṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ haṃ hauṃ saḥ! The vital breaths (prāṇas) of the deity [Name], here present! Likewise, Āṃ 13! The life-force (jīva) of the deity [Name] is established here!
Āṃ 13! May all the senses of the deity [Name], Āṃ 13!

may the speech, mind, eyes, ears, nose, and vital breath of the deity [Name] come here and remain happily and for a long time; Svāhā! Having thus established the vital breaths (prāṇas) and invoked the primary deity, [one should proceed].
Having worshipped with the sixteen types of offerings (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*) and so forth, one should worship with the six-limbed rite (*ṣaḍaṅga*).
Then, having offered the silk thread (*paṭṭasūtra*) and other items, one should recite the mantra one thousand and eight times (*aṣṭottarasahasra*).
If one is unable [to do this], one should offer a sacrificial oblation (*bali*). Then, having performed one hundred and eight fire-offerings (*aṣṭottaraśata-homa*), [one should proceed].

One should offer oblations according to the number of responses received. In the event of being unable to perform the fire sacrifice (*homa*), twice the amount of recitation (*japa*) must be performed.
Then, one should offer a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) and perform the inspection for defects; this is the consecration of the yantra.
Now, regarding the consecration of the Sundarī-yantra, one should touch it with the tip of *kuśa* grass while reciting "Ām" and so forth in the general manner.
First, having performed the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of the vital breaths), one should recite the *jīvākarṣiṇī-vidyā* according to one's capacity. For example:
*oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hyauṃ shauḥ shauḥ āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ klīṃ gaṇapatikālike sauḥ | sakala hrīṃ klīṃ klīṃ hrīṃ shauḥ hyauḥ śrīṃ*.

One should recite the root Gāyatrī mantra: *hrīṃ aiṃ oṃ*. One should also recite the root mantra (*mūlamantra*). Then, having visualized the Goddess as having arrived in the center of the yantra, one should worship her with the sixteen services (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*); this is the remainder [of the instruction].
There was the excellent scholar Śrī Karuṇākara, a mine of compassion and generosity,
skilled in the essence of scriptural tradition, conduct, and inquiry, and the foremost among astrologers.
His son was the accomplished Śrī Śambhunātha, whose feet were honored by the lords of the earth.
Through the power of meditating upon Śambhu, he attained equality with Śambhu out of devotion in Kāśī.
But his son, having beheld the pure Tantras proclaimed by Śiva through the grace of Śambhu,
[composed] the *Dīkṣāprakāśa* by Jīvanātha—
He composed this wonderful work for the delight of those who know the tantras.
In the Śaka year numbered by the sky, the moon, the limbs, and the earth (1790), on the lunar day of the auspicious Rāmanavamī,
there was a venerable Maithila twice-born residing near the bank of the Jāhnavī.
Thus ends the *Dīkṣāprakāśa*, composed by Śrī Jīvanātha, the son of Śrī Śambhunātha.
Now follows another specific point stated by Śrī Kṛṣṇadatta.
First, regarding the majesty of Śiva:
likewise, in the Brahma Purāṇa—
on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Māgha, at the dead of night, the Primordial God [manifested].
Born from the Śiva-liṅga, he possesses a splendor equal to ten million suns.
Likewise, in the Saurāgama:
"At every watch of the day, one should perform the ritual bath and worship of the Śivaliṅga according to the injunctions, and offer the water libation (argha) with devotion."
By performing a single fast on this lunar day, the Lord Śiva,
the divine one who bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, is pleased.
Likewise, Nandikeśvara says:
"Upon seeing the Liṅga of Maheśa, an embodied being is liberated from all sins committed throughout birth after birth, arising from the actions of mind, speech, and body."
Thus it is said in the Skanda Purāṇa: "He who worships the Liṅga when the sun has reached the meridian shall obtain that fruit which is gained by giving away the entire earth."
He who performs the worship of Śiva every day at the three junctions [of the day] and utters His names—he is indeed Śiva; there is no doubt about this.
He who worships Śiva one hundred and eight times every day—
whether once or three times a day— purifies three generations of his lineage.
Better is the abandonment of life or even the cutting off of one's head than to eat without having first worshipped the Śivaliṅga, the Great Lord Maheśvara.
By uttering the name "Mahādeva," one obtains the fruit of a thousand times a thousand horse-sacrifices.
Even those men who constantly remember Maheśvara by means of recitation go,
upon casting off the body, to the stainless world of Śiva.
Having approached a crystal linga, one who performs japa obtains wealth, long life, prosperity, sons, and whatever else is desired by the mind.
Whoever rises early in the morning and worships the Liṅga even once with devotion shall obtain that fruit which is gained by giving a hundred tawny cows in charity.
One should not abandon the worship of Śiva during periods of birth or death;
one should worship Śiva according to the prescribed rite continuously for six months.
One obtains that entire merit from the worship at the Viṣuva;
this same [merit] is to be known [as obtained] during an eclipse and at the Uttarāyaṇa.
On the full moon day of Kārttika, on the Yugādi days, and especially on the day of Ṣaḍaśīti,
he who bathes on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight and [worships] the god Pinākin—
O best of the twice-born, he who propitiates [the deity] in this way shall have no further rebirth.

A great ablution (mahāsnāna) with fruits is proclaimed to yield two thousand-fold merit; however, when performed with clay, copper, gold, and silver, the merit increases respectively by ten million times ten million.
In this regard, there is also another point: regarding water-born flowers and indeed the bilva leaf,
one should entertain the suspicion that they have become stale after five days have passed.
Kanakas and kadambas should be offered to Śaṅkara at night;
all other flowers [should be offered] during the day, and mallikās both by day and by night.
In the absence of flowers, one should offer even leaves;
and in the absence of fruits, one should offer grass and shrubs.
Even in the absence of these, he becomes worshipped through devotion;
however, one should personally discard flowers that have fallen or are defiled.
But those of dull intellect who, having performed their ablutions, take up a flower [for themselves].
The deities do not accept that, nor do the ancestors likewise;
one should worship with a bud, and one should not offer what is unripe.

One should carefully discard a fruit that is overripe or damaged. By lighting a lamp with ghee, sesame oil, or the juices of medicinal herbs before the Lord of Gods with devotion, one shall become the lord of heaven.
Just as food is eaten, so indeed should one present it.
Otherwise, by giving that [gift], one would not obtain its fruit;
for by whomsoever the auspicious five-syllabled mantra has been uttered even once.
One is liberated from the sins committed over seven lifetimes; there is no doubt about this.
Whether impure or pure, or even having fallen into any state whatsoever.
Even one joined with great sins becomes pure by the recitation of this mantra;
having performed a circumambulation of Śiva’s abode with devotion, a person [attains purity]. (p. 129)
He who worships with a prostration on the ground, reaching as far as the length of his staff, obtains the fruit of a thousand excellent horse-sacrifices.
The destination that one attains through that cannot be reached even by hundreds of sacrifices,
nor by thousands of millions of sacred fords, nor by hundreds of millions of sacrifices.
Sacrificial threads, garments, bells, fans, and chowries do not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of prostrating before Mahādeva.
Having given cows, land, female slaves, a city, a village, a garden, a banner, and so forth,
one shall become an attendant of Śiva until the dissolution of the eon.
Whoever constructs a temple of Śiva out of clay, wood, brick, or stone,
is honored in the world of Śiva together with twenty-one generations of their kin.
Having performed the installation of a *liṅga*, one shall uplift ten million members of one's lineage;
O best of the twice-born, all rivers are situated near the sacred field of Śiva.
The step-wells, wells, and tanks are remembered as the Śivagaṅgās;
it is declared that bathing there yields merit equal to bathing in the Gaṅgā.
In that land there shall be no famine, nor does Māra prevail;
no one dies prematurely where Śaṅkara is worshipped.
If anyone should see any Śiva-liṅga that has not been worshipped,
he who goes away after first worshipping it attains the supreme goal.
Whoever removes a garland that has been worn for a long time from Śiva shall obtain the merit of donating a thousand cows; of this there is no doubt in this world.
In the offering of oblations such as cows, land, gold, garments, and other gifts,
the mantra "Namaḥ Śivāya" should be known as the accomplisher of all aims.
This six-syllabled mantra, beginning with Oṃ, is superior to all mantras;
one who recites that mantra, delights in its ritual practice, and has a mind intent upon it [attains success].
O King, the man who is free from desire attains the state of Rudra.
Thus ends the description of the majesty of Śiva.
This work is completed.
